
# Sentences 1

Analyze the following sentences:

*ay mard tō kē hē* "O man, who are you?"

*an Kay Husrōy* *ham* = *an ham Kay Husrōy* "I am Kay Husrōy"

*ašmāh kē hēd* "Who are you (all)?"

*amāh mazdēsn hēm* "We are Mazdayasnians"

*ašmāh driyōš mardōm hēd* "you (all) are poor people"

*awēšān mard hēnd zan nē hēnd* "they are men, not women"

*dēw hēnd nē mardōm* "they are demons, not humans."

*andar mardōm ērtan ud čarb ud hučašm bāš* "among people, be humble and
amenable and benevolent!"

*ašmāh pad kār ud kerbag tuxšāg bawēd* "(you all), be diligent in (your)
work and good deeds!"

*pad Ahrimen wistāx ma bawēd* "do not be confident in (= rely on)
Ahrimen (the Evil One)!"

*pad gētīy nē būd ham* "I have not (always) been in this world"

*andar mān mār būd* "(there) was a snake in the house"

*fradom mardōm andar abēgumānīh būd hēnd* "the first humans were in a
state of non-doubt"

*andar šahr was mazdēsn būd hēnd* "In the land, there were many
Mazdayasnians"

*dušdānāg dēw-ēd* "you are stupid demons"

## Grammar 2

### The use of *-ēw* "one" to specify

There is no indefinite article in Pahlavi, but the numeral !- \<-1\>
*-ēw* "one" can be added to a noun to signify "one particular, a
certain" and similar. Sometimes it comes close in function to the
English indefinite article, but one should not make it a habit to
translate every English indefinite article by Pahlavi *-ēw*! E.g.:

*rōd-ēw* !WTwL "a (certain) river" *gyāg-ēw būd* WTWB !WkAwïD "there was
a (special) place (where)"

*kanīzag-ēw* !WKcDWK "a (certain) girl" *čiyōn mard-ēw ī* Y 1AWvY WwSC
"like a man who"

### Singular and plural

Normally, the verb agrees with the subject in number.

When plurality is not emphasized, but rather species, the singular is
normally used, e.g.:

*pad āsmān stārag ud axtar ud abāxtar ast*

"there are \[*ast*: see below\] stars, constellations, and planets in
the sky" (not *hēnd*)

When two or more 3rd plural past tense forms follow, the plural may be
indicated on the last only, e.g.:

*pad kerbag kerdan tuxšāg [būd]{.underline}*

*ud az wināh pahrēxtār [būd hēnd]{.underline}*

"they were (*būd*) diligent (*tuxšāg*) in performing (*kerdan*
\[infinitive\]) good deeds

and kept away (*pahrēxtār būd hēnd*) from sin (*az* *wināh*)"

The noun *mardōm* "people, humans" is always plural:

*ēn mardōm kadām hēnd*

"which (= who) are these people?"

####  The plural ending *-ān* with plural nouns governed by prepositions.

The plural ending *-ān* is used when nouns are governed by prepositions
(postpositions), e.g.:

*ēn kanīg ō abārīgān kanīgān nē homānāg*

"this young woman is not like (other) young women"

*Zarduxšt pad mardōmān rād ud rāst būd*

"Zarduxšt was generous and straight/truthful toward people"

More examples of the ending *-ān* are given below. See also Lesson 11.

### 

### The adjective/adverb *was* "much, many, very"

This adjective is very commonly used to qualify nouns and adjectives,
e.g.,

*andar ērān šahr was mazdēsn būd hēnd*

"in the land of the Iranians (= Iran), there were many Mazdayasnians"

*ēn kanīzag was hučihr ān rēdag was huwīr*

"this girl is very pretty, that boy is very manly"

Note the alternative word order, in which *was* is the predicate of the
noun it qualifies:

*andar ērān šahr was mowmard hēnd*

"in the land of the Iranians, there are many Zoroastrian priests"

beside

*andar ērān šahr mowmard was hēnd*

"in the land of the Iranians, Zoroastrian priests are many"

### Possession 1

Possession can be expressed by simply putting the possessor in front of
what is possessed, similar to English *In God's name* (as opposed to *In
the name of God*).

If the possessor is a plural noun, it usually [takes the ending
*-ān*]{.underline}, e.g.:

*pad Ohrmazd nām* "in Ohrmazd's name"

*pad yazdān nām* "in the gods' name"

*dēwān dām* "the creation of the evil gods."

*andar mardān ruwānān* "in men's souls"

###  "To be" and "not to be"

To express existence, the verbs *ast* "exists" and *nēst* "does not
exist" are used, past tense *būd*, future *bawēd* "there will be.

These forms are also used to express "there is, there are."

The plural forms *hēnd*, *nē hēnd*, *būd hēnd* are used when plurality
is emphasized.

Examples:

*wahišt ast ud dōšox ast*

"Paradise exists, and Hell exists; there is a Paradise and there is a
Hell"

*Ahrimen andar gētīy nēst*

"Ahrimen does not exist in this world"

*andar wahišt bazzakkar nēst*

"there is no evil-doer in Paradise, there are no evil-doers in Paradise"

*andar dōšox kerbakkar nē hēnd*

"there are no doers of good deeds in Hell"

*andar dōšox yazd nē būd hēnd*

"there have been no gods (ever) in hell, there have never been any \..."

###  "To have"

The verbs "to be" and "not to be" are also used to express
[possession]{.underline}. Grammatically, we could say that the possessor
is indirect object. Plural nouns take [the ending *-ān*]{.underline},
e.g.:

*amāh ēč nēst*

"we have nothing" ("there is nothing for us")

*murwān* *parr ast*

"birds have wing(s)" ("for the birds there are wings")

# Sentences 2

*andar Ohrmazd mān wazurg šādīh ast* "in Ohrmazd's house, there is great
joy"

*wad dēw hēnd wad yazd nē hēnd* "there are bad demons, there are no bad
gods"

*pad Ohrmazd warz yazdān dušmen nē hēnd* "By Ohrmazd's miraculous power,
the gods have no enemies"

*Wištāsp šāhān šāh ud Ērān šāh būd* "Wištāsp was king of kings and (the)
king of the Iranians"

*ēn Wištāsp būd wazurg šāh* "this was Wištāsp, a great king"

*pad gētīy mardōm was hēnd* "there are many people in this world"

*andar am xwadāyīh haft-kišwar mardōm pad* "during am's kingdom
(rule), the people of the seven

*abēgumānīh bud hēnd* continents were in absence of doubt" ("had no
doubts")

*mardōmān tan ud gyān ud ruwān ast* "humans have bodies, vital spirits
(souls), and (immortal) souls"

*gōspandān ud dadān ruwān nēst* "domestic and wild animals have no
souls"

*andar wahišt rōšnīh widerdagān ruwān was hēnd* "in the light of
Paradise, there are many souls of the departed"

*pad gētīy kōf ud rōd ud zrēy was ast bē stārag nēst* "in this world,
there are many mountains, rivers, and oceans, but there are no stars"

*andar ēn zrēy ud rōd māhīg ast* "in this ocean and river there are
fish"

*xwaršēd ud māh ud stārag pad āsmān hēnd* "the sun, moon, and stars are
in the sky"

*bazzakkarīh mardōmān wattar kunišn* "evil-doing (is) humans' worst deed
(act, action)"

*andar mazdēsnān bazzakkar was nēst* "there are not many evil-doers
among the Mazdayasnians"

## Grammar 3

### Adjectives

Adjectives can qualify a noun directly or as predicate of "to be" (many
examples in lessons 1-2).

Adjectives can be placed before the noun they qualify, as in English,
e.g.:

*pad zarrēn gāh* *pad wazurg šādīh*

"on a golden throne, on a throne of gold" "in great joy"

More commonly adjectives follow the noun, being attached to it by [the
particle *ī*]{.underline} ( Y \<Y\>), often referred to as the *izafe*,
e.g.:

*wistarg ī xūb* *Rašn ī rāst*

"a good carpet" "the straight Rašn" (a god of judgment)

*kanīzag ī was hučihr ud rēdag ī was huwīr*

"a very pretty girl, a very manly boy"

The particle can also be used after the "specifying" *-ēw*, e.g.:

*rōd-ēw ī wazurg*

"a (certain) big river"

It can also be placed after an intervening verb, e.g.:

*andar mān ātaxš-ēw būd ī wazurg*

"in the house, there was a great fire"

The particle is also used with appositions and similar expressions such
as:

*Ohrmazd ī xwadāy* *kōf ī Harburz*

"Ohrmazd, the Lord" "the mountain Harburz, Mount Harburz"

*kerbag ī gētīy*

"the good deeds (performed) in this world"

Several adjectives with one noun:

*kanīg ī nēk ī was amāwand ī hu-rust ī āzād*

"a beautiful woman, very powerful and well-grown (of tall stature),
noble"

With appositions:

*šahr ī wazurg ī Bābēl* *Ohrmazd ī xwadāy*

"the great land (of) Babylon" "Ohrmazd the lord"

The particle is also used before prepositional phrases:

*nēkīh ī pad wahišt ud anāgīh ī pad dōšox*

"the goodness in Paradise and the evil in Hell" (*AWN*.5.7)

*kanīg-ēw ī ō kanīgān nē homānāg*

"a young woman not like (other) young women" (*MX*.1.167)

##### *ān ī* ( Y ã \<ZK Y\>):

The Pahlavi expression for "[the X one]{.underline}," is *ān ī X*
literally, "that X one." This expression can also be used to attach
adjectives to nouns, e.g.:

*ān ī pahlom axwān* "the best existence" = *pahlom axwān* = *axwān ī
pahlom*

*ān ī wattar axwān* "the worst existence" = *wattar axwān* = *axwān ī
wattar*

*ān ī meh kerbag ud ān ī keh* "the greater good deed and the smaller
one"

[The construction with *ān ī* is very common and important, so learn it
well!]{.underline}

### Possession 2

### 

#### The possessive particle *ī* ( Y \<Y\>)

We have already seen expressions such as *man pid* "my father" and *ērān
šāh* "(the) king of the Iran(ians)." [More commonly]{.underline},
genitives are connected to their nouns by means of the particle *ī*,
which we also saw used with adjectives. In this case, too, plural nouns
(and sometimes their adjectives) take the ending *-ān*.

[Note that, in this construction, the *ī* is in the same position as
English *of*.]{.underline}

*gyāg ī Ohrmazd ud abārīgān yazdān*

"the place of Ohrmazd and the other gods \> Ohrmazd's and the other
gods' place"

(beside: *Ohrmazd ud abārīgān yazdān gyāg*).

#### *X xwēš* "belonging to X"

Note the common possessive expressionx *X xwēš* "belonging to X,"
literally "X's own." See more in Lesson 5.

Plural nouns take [the ending *-ān*]{.underline} before *xwēš*, e.g.:

*kē xwēš ham* *Ahrimen ud dēwān xwēš nē ham*

"whose am I?" ("who do I belong to?") "I do not belong to Ahrimen and
the demons"

# Sentences 3

*Ohrmazd man xwēš ud an Ohrmazd xwēš ham*

"Ohrmazd belongs to me, and I belong to Ohrmazd"

*andar zrēy ī Warkaš xar-ēw ast ī 3-pāy* (*sē-pāy*)

"in the Warkaš sea (ocean), there is a three-legged donkey (*xar*)"

*Ērān šahr andar kišwar ī Xwanīrah*

"the land of the Iranians is in the continent (*kišwar*) of Xwanīrah"

*xarbuz ī spēd buzān rad*

"the white oryx \[*oryx leucoryx*\] is the *rad* 'chief' of 'goats' (=
of the 'goat' species)"

*anōšag-ruwān Ādurbād ī Mahrspandān mazdēsnān sālār būd*

"Ādurbād son of Mahrspand of-immortal-soul (*anōšag-ruwān*) was a leader
of the Mazdayasnians"

Note the ending *-ān* in *Mahrspand-ān* meaning "son of."

*ahlawān widerdagān ruwān hamāg abāg Ohrmazd ud amahrspandān andar
Garōdmān pad wazurg šādīh hēnd*

"the souls of the Righteous departed are all (*hamāg*) in Garōdmān
together with Ohrmazd and the *amahrspand*s in great joy"

##### Appositions:

Appositions are not marked in Pahlavi and can at times be not so easy to
identify (at first glance):

*asar rōšnīh gāh ī amahrspandān ud Garōdmān ud āsmān* *awināh*

"the Endless Lights, the place of the *amahrspand*s, Garōdmān, and the
sky are sinless (free from sin, *awināh*)"

*ēk ast rāh ī ahlāyīh rāh ī pōryōtkēšīh ud ān ī abārīg rāh hamāg nē-rāh*

"one (*ēk*) is the road (path, *rāh*) of Righteousness, (namely) the
road of the teachings of old (*pōryōtkēšīh*); the other (*abārīg*) roads
are all 'non-roads'"



##  Grammar 4

### Possession 3

#### *ān ī X* "that of X"

As in the case of adjectives, one can also use the formula [*ān ī X*
"that of X"]{.underline} to express possession, e.g.:

*[ān ī šāh]{.underline} pus*

"[the king's]{.underline} son"

*[ān ī murwān]{.underline} parr*

"[the birds']{.underline} feathers/wings"

*tan ī pasēn [ān ī Ohrmazd]{.underline} abdom dām*

"the Final Body (is) [Ohrmazd's]{.underline} last (*abdom*) creation"

*gāh ī rāstān ud [ān ī drōzanān]{.underline}*

"the place of the truthful ones and [that of the liars]{.underline}"

*[ān ī ahlawān]{.underline} kerbag ud [ān ī druwandān]{.underline}
wināh*

"the good deeds [of the Righteous ones]{.underline} and the sins [of the
wicked ones]{.underline}"

*pad [ān ī Ohrmazd]{.underline} āmurzīdārīh ud pad [ān ī
Ohrmazd]{.underline} rādīh*

"by [Ohrmazd's]{.underline} mercy and by [Ohrmazd's]{.underline}
generosity" (after *Bd*.26.9)

*menišn ud gōwišn ud kunišn [ān ī harw dō]{.underline} kē weh ud kē-iz
wattar*

"thinking, speaking, and acting (are) '[both's' = belongs to
both]{.underline} (*harw dō*): (the one) who is good and also (*-iz*)
(the one) who is bad"

*ōy [ān ī kē]{.underline} ruwān*

"[whose]{.underline} soul (is) he (*ōy*)?" (Ardā Wirāz's question on his
trip to hell)

The construction sometimes has more pronounced deictic ('pointing')
function, "[that]{.underline} of," which can then be con­trasted with
*ēn* (*ēd*) *ī X* "[this]{.underline} one of X's," which usually has
pronounced deictic function (on *ōy ī*, see below), e.g.:

*mizd ī gētīy ān-iz ī mēnōy*

"the reward of (= in) this world (and) [that]{.underline} of the other
world, too (*-iz*)"

*[ēn]{.underline} ī man dēn ud [ān]{.underline} ī tō kerb*

"[this]{.underline} *dēn* of mine and that body/shape of
[yours]{.underline}"

*[ēd]{.underline} ī mardōmān zīndagīh*

"[this]{.underline} people's [life]{.underline} (this life that people
lead)"

#### *xwēš* (nÍPW \<NPŠE\>) "own, belonging to"

As we saw in Lesson 3, the pronoun *xwēš* "own" can be used in the sense
of "belonging too." Plural nouns as possessor take the ending *‑ān*. It
can be combined with *ān ī* (*ēn ī*, *ēd ī*), e.g.:

*harw gul-ēw amahrspand-ēw xwēš*

"each flower (*gul*) belongs to one *amahrspand*"

*drōš hamēmālān xwēš*

"branding (*drōš*) belongs to (his) fellow men" (*MHD*.5.1) (i.e., they
decide whether he should be branded)

*ān ī Ohrmazd xwēš*

"[Ohrmazd's]{.underline}, that of Ohrmazd's, that which is that of =
belongs to Ohrmazd"

*ēd ī amahrspandān xwēš*

"this that belongs to the *amahrspand*s"

In the construction *ī* \... *xwēš*, *ī* is actually a relative pronoun,
but is often used for emphasis:

*pas az 10 (dah) sāl xwāstag ī [man xwēš tō xwēš]{.underline}*

"after 10 years, the property that (is) [my own]{.underline} (belongs to
me) (is) [your own]{.underline} (belongs to you) (*MHD*.24.3)



#### *ōy ī*

Note also *ōy ī* used like *ān ī*. This construction can sometimes be
rendered by the English definite article e.g.:

*[ōy ī mazdēsn]{.underline}*

"[the Mazdayasnian]{.underline} (one/ones)"

*[ōy ī druwand]{.underline} Ganāg Mēnōy*

"[the/that wicked]{.underline} Foul Spirit"

*ōy ī abārōn-dād ī wēš-wināh*

"the one with evil law and greater sin"

*mihr ī šōy drōzēd ī abāg [ōy ī bazakkar]{.underline} mard xufsēd*

"she belies (*drōzēd*) the love (*mihr*) of the husband (*šōy*) who
sleeps (*xufsēd*) with [a man who-does-evil-deeds]{.underline}"

*[ōy ī]{.underline} abardom rōšnān [xwadāy]{.underline} Ohrmazd ī dādār*

"[the lord]{.underline} (*xwadāy*) of the highest (*abardom*) lights
(*rōšnān*) (is) Ohrmazd the Creator" (*DD*.36.10)

Note the use of both *ān ī* and *ōy ī* in the following sentence:

*ruwān ka ō ham rasēnd ān ī [ōy ī nēk dastwar]{.underline} ī ruwān-dōst
ruwān burzēnd*

"the souls, when they come together (in paradise), praise the soul of
the good *dastwar* who loves (his) soul" (*Dk*.9.20.1)

Here *ān ī* expresses possession: *[ān ī]{.underline} dastwar
[ruwān]{.underline}* "[the soul of]{.underline} the *dastwar*"; *ōy ī*
is used to connect the adjective *nēk* to the noun *dastwar*: *ōy ī nēk
dastwar* "[the]{.underline} god *dastwar*"; and *ī ruwān-dōst* is a
regular adjective construction."

The enclitic pronouns must be attached to another word, most commonly
the first word of a clause (in which case they are often separated from
the words they qualify); examples with *ā-* "then," *agar* "if";
particle *ī*; *bē* "but" and verbal particle; *ī* relative pronoun,
etc., *kū* "that" etc.; *u-* "and"; *ēg* "then":

ÂAWV \<BRAm\> *bē-m* MtÅ \<HTm\> *agar-im*

mï¸ \<ZYm\> *ī-m* WwaHWN \<MNWš'n\'\> *kē-šān*

Wt∂¸ , t∂¸ \<ZYt(\')\> *ī-t* Wwa˜à \<AYKm'n\'\> *kū-mān*

˙∂¸ \<ZYš\> *ī-š* Wwa˜cÅ \<APm'n\'\> *u-mān*

ßMA \<'-mš\> *ā-m-iš* WwATWwsA \<ADYNt'n\'\> *ēg-itān*

Note the following common spellings, in which the enclitic pronouns are
added without ligature; with *ā-* "then": MA, TA \<'-m, '-t\> *ā-m*,
*ā-t*, etc.; with *tā* "up to," etc. MY\>W, T Y\>W \<OD-m, OD-t\>
*tā-m*, *tā-t*, etc. (beside ÂY\>W, tD\>W)

Some scribes write ßï¸ \<ZYš\> and wahï¸ \<ZYš'n\> instead of ˙∂¸ and
waÔ∂¸, in which case they are mostly indistinguishable from aå¸ \<z''\>
and waåå¸ \<z'''n\>.

The particle *ā-* and the negation *nē* \<LA\> can be attached to a
following word, e.g., *ā-šāyēd* "is then appropriate," *nē-tuwān* "is
not possible."

The enclitic pronouns can alternate with the full pronouns.

Enclitic pronouns are sometimes attached (in the manuscripts) to other
words, notably prepositions, and rarely to nouns, e.g.:

*abāg-[išān]{.underline} ham-wināh* *pad ān anāgīh-[iš]{.underline}*

"together with [their]{.underline} fellow sinner" "by that evil [of
his]{.underline}"

[Examples with *u-*:]{.underline}

*Zarduxšt mād nām būd Dugdōw u-[š pid]{.underline} nām Pōrušasp*

"Zarduxšt's mother's name was Dugdōw and [his father's]{.underline} name
(was) Pōrušasp"

*frahang tōhm ī dānišn u-[š bar]{.underline} xrad*

"learning is the seed of knowledge, and [its fruit]{.underline} is
wisdom" (*PN*.41)

*u-[m dēn]{.underline} kadām u-[m]{.underline} kē [dōst]{.underline}
u-[m]{.underline} kē [dušmen]{.underline} u-[m]{.underline} čē
[xwēškārīh]{.underline} ī gētīy ud čē mizd ī mēnōy*

"Which is [my]{.underline} *dēn*? Who is [my friend]{.underline}? Who is
[my enemy]{.underline}? And what is [my duty]{.underline} (of =) in this
world, and what is (my) reward in the other world?" (*PN.*1)

*pad gōwišnīh ī Ohrmazd paydāg kū ēd [tō]{.underline} Mašīy
[gāw]{.underline} u-[t]{.underline} ēd [ǰōrdā]{.underline}*

"by the statement of Ohrmazd (= from what Ohrmazd has said) it is
manifest (well-known) that: This (is) [your cow]{.underline}, Mašīy, and
this (is) [your barley]{.underline}" (*Dk*.7.1.11)

Other examples:

*ān [ī-š]{.underline} andar dānišn*

"that [which]{.underline} (is) within [his]{.underline} knowledge"

*ēn ruwān ī awēšān mardōmān hēnd [kē-šān]{.underline} kerbag ud wināh
rāst būd*

"these are the souls of those people [whose]{.underline} good deeds and
sins are equal (in weight)" (after *AWN*.6.3)

*[ēg-im]{.underline} mang ma dahēd*

"[then]{.underline} do not give [me]{.underline} hashish!" (after
*AWN*.1.20)

*būšāsp ma warz [kū-t]{.underline} kār ud kerbag akerd nē mānēd*

"do not practice sloth, [so that your]{.underline} work and good deeds
do not remain undone" (*MX*.1.29-30)

The conjunction *u-* "and" is also often used simply as a particle to
attach the pronoun to, alternating with the particle *ā-* "then," e.g.:

*gētīy ham [u-m]{.underline} mēnōy kunēd*

"I am (a creature) of this world. Make [me]{.underline} (one) of that
world!"

*ān haft amahrspand u-[šān]{.underline} nām ēn* = *ān haft amahrspand
ā-[šān]{.underline} nām ēn*

"those seven *amahrspand*s---[their]{.underline} names are these"

*kē kerbakkar ā-[š]{.underline} mizd wahišt*

"he who does good, [his]{.underline} reward is Paradise"

Note that enclitic pronouns can be governed by a postposition, which can
follow it directly or come later in the clause:

*u-[šān]{.underline} [mayān]{.underline} tuhīgīh būd*

"and [between]{.underline} [them]{.underline} was emptiness" (*Bd*.1.5)

*ōy ī mazdēsn agar-[iš]{.underline} āb [abar]{.underline} hilēnd \...*

"the Mazdayasnians -- if they release water [upon it]{.underline} \..."
(*PV*.6.3)

*u-[š]{.underline} 7 rōd [andar]{.underline}*

"and (the castle Kang) has seven rivers [inside it]{.underline}" (after
*PR*.49.7)

*čē-[t]{.underline} abdom margīh [abar]{.underline} rasēd*

"for, in the end, mortality will come [upon yo]{.underline}u"
(*MX*.1.111)

Enclitic pronouns are often found in impersonal constructions:

*u-[š]{.underline} haft murw andar kē-š pānagīh pad xwadāyīh šāyēd
kerdan [andar]{.underline}*

"and (the castle Kang) has seven birds [inside it]{.underline}, which
[it can]{.underline} protect by its reign" (*-š \... šāyēd* "it is
possible for it = it can") (after *PR*.49.7)

### "To be" and "to have" 2

As already mentioned, the verb "to be, become" is also used to express
possession "there is an X for Y" = "Y has an X." Nouns as possessor
often take [the postposition *rāy*]{.underline}:

*agar-[it]{.underline} hambun-iz mihr ī amāh [ast]{.underline}*

"if you have any love for us at all (*hambun-iz*)" (*KN*.10.3/9.8)

*[Pābag rāy]{.underline} ēč frazend [nē būd]{.underline}*

"Pābag had no (*ēč \... nē*) child(ren)" (after *KN*.1.5)

##### *ast* "is":

We find *ast* in certain contexts (not yet entirely defined), referring
to some preceding discussion or explanation, meaning something like
"that is (*id est*)" or "and that is X," sometimes simply "is, are"
e.g.:

*ān [ast]{.underline} Ohrmazd*

"(Wahman said:) That (one)/[*he* is]{.underline} Ohrmazd" (*AWN*.11.3b)

*az asrō-kerb Ahunwar frāz būd [ast]{.underline} dēn*

"From the fire form the *Ahunwar* originated, [that is]{.underline}, the
*dēn*" (*Bd*.1.49)

*stārag ī kōdag was hēnd kē-šān nām ēn [ast]{.underline}*

"there are many small stars, whose (*kē-šān* 'who their') names
[are]{.underline} these (= as follows)"

### The verb

#### The present indicative and the imperative

Pahlavi verbs are conjugated in three persons and two numbers (1st, 2nd,
3rd person singular and plural), as in German, French, Persian (Farsi),
etc.

The present and imperative are formed from the present stem, which
differs from the past stem in various ways (see Lesson 5). In the
Glossary, the present stem is followed by a hyphen and then the past
stem, e.g., *purs- pursīd* "ask, asked."

#### Present indicative

The endings of the present indicative are those of the verb "to be":
*ham*, *hē*, etc., except the 3rd person.

In this and subsequent lessons, we shall mainly use the 3rd person
singular and plural forms. Other forms will be used from Lesson 7 on.
Note that the present is also used to express future.

Subjects normally take no ending (*mard*, not *mardān*).



Examples:

*Zarduxšt az Ohrmazd ēdōn [pursēd]{.underline} kū tō kē hē*

"Zarduxšt [asks]{.underline} Ohrmazd thus: who are you?"

Note *purs-* + *az*, literally "ask (something) 'from' somebody."

*mard az mard [pursēnd]{.underline} kū-t pad ruwān dādestān čē būd*

"men [ask]{.underline} men: what was the judgment (*dādestān*) upon your
soul?" (after *Bd*.34.20)

Note the use of the form *mard* + plural verb *pursēnd* (not *mardān*! )

*amahrspand andar Garōdmān pēš ī Ohrmazd [estēnd]{.underline}*

"the *amahrspand*s [stand]{.underline} before Ohrmazd in Garōdmān"

*ahlawān kerbag ō yazdān [rasēd]{.underline} ayāb ō dēwān*

"does the good activity (the good deeds) of the Righteous ones
[come]{.underline} to the gods or to the demons?" (after *AWN*.1.15)

*win wāng ān ast kē ahlaw [srāyēnd]{.underline} ī Abestāg abar
[gōwēnd]{.underline}*

"the sound (*wāng*) of the lute (*win*) is that which the Righteous ones
[sing]{.underline} who [recite]{.underline} (*abar gōwēnd*) the Avesta"
(*Bd.*20)

####  Imperative 2nd person singular and plural

The imperative has no ending in the singular and in the plural is
identical with the indicative ending *-ēd*.

The negation is *ma* 'do not \...!"


Examples:

*pas Srōš-ahlaw ō man gōwēd kū [ma tars]{.underline}*

"then Srōš-ahlaw says to me: [do not fear]{.underline}!" (after
*AWN*.53.4)

*ō ān wināhkār zahr [dahēd]{.underline} tā andar zamān mīrēd*

"[give]{.underline} that sinner poison, so that (*tā*) he dies in time =
on the spot!" (*KN*.10.3/9.8)

*rāst [gōwēd]{.underline} ān ī drōw [ma gōwēd]{.underline}*

"[Speak]{.underline} the truth! [Do not speak]{.underline}
untruth/lies!"

*ay bazzakkar Ohrmazd dām [ma zanēd]{.underline} čē ō dōšox rasēd*

"O evil-doers, [do not smite]{.underline} Ohrmazd's creation, because
you will come to Hell!"

#### Double negations

Note the use of double negations: *nē nē* "not at all"; *nē \... (ud)
nē*, *ma \... ma*, "neither \... nor," e.g.:

*ka-š bīm ī pad margīh ēwar ud kasān-iz bīm ī pad margīh ēwar ā pādixšāy
ka [nē nē]{.underline} kunēd*

"when fear (*bīm*; i.e. danger) of death (*margīh*) for him (*-iš*) (is)
certain and fear for the death of other people (if he does not help
them) (is) certain, then he is authorized (*pādixšāy*) [not]{.underline}
to do it [at all]{.underline}" (*PR*.17d.12)

*[ma-iz]{.underline} pas-iz mazdēsn ān zamīg kārēnd [ma]{.underline} āb
abar hilēnd kū pad ān abar sag ayāb mard widerd*

"also, afterward, let the Mazdayasnians not till that earth, let them
not release water on (it), on which (*kū pad ān abar*) a dog or a man
has passed away!" (*PV*.6.2)

Also note the use of negation in negated + positive clauses with
identical verb:

*ān mard dušmen [nē]{.underline} [bē]{.underline} dōst bawēd*

"that man does [not]{.underline} become an enemy, [but]{.underline} a
friend"

###  Reported (direct and indirect) speech

Pahlavi does not have indirect speech, like English. That is, we cannot
say "he said that they should go and tell him that he must come." This
sentence would have to be put as "he said: you go and tell him: you must
come." This is how it is said in Persian, as well.

*an nē dānam [kū]{.underline} pad handarz-nāmag čē nibišt estēd*

"I do not know: what stands (= is) written in the will?" = "I do not
know what is written in the will" (after *REA*.7.3)

*an dādār Ohrmazd framāyam ō amahrspandān [kū]{.underline}*

*gōwēd ō hamāg yazdān ud mēnōyān kū*

*rawēd ud rasēd ō hayārīh ī Pišišōtan ī bāmīg*

"I, Ohrmazd the creator, command the *amahrspand*s:

tell all the gods and (all others) in the other world:

go and come to the aid of Pišišōtan the bright!" (*ZWY*.7.27)

= "I, Ohrmazd the creator, command the *amahrspand*s to tell all the
gods and (all others) in the other world to go and come to the aid of
Pišišōtan the bright"

In "disjunctive" questions *kū* should be translated as "whether":

*nē dānēnd kū rāst gōwēd ayāb nē*

"they do not know: 'is he speaking the truth or not?"

= "they do not know whether he is speaking the truth or not"



# Sentences 4

*u-m dēn kadām u-m kē dōst u-m kē dušmen u-m čē xwēškārīh ī gētīy ud čē
mizd ī mēnōy*

"Which is my *dēn*? Who is my friend? Who is my enemy? And what is my
duty (of =) in this world, and what is my reward in the other world?"

*Spandarmad zamīg rādīh ēd kū hamāg dāmān az ōy zīyēnd*

"Spandarmad the earth's generosity is this: all creatures (*dāmān*) live
from her" (after *Bd*.26.83)

*pad ān ī Ohrmazd āmurzīdārīh dāmān zīyēnd ud pad ān ī Ohrmazd rādīh ō
ān ī pahlom axwān rasēnd*

"by Ohrmazd's mercy (*āmurzīdārīh*) the creatures live, and by Ohrmazd's
generosity they (will) come to the best existence" (*Bd*.26.9)

*gyān ō sag ud way pahikārēd kū ma ēn ī man kerb frāz xwarēd*

"the soul argues with (*ō*) the birds and dogs: Do not eat up this body
of mine!" (after *WZ*.30.32)

*ēn az Abestāg paydāg ān bawēd ka nē nān ud nē gōšt nēst*

"This is manifest from the Avesta. That is/will be (the case) when (he
has) neither bread nor meat."

*mardōm abēr tuxšāg bawēd kū tā Ohrmazd framān-burdār bawēd kū-tān mizd
az Ohrmazd ī xwadāy bawēd*

"people! be very diligent so that (*kū tā*) you will be obedient to
Ohrmazd, so that you will have a reward from Ohrmazd the lord!' " (after
*Dk*.6.249)

#  Text 4

Adapted from the *Ardā Wirāz-nāmag* "Book of the Righteous Wirāz" (the
'Zoroastrian *Divina Commedia*'):

*Ardā Wirāz az Mihr ud pērōzgar Srōš-ahlīy ud Ādur yazd pursēd kū*

*awēšān kē hēnd ud čē rāy ēdar estēnd*

*gōwēd Srōš-ahlīy ud Ādur yazd kū ēn gyāg hamēstagān xwānēnd*

*ud ēn ruwān tā tan ī pasēn ēn gyāg estēnd*

*ud ruwān ī awēšān mardōmān hēnd kē-šān kerbag ud wināh rāst būd*

*u-šān pādifrāh az wardišn ī andarwāy sardīh ayāb garmīh*

*u-šān anīy petyārag nēst*

Ardā Wirāz asks Mihr, the victorious Srōš-ahlīy and the divine Fire:

Who are those (souls) and why are they standing here?

Srōš-ahlīy and the divine Fire say: This place they call Hamēstagān.

These souls stand (in) this place until the Final Body.

They are the souls of those people whose (*kē-šān*) good deeds and sins
are equal (in weight).

And their punishment is from (results from) the turning of the
atmosphere: coldness and heat.

And they do not have (any) other adversary.



##  Grammar 5

### The relative pronouns

The relative pronouns *ī* (Y \<Y\>) and *kē* (WN \<MNW\>) are both of
them common in the functions of "who, whom, which."

Note that relative clauses introduced by *ī* usually contain a verb,
which helps distinguish them from *izafe* constructions.

Examples:

*ast [kē]{.underline} ēdōn gōwēd* *ān ī dānēd ud ān ī nē*

"there is one [who]{.underline} says thus (as follows) \..." "the one
who knows and the one who does not"

*mardōm [ī]{.underline} andar ēn šahr hēnd mazdēsn hēnd*

"the people [who]{.underline} are in this town are Mazdayasnian"

*ātaxš ī Burzisawang ātaxš [ī]{.underline} pēš ī Ohrmazd ī xwadāy estēd*

"the Burzisawang fire is the fire [which]{.underline} stands before
Ohrmazd the Lord" (after *Bd*.18.1)

Note: The four particles in this last sentence have three different
functions. What are they?

Relative pronouns with enclitics, e.g.:

*ān ī-[š]{.underline} andar dānišn*

"that which (is) within [his]{.underline} knowledge"

#### "Whose"

The relative pronoun *kē* can be direct or indirect object, as well as
possessive "whose," e.g.:

*Ardaxšīr az awēšān pursīd kū ēn rēdag [kē]{.underline} ast*

"Ardaxšīr asked them: whose (son) is this boy?" (*KN*.14.9)

*ān [kē]{.underline} kār abāg wehān wehīh kunēd ud [kē]{.underline} abāg
wattarān wattarīh kunēd*

"he [whose]{.underline} business (is) with good (people) does good
things (goodness); and (he) [whose]{.underline} (business is) with bad
ones does bad things (badness)" (after *MX*.59.12-14)

The possessive "whose" can also be expressed by attaching an enclitic
pronoun to the relative pronoun, e.g.:

*Ardawān kanīzag būd [ī-š]{.underline} kerb was nēk*

"Ardawān had a (servant) girl, [whose]{.underline} (lit. who her) shape
(was) very good (beautiful)"

*u-šān čē wināh būd [kē-šān]{.underline} ruwān ōwōn garān pādifrāh
bawēd*

"and what (*čē*) sin was theirs [whose]{.underline} soul gets (lit. who
for their soul = for whose soul there will be) such a heavy punishment?"
(after *AWN*.99.3)

The relative pronoun *čē* (nM \<ME\>) is most often used indefinitely:
"that which," *harw čē* "everything that," etc., e.g.:

*ud [čē]{.underline} andar ān dar*

"and (that) [which]{.underline} (is) in that chapter"

*[harw čē]{.underline} andar dānišn ī Ohrmazd kanāragōmand*

"[everything that]{.underline} (is) in Ohrmazd's knowledge is limited"
(after *Bd*.1.9)

Note: be careful to distinguish the various functions of *kē*, *cē*, and
*kū*:


Examples:

*ka Ardašīr ō dād ī 15-sālag [rasīd]{.underline} āgāhīh ō Ardawān
[mad]{.underline}*

"when Ardašīr came to (= reached) the age of 15, information came to
Ardawān" (*KN*.2.5/1.24)

*dēw gōwēnd kū amāh hagriz andar Ērānwēz [nē būd hēm]{.underline}*

"the *dēw*s say: we have never (*hagriz \... nē*) been in Ērānwēz"

# Texts 5

Adapted from the *Ardā Wirāz-nāmag*:

*ēdōn gōwēnd kū pas az marg ī ahlaw Zarduxšt tā bowandagīh ī 300 (sē
sad* or *tīrēst) sāl dēn andar abēzagīh ud mardōm andar abēgumānīh būd
hēnd*

*ēg ān gizistag Aliksandar ī hrōmāyīg pad garān zyān ud anāštīh ō Ērān
šahr āmad*

*pas az marg ī Aliksandar mardōmān ī Ērān šahr ēk abāg did was āšōb ud
pahikār būd*

*čiyōn-išān xwadāy ud sālār ud dastwar ī dēn-āgāh nē būd*

*ud mowmard-iz pad tis ī yazdān gumān būd hēnd*

*ud was ǰud-dādestānīh andar gēhān bē ō paydāgīh āmad*

So they say: After the death of Righteous Zarduxšt until the completion
of 300 years, the *dēn* (was) in purity, and people were in a state of
non-doubt.

Then that accursed Alexander, the Roman, came to Iran with (= bringing)
severe harm and lack of peace (= war).

After the death of Alexander, there was much turmoil and strife among
the people of Iran (lit. "the people of Iran had much turmoil and strife
one with the other")

since they had no lord (king), governor, and teacher knowledgeable in
the *dēn*.

And the high priests, too, were doubtful about the matters of the gods.

And much disagreement appeared \[Lesson 4\] in the world.


## Additional readings 5

From the *Zand ī Wahman Yasn*: *ZWY*.7.36. Note that the text probably
goes back to Pahlavi versions of Avestan texts, which accounts for some
of the unusual syntax and word order.

*ud wāng kunēd Mihr ī frāy-gōyōd ō Pišišōtan ī bāmīg kū*

*bē kan bē zan ān uzdēstčār ī dēwān nišēmag*

*raw ō ēn ērān dehān ī man ohrmazd-dād*

*abāz wirāy gāh ī dēn ud xwadāyīh*

*abar druwandān ka tō wēnē bē škennē*

*ud abar rasēd Pišišōtan ī bāmīg*

*ud ādur Farrbay ud ādur Gušnasp ud ādur Burzēnmihr ī pērōzgar bē zanēd
ān druz ī was-ōz*

*bē kanēd ān uzdēstčār kū nišēmag ī dēwān*

*ud yazišn frāz sāzēnd barsom frāz wistarēnd ud yazēnd dwāzdah-hōmāst*

*33-ēw* (*sī ud sē-ēw*) *stāyēnd man Ohrmazd abāg amahrspandān*

And Mihr Frāy-gōyōd calls to the radiant Pišišōtan:

"Pull down, strike that place of idols, the dwelling of *dēw*s!

Go to these towns of the Iranians---mine---established by Ohrmazd!

Redress the throne of *dēn* and royalty!

Smash (*abar \... škennē*, 2nd sg.) the wicked when you see (them)!"

And the radiant Pišišōtan arrives;

and the Farrbay fire, the Gušnasp fire, and the victorious Burzēnmihr
fire, and he strikes that mighty Lie.

And he pulls down (destroys) that place of idols, where the dwelling of
*dēw*s (was).

And they prepare a sacrifice, spread out the *barsom*,

and they sacrifice (= perform the sacrifice of) the Twelve Hōmāst.

They praise (= offer in praise) one Thirty-three to/for me Ohrmazd,
together with the *amahrspand*s.

# Texts 6

## Text 6.1

From *Pand-nāmag ī Zarduxšt* "Zarduxšt's Book of Advice":

*paydāg kū xwaršēd harw rōz 3 bār ō mardōm ī gētīy framān dahēd. bāmdād
ēn gōwēd kū*

*Ohrmazd ō ašmāh kē mardōm hēd hamē gōwēd kū pad kār ud kerbag tuxšāg
bawēd tā-tān man zīyišn ī gētīy pad mayān kunam*

It is well known that, every day three times, the sun commands the
people of this world. At dawn it says:

"Ohrmazd keeps saying to you, who are people: 'Be diligent in all (your)
activities so that I (can) place (*kunam*) among you life in this
world!'"

Note: *kē mardōm hēd* "(you) who are people" is an Avestan-type phrase
and means only "(you) people."

## Text 6.2

Adapted from the *Ardā Wirāz-nāmag*:

*fradom gām pad humad ud didīgar gām pad hūxt ud sidīgar gām pad
huwaršt*

*frāz ō Činwad puhl mad ham ī was-pahnāy ī amāwand ī Ohrmazd-dād*

*čahārom gām frāz niham ō ān ī rōšn Garōdmān ī hamāg-xwārīh*

*u-mān ō padīrag āmad awēšān widerdagān ruwān*

*ud drōd pursēnd ud āfrīn kunēnd ud ēn gōwēnd kū*

*čiyōn tō ahlaw bē mad hē az ān ī was-anāgīh axwān ud abar ō ēn axwān ī
apetyārag āmad hē*

*ud anōš xwar čē dagr zamān ēdar rāmišn wēnē*

The first step with good thought, the second step with good speech, and
the third step with good action---

I came forth to the very wide and powerful Činwad bridge established by
Ohrmazd.

The fourth step I place forth to the luminous Garōdmān, full of bliss.

And those souls of the departed came to meet us.

And they ask (us about our) health; they applaud (us); and they say
this:

How did you, O Righteous one, come from that existence with much evil
and came to this existence, free from adversity?

And drink nectar! For you shall see (= experience) joy for a long time.

## Additional readings 6.1

From the *Bundahišn*: *Bd*.26.34. -- About the duties of the various
divine beings.

*mēnōy-ēw ī abāg Mihr hamkār Sōg xwānēnd.*

*hamāg nēkīh ka az abargarān ō gētīy brēhēnīd nazdist ō Sōg āyēd*

*Sōg ō Māh abespārēd Māh ō Ardwīsūr abespārēd*

*ud Ardwīsūr ō Spahr abespārēd ud Spahr pad gēhān baxšēd*

*kē wēš dahēd nēkīh Spahr ud kē kem dahēd wad Spahr xwānēnd*

*ud ān-iz baxšišn pad Zamān rasēd kē Wāy ī dagrand-xwadāy ī ast ī
Zurwān*

One being in the *mēnōy* who collaborates with Mihr they call Sōg.

All goodness, when it is fashioned (to be sent) from those who work
above to this world, first comes to Sōg.

Sōg transfers it to the Moon. The Moon transfers it to Ardwīsūr.

And Ardwīsūr transfers it to the Firmament. And the Firmament
distributes it among living beings.

The one who gives the more goodness is the Firmament, and the one who
gives less they call the bad Firmament.

And that distribution (of goodness), too, comes through Time, who is Wāy
"of long-lasting lordship," whom some (call) Zurwān.

## Additional readings 6.2

From the *Bundahišn*: *Bd*.26.35-36.

*Ardwahišt xwēškārīh ēd kū ruwān ī druwandān andar dōšox dēwān wēš az
wināh ī-šān ast pādifrāh nē hilēd kerdan u-šān was abāz dārēd.*

*čiyōn gōwēd kū Ašwahišt ašāyīh ī pahlom ī amarg ī abzōnīg.*

Ardwahišt's special duty is this: He does not permit the demons to exact
more punishment on the soul of the wicked in Hell than their sins
(warrant), and he holds many of them back.

As it says: Ardwahišt: the best Righteousness, undying and making
increase.



## Grammar 7

### Comparisons with *čiyōn*

The conjunction of comparison *čiyōn* "as, like, that is; how?" is
usually combined with an adverb meaning "such, in this/that manner." The
constructions can rarely be translated literally into English.

The commonest combinations are:

WWwYwA \<'wgwn\'\> *ōwōn* "in that way, so" WWwïDC \<cygwn\'\> *čiyōn*
"as"

WWWtdA \<'ytwn\'\> *ēdōn* "in this way, so"

Note: Both WWwYwA and WWwïDC tend to be written without final stroke and
even without the final *-n* as WwYwA, wYwA, WwïDC, wïDC.

##### Only *čiyōn*:

*[čiyōn]{.underline} gōwēd kū*

"[as]{.underline} it says (in the *dēn*): \..."

*dōšox zofr [čiyōn]{.underline} ān ī sahmgentom čāh*

"hell is deep, [like]{.underline} the most terrifying well" (*AWN*.18.3)

*xwaršēd gardišn [čiyōn]{.underline} abesar pērāmōn ī gēhān*

"the turning of the sun is [like]{.underline} a crown around the world"
(*Bd*.5b.1)

*ōy Wirāz rāy haft xwah būd ud awēšān harw haft xwahān Wirāz
[čiyōn]{.underline} zan būd hēnd*

"that Wirāz had seven sisters, and all of those seven sisters were
[like]{.underline} a wife to Wirāz" (*AWN*.2.1)

##### *ciyōn* "that is":

*ēn dēn [čiyōn]{.underline} hamāg Abestāg ud zand abar gāw pōstīhā
nibišt estād*

"this *dēn*, [that is]{.underline}, the Avesta and (its) *zand*
(commentary) was written on bull-hides" (after *AWN*.1.5)

##### *čiyōn ka* "as when/if":

*mār ān-iz ast kē zahr pad čašm dārēd pad nigerišn mardōm bē ōzanēd
[čiyōn ka]{.underline} gazīd estēd*

"there is that snake, which has venom in the eyes; it kills a person
with (its) look, [just as when]{.underline} he is bitten" (*Bd*.22.19)

The adverbs may precede *čiyōn* directly or at a distance, and *homānag*
"like, similar," may be added e.g.:

##### *ōwōn čiyōn*, *ōwōn \... čiyōn* "as, like, in that way that":

*[ōwōn čiyōn]{.underline} pad dēn gōwēd kū*

"[as/in the way that]{.underline} it says in the *dēn*"

*[ōwōn]{.underline} saxt [čiyōn]{.underline} sang-ēw*

"[as]{.underline} heavy [as]{.underline} a stone"

*Ardā Wirāz [ōwōn]{.underline} būd [čiyōn]{.underline} mard-ēw ī huram*

"Ardā Wirāz was [like]{.underline} a happy man"

*tō [ōwōn]{.underline} kerbag kun [čiyō]{.underline}n-it Ohrmazd
framāyēd*

"perform good deeds [in the way that]{.underline} Ohrmazd commands you!"

##### *ēdōn čiyōn*, *ēdōn \... čiyōn* "like, in this way that"

*ēdōn čiyōn tō* "like you"

*mēnōy āsmān [ēdōn]{.underline} estād [čiyōn]{.underline} gurd ī
artēštār*

"the divine sky stood like a warrior hero" (after *Bd*.1a.7b)

*an [ēdōn]{.underline} dušxwār būd ham [čiyōn]{.underline} mard-ēw ka-š
mān kanēnd*

"I was [as]{.underline} unhappy [as]{.underline} a man when they destroy
his house"

*pad ēč nēkīh ī gētīy wistāx ma bāš čē nēkīh ī gētīy [ēdōn homānāg
čiyōn]{.underline} abr ī pad ābsālān rōz āyēd kē pad ēč kōf abāz nē
pāyēd*

"have confidence in no goodness of this world, for the goodness of this
world is [just like]{.underline} a cloud that comes on a spring day
(and) which does not linger on any mountain" (*MX*.1.98--99)

In similes, *homānāg* "resembling" can be used as a postposition:

*dām ī Ohrmazd pad mēnōyīh [ēdōn]{.underline} parward \...
[čiyōn]{.underline} šusr [homānāg]{.underline}*

"the creation of Ohrmazd was nurtured in *mēnōy* state,
[like]{.underline} semen" (*Bd*.1.57)

Note that *ōwōn* and *ēdōn* are commonly used with adjectives and
adverbs to mean "as, so," e.g.:

*arz ī kerbag [ōwōn]{.underline} wazurg ud akanārag ([kū]{.underline}
\...)*

"the value good deeds is [so]{.underline} great and immeasurable (that
\...)" (*PN*.53)

###  The verb

The present indicative and the imperative are formed from the present
stem. As in English, the present indicative is commonly used to express
present and future action or state.

There is also a [1st plural imperative]{.underline} (=1st plural
indicative), which is used to express "let us \...!" ("cohortative").

#### The present indicative

##### Endings:

Singular Plural

1st µY--, M-- \<-m\>, \<-ym\> *-am*, *-ēm* µY-- \<-ym\> *-ēm*

2nd E-, aÅ-, ∫Y-, ì-- \<-yḏ, -[ydy]{.underline}\> *-ē* WtD-- \<-yt\'\>
*-ēd*

3rd WtD-- \<-yt\'\> *-ēd* Y--, YwY-- \<-ynd\> *-ēnd*

Note: On the spellings of the 2nd singular ending *-ē* and \<-dt\'\> for
\<-yyt\'\>, see Lesson 5.

##### The 1st singular:

1st-singular discourse is relatively rare and phonetically written forms
even rarer.

The most common ending is *-am*, e.g. Mwï˜ \<mynm\> *menam* "I think,"
McD\<ycm\> *yazam* "I sacrifice," but the ending *-ēm* appears to be
found with certain kinds of present stems, e.g.:

present stems in *-s-*:µïJWWP \<pwrsym\> *pursēm* "I ask," µïjAwÍ
\<šn'sym\> *šnāsēm* "I know";

present stems in -*š*-: µïhAW \<whšym\> *waxšēm* "I grow," µïhAWT
\<twhšym\> *tuxšēm* "I strive";

present stems in *-y-*: µïå¸ \<z'ym\> *zayam* or µsa¸ *zayēm* "I ask
for" and µïÅtJ \<st'ym\> and µsAtJ \<st'dym\> *stāyam* or *stāyēm* "I
praise"

Note: some of these may be caused by uncertainty about how to connect
with the \<-m\>.

There are also examples of an ending *-om*, e.g., MwlYKW \<nkylwm\> "I
look at."

In arameograms, the 1st singular and 1st plural endings are always
distinguished: sing. \<-m\>, plur. \<-ym\>.

##### The 2nd singular:

For îJWWP \<pwrsyḏ\> "you ask," we also find îŸJWWP \<pwrsyyḏ, etc.

The 2nd singular of *zay-* is ísa¸ \<z'dyḏ\>, aŸŸ©a¸ \<
z'dy[ydy]{.underline}\>, etc., "you ask (for)."

##### The 1st plural:

The 1st plural occasionally has the endings *-am* or *-om*, e.g., McD
\<ycm\> *yazam* and MWcD \<ycwm\> *yazom* "we sacrifice," *abespāram*
"we shall hand over" (*AWN* 2.7), MwLwmEwA \<'wšmwlwm\> *ōšmurom* "we
enumerate" (PY.31.1).

##### The 3d plural:

The 3rd plural is not infrequently written with \<-nd\>, e.g.,
\<wcynnd\> *wizīnand*, \<lwnd\> *rawand* (MK 4r).

Some scribes often simplify the endings of present stems in *-ēn-*,
e.g., \<'k'synynd\> *āgāhēnēnd* "they inform" to \<'k'synd\>,
*paydāgēnd* for *paydāgēnēd* "he makes manifest."

In arameograms, the ending is always \<-d\>.

#### The imperative

The imperative has no ending in the 2nd singular and is identical with
the present indicative in the 1st and 2nd plural.

The 2nd singular present indicative is also sometimes used as
imperative.

Paradigms of *ōbār-* (-lAPwA \<'wp'l-\>) "swallow," *purs-*, *framāy-*,
*gīr-*, and *šaw-*:

##### Paradigms:

Singular

2nd lAPwA \<'wp'l\> *ōbār* "swallow!" SWWP \<pwrs\> *purs* "ask!"

Plural

1st µï¬APwA \<'wp'lym\> *ōbārēm* "let us swallow!" µïJWWP \<pwrsym\>
*pursēm* "let us ask!"

2nd WtdlAPwA \<'wp'lyt\'\> *ōbārēd* "swallow!" (you all) WtŸJWWP
\<pwrsyt\'\> *pursēd* "ask!" (you all)

Singular

2nd áÂLP \<plm'd\> *framāy* "order!"

Plural

1st µïdaÂLP \<plm'dym\> *framāyēm* "let us order!"

2nd WtdaÂLP \<plm'dt\'\> *framāyēd* "order!" (you all)

##### Arameograms:

Singular

2nd WwˆÅW \<OHDWN\> *gīr* "take!" WwlZW \<OZLWN\> *šaw* "go!"

Plural

The verb *baw-* "become, be" has the irregular 2nd singular imperative:
ßAWWwE , ÍWWwE \<YHWWN(')š\> *bāš* "be!"

For 2nd sing. \<-'ḏ\> *-āy*, e.g., áÂLP \<plm'ḏ\> "command!" we also
find \<-''\>, e.g., aåÂLP \<plm''\> (perhaps for *framāyē*) "command,
order!"

### Uses of the present and the imperative

#### Present indicative

The present indicative is used for actions taking place in the present
or future and for general statements, e.g.:

*ēdōn [gōwēnd]{.underline} kū*

"thus they say (are saying): \..."

*agar ašmāh [stāyēd]{.underline} weh dēn ī abēzag ī Spitāmān ahlaw
Zarduxšt amāh ō tō [dahēm]{.underline} dagr-xwadāyīh*

"if you (and your followers) [praise]{.underline} the good, pure *dēn*
of the Righteous Spitamān Zarduxšt, (then) we [shall give]{.underline}
to you long-lasting kingship" (*Dk*.7.4.81)

*az dēwān ud druzān garān zyān ud wizend pad Ohrmazd dāmān
[bawēd]{.underline}*

"[there will be]{.underline} heavy damage and harm to Ohrmazd's
creatures from the demons and lie-demons" (after *AWN*.33.3)

*Gannāg Mēnōy hagriz az petyāragīh nē [wardēd]{.underline}*

"the Foul Spirit [will]{.underline} never (*hagriz \... nē*) [turn
away]{.underline} from being the Adversary (of Ohrmazd's creation)"
(*Bd*.1.35)

*ātaxš gōwēd kū nē [waxšēm]{.underline} ud āb [gōwēd]{.underline} kū nē
[tazam]{.underline}*

"the fire says: '[I will]{.underline} not [blaze]{.underline}!' the
water says: '[I will]{.underline} not [run/flow]{.underline}!' "
(*ZWY*.9.19)

#### Imperative

The imperative expresses commands, e.g.:

*andar hamēmālān ērtan ud čarb ud hučašm [bāš]{.underline}*

"be humble and amenable and benevolent with respect to (= toward) your
fellow men!" (*MX*.1.7)

*Sōšāns gōwēd kū Kay [raw]{.underline} ud dēn [stāy]{.underline} Kay
Husrōy dēn bē stāyēd*

"Sōšāns says: '[Go]{.underline}, Kay, and [praise]{.underline} the *dēn*
(*dēn*)!' --- Kay Husrōy praises the *dēn*" (*PR*.48.48)

The 1st plural expresses an exhortation to oneself ("cohortative"),
e.g.:

*tā šab kārēzār [kunēm]{.underline}*

"[let us do]{.underline} battle until night(-fall)!" (*Bd*.1.26)

*Zarduxšt bē ō gētīy bē [dahēm]{.underline}*

"[let us give]{.underline} Zarduxšt to the world!"

The imperative is negated with *ma* "do not," which usually precedes the
verb but can also be separated from it, e.g.:

*Sāsān ō Pābag guft kū-m wizend ud zyān [ma kun]{.underline}*

"Sāsān said to Pābag: [do not do]{.underline} harm and damage to me!"
(*KN*.1.15)

*pad ēč nēkīh ī gētīy wistāx [ma bāš]{.underline}*

"[do not be]{.underline} confident in (do not rely upon) any goodness of
this world!" (*MX*.1.98)

*ēč zamān [ma pāy]{.underline} u-š [ōzan]{.underline}*

"[do not linger]{.underline} (hesitate) any (amount of) time, and (=
but) [kill]{.underline} him!" (*KN*.10.15)

*ašmāh mard [ma]{.underline} dēwān [yazēd]{.underline}*

"you, men, [do not sacrifice to]{.underline} the *dēw*s!" (*Dk*.7.1.9)

##### With 2nd singular indicative:

*Mihr [ma]{.underline} abar-druxtār [bawē]{.underline}*

"do not belie Mihr = the contract!" (*abar-druxtār baw-* "belie")

### Subject and verb agreement

When the subject is the plural of an [animate]{.underline} noun (humans
or animals) the predicate is usually in the plural, but in the past
tense the auxiliary (*hēnd*) is sometimes omitted. When there are
several inanimate subjects, the verb normally agrees with the closest
one. When the subject is not expressed, the auxiliary can not usually be
omitted:

*čand [āyēnd]{.underline} xyōn az bunag čand aswār [āyēnd]{.underline}
čand [mīrēnd]{.underline} ud čand abāz [šawēnd]{.underline}*

"how many Xyōns [will be coming]{.underline} from the camp? How many
[will come]{.underline} on horseback? How many [will die]{.underline}?
And how many [will go back]{.underline}?" (*AZ*.65)

*ud pas awēšān [haft mard bē nišast hēnd]{.underline}*

"and then those seven men sat down" (*AWN*.1.19)

*u-mān ō padīrag [āmad]{.underline} awēšān widerdagān
[ruwān]{.underline}*

"and [the souls]{.underline} of those departed [came]{.underline} to
meet us" (after *AWN*.10.2)

#### Collective nouns

Collective nouns in the singular can take a plural verb:

*[grōh-ēw āyēnd]{.underline} \... ud rōdestāg ī Ērān šahr tā Bābēl
[gīrēnd]{.underline}*

"[one group will come, and they will take]{.underline} the provinces of
Iran (all the way) to Babylon" (after *Bd*.33.29)

*az dašn wēnīg ī ōy [snexr padīd hēnd]{.underline}*

"from his right nostril, snow fell" (*Dk*.9.21.22)

When the subject is an inanimate noun, the predicate is usually in the
plural only when [individuality]{.underline} is emphasized, otherwise in
the singular:

*gōwēd pad dēn kū nazdist kōf frāz rust Hariburz \... az ān pas hamāg
kōf frāz [rust hēnd]{.underline} pad 18 sāl*

"it says in the *dēn*: the first mountain (that) grew up (is) Hariburz;
from that, afterward, all the mountains [grew up]{.underline} in 18
years" (*Bd*.9.1)

## Verbal particles

There are two particles of negation, *nē* and *ma*, and three verbal
particles with modal functions: *hamē*, *bē*, and *ē*.

#### Negations

To recapitulate: The normal negations are *nē* (aÒ , âL \<LA\>) "not"
and *ma* (oA , øA \<AL\>) "(do/let) not!," both of which we have seen
many times, e.g.:

*ēg-im akāmagōmand mang [ma dahēd]{.underline}*

"then [do not give]{.underline} me hashish unwillingly!" (i.e., if I do
not want it) (*AWN*.1.20)

*[ma]{.underline} Xyōn [rasēnd]{.underline}*

"[let not]{.underline} the Xyonians [come]{.underline}!" (*AZ*.81)

Note repeated *nē* and *ma*, often with *-iz* "either," e.g.:

*ān tarāzūg ēč kustag ōgrāy [nē]{.underline} kunēd [nē]{.underline}
ahlawān rāy ud [nē-iz]{.underline} druwandān [nē]{.underline} xwadāyān
rāy ud [nē-iz]{.underline} ān ī dahībedān*

"that balance does [not]{.underline} dip to any side (i.e., the wrong
way): [neither]{.underline} for the Righteous [nor]{.underline} the
wicked, [neither]{.underline} for lords nor governors" after *MX*.1.120)

*ān ēk rāh gīrēd ī ahlāyīh ud [ma]{.underline} pad frāxīh ud
[ma]{.underline} pad tangīh ud [ma]{.underline} pad ēč rāh az-iš wardēd*

"take that one path, that of Righteousness, and [do not]{.underline}
turn from it in any way, [(n)either]{.underline} in well-being
[(n)or]{.underline} (when) in a tight spot (distress)!" (*AWN*.101.8)

Note *hambun-iz* \<hmbwnc, hmbwnyc\> "altogether," *hambun-iz*
(*hāmbun-iz*) *\... nē* "not at all":

*agar-it [hambun-iz]{.underline} mihr ī amāh ast* *Ardawān [hambun-iz
nē]{.underline} pād*

"if you have any love for Us [at all]{.underline}" (*KN*.10.3) "Ardawān
did [not]{.underline} linger at [all]{.underline}" (*KN*.4.13)

#### The particle *hamē*

The particle *hamē* (áÂA \<hm[ydy]{.underline}\>) literally meant "ever,
forever" and is used to express continuing action. With verbs, it can be
rendered by "keep doing" or similar. With nouns and adjectives, it may
mean "still," e.g.:

*kāmag ī Ganāg Mēnōy [hamē warzēnd]{.underline}*

"[they keep performing]{.underline} the will/wish of the Foul Spirit"
(*Bd*.1.24)

*Ohrmazd ō ašmāh kē mardōm hēd [hamē gōwēd]{.underline} kū pad kār ud
kerbag kerdan tuxšāg bawēd*

"Ohrmazd [keeps saying]{.underline} to you (who are) people: Be diligent
in performing (*kerdan* infinitive) (your) work and good deeds!"
(*PN*.49)

*anšahrīg ī ag-dēn ka abāg xwadāy ayāb pas az xwadāy ō hudēnīh ā329*

*ēd [hamē]{.underline} anšahrīg*

"if a slave belonging to one of an evil *dēn* comes to (joins) the
community of those of the good *dēn* (= Zoroastrians) together with
(his/her) master or after the master, [he/she will still]{.underline} be
a slave" (*MHD*.1.8)

##### *hamē ka* "(for) as long as"

*[hamē ka]{.underline} wārišn wārēd xrafstar ēdōn wārēd čiyōn wārišn*

"([for) as long as]{.underline} it rains, it rains evil animals like
rain" (*MX*.61.36)

[Note *tā hamē ud hamē-rawišnīh* "forever and ever."]{.underline}

#### 

#### The particle *bē* 

As an adverb, *bē* (AWB \<BRA\>) means "out (from), away (from)," and is
often used with prepositions, as in *bē ō* "to, all the way to."

As a verbal particle, one of its most common functions seems to be to
express beginning or end of an action or state, especially with past
tenses, but also with the present, and imperative. It is often unclear
whether we are dealing with the adverb or the particle, e.g.:

##### With the present:

*ka 9000* (*nō hazār*) *sāl bowandag bawēd Srōš-ahlīy Xešm [bē
zanēd]{.underline}*

"when the nine thousand years are complete, Srōš-ahlīy [will
smite]{.underline} Wrath" (after *MX*.7.13)

*pad abdom Gannāg Mēnōy nē bawēd andar dām ī Ohmrazd ud pad frazām [bē
abesihēd]{.underline}*

"in the end, the Foul Spirit will not be (exist) in Ohrmazd's creation,
and, for (all) future, [he will be destroyed]{.underline}"

##### With the imperative:

*bē nigerēd* "look!"

*wināh andar hāsr [bē ma hilēd]{.underline}*

"[do not let]{.underline} a sin within a 'mile' (of you)!" (*PN*.36)

##### With the past tense:

*Hōšang dēw [bē ōzad]{.underline}*

"Hōšang [killed]{.underline} the *dēw*" (after *Bd*.33.1)

*Ganāg Mēnōy abesinnēnišnīh ī dēwān agārīh ī xwēš rōšn [bē
dīd]{.underline}*

"the Foul Spirit [saw]{.underline} the destruction of the *dēw*s (and)
his own undoing clearly" (*Bd*.6a.4)

##### Repetition of *bē* without verb:

*[bē]{.underline} abar ō ān deh ān ī guxrūn anāštīh [padēd]{.underline}
[bē]{.underline} ān ī abārōn snōhišn [bē]{.underline} ān ī abārōn
spazgīh*

"upon that town bloody discord [will fall]{.underline} (*bē \...
padēd*), (as well as) immoral lamentation and immoral slander"
(*Dk*.7.7.36)

#### The particle *ē* 

The particle *ē* (Ä , íA \<'y, '[d]{.underline}\>; inscr. *ēw* wya, Man.
*hēb*) is used with the present to express exhortation to other than 2nd
person. It can usually be translated with "let \... !"

It is negated with *ma* (*ma ē*) e.g.:

Note: In the manuscripts, *ē* is frequently spelled \<HNA\> *ēd*, which
indicates that at the time the manuscripts were written, the pronoun
*ēd* had lost its final *-d* and become *ē*.

*paydāg kū mard menišn az zan [ē bandēd]{.underline}*

"it is manifest: [let]{.underline} a man [close]{.underline} his mind to
women!" (after *PR*.10j.1)

*ka meh ruwān-dōstar* *meh [ē šawēd]{.underline}*

"when the older loves (his) soul more, [let]{.underline} the older
[go]{.underline}!" (*Herb*.1.3.1)

*aškamb rāy ēdōn [ma ē tuxšēd]{.underline}*

"[let]{.underline} [him]{.underline} [not labor]{.underline} so for the
sake of his belly!" (*PR*.10j.1)

*awēšān [ē ōšmurēnd]{.underline} kē sūdōmand hēnd*

"[let them enumerate]{.underline} (recite, i.e., the *dēn*), they who
are the Profit-makers!" (*Dk*.9.46.2)

*Spitāmān Zarduxšt tēz ō man [bē ē rasēd]{.underline} \... ud ō man [ē
nigēzēd]{.underline} dēn ī Ohrmazd ud Zarduxšt*

"[let]{.underline} Spitāmān Zarduxšt [come]{.underline} quickly to me,
and [let him teach]{.underline} me the *dēn* of Ohrmazd and Zarduxšt!"
(*Dk*.7.4.86)

# Texts 7

## Text 7.1

From the *Bundahišn*: *Bd*.34.9. -- Account of the last days.

*pas mardōm mardōm bē šnāsēnd kū ruwān ruwān tan tan bē šnāsēd kū ēn man
ast pid ēn man ast brād ud ēn man ast zan.*

*pas bawēd hanǰaman ī Isadwāstarān kū mardōm pad ēn zamīg bē estēnd.*

*andar ān hanǰaman harw kas nēk-kunišnīh ud wad-kunišnīh ī xwēš wēnēnd.*

*ahlaw andar druwand ōwōn paydāg čiyōn gōspand ī spēd andar ān ī syā
bawēd.*

*pas ahlaw az druwand ǰudāg kunēnd ud ahlaw ō Garōdmān nayēnd ud druwand
abāz ō dōšox abganēnd.*

*ud 3 (sē) rōz šab dōšoxīg tanōmand gyānōmand andar dōšox pādifrāh
widārēnd ud ahlaw andar Garōdmān tanōmand ān 3 rōz šab urwāhmenīh
wēnēd.*

Then people will know (recognize) people, i.e., souls will know souls
(and) bodies bodies (knowing that) this is my father, this is my
brother, and this is my wife.

Then comes the assembly of Isadwāstar, where (= in which) people will
stand on this earth.

In that assembly, all will see what good they did and what bad they did.

The Righteous will be as manifest among the wicked as a white sheep
among the black.

Then they will separate the Righteous from the wicked. And they lead the
Righteous to Garōdmān and throw the wicked back into Hell.

And, for three days (and) nights, those hell-bound will suffer
punishment in hell in body and soul, and the Righteous (one) in Garōdmān
will see (= experience) bliss in body for three days (and) nights.

##  Text 7.2

From the *Māh nyāyišn* "Hymn to the Moon": *Ny*.3.4. -- Pahlavi
rendering of the Avestan in **bold**.

***čiyōn ka māh waxšēd čiyōn ka māh nirfsēd***

***15*** (*panzdah*) ***ka māh waxšēd 15 ka māh nirfsēd***

*15 rōz az gētīyān kār ud kerbag padīrēd ud az mēnōyān mizd ud pādāšn*

*ud 15 rōz ō mēnōyān kār ud kerbag bē abespārēd ō gētīyān mizd ud
pādāšn*

*nēkīh ī māh ī pērōzgar az ēk tā 15 rōz az mēnōyān nēkīh ud farroxīh
padīrēd*

*ud az 15 tā bowandagīh ī 30* (*sī*) *rōz pad gētīyān baxšēd*

*ud az ān ēk rōz ka nōg bē abzōn pad māh bawēd tā bowandagīh ī 30 rōz
rōšnīh ud nēkīh az mēnōyān padīrēd ō gētīyān abespārēd mizd ud pāddāšn*

'How (is it) when the moon waxes? How (is it) when the moon wanes?

Fifteen when the moon waxes. Fifteen when the moon wanes.'

For fifteen days, it receives all the activities of those in this world
and rewards and countergifts from those in the other world.

And for fifteen days, it transfers all the activities to those in the
other world, (and) to those in this world the rewards and countergifts.

The goodness of the victorious moon: from day one to (day) fifteen, it
receives from those in the other world goodness and good fortune.

And from day fifteen to the completion of thirty days, it distributes it
among those in this world.

And from that day one, when (it is) new, there is (*bē \... bawēd*)
increase in the moon, to the completion of thirty days, it receives
light and goodness from those in the other world (and) transfers rewards
and countergifts to those in this world.

1.  Gayōmard's life was 30 years. After that he died.

2.  Zarduxšt, the Mazdayasnians' messenger, will bring Ohrmazd's *dēn*
    to King Wištāsp.

3.  Now, Ohrmazd, show me heaven and hell and the reward of the
    Righteous and the punishment of the wicked!

    after death! \[*singular and plural*\]

    and scorns them!

    opponents.

    Heaven.

    enemies!

9.  Do not let the Xionians strike the heros of Iran!

10. Everybody in this world has (lit., there is for \...!) sins in (his)
    hand and foot (= commits sins with his hands and feet).

# Additional readings 7

## Additional readings 7.1

From the *Mēnōy xrad*: *MX*.2.110-115

*pad zīndagīh wistāx ma bāš čē-t abdom margīh abar rasēd*

*ud nasāy sag ud way kirrēnēd ud astag ō zamīg ōftēd.*

*ud tā 3 (sē) rōz-šabān ruwān pad bālēn ī tan nišīnēd.*

*ud rōz ī čahārōm andar ōšbām pad abāgīh ī Srōš-ahlīy ud Wāy ī weh ud
Wahrām ī amāwand*

*ud hamēstārīh ī Astwihād ud Wāy ī wad ud Frazišt dēw ud Wizišt dēw*

*ud duškām-kerdārīh ī Xešm ī anāg-kerdār ī xurdruš*

*tā ō Činwad puhl šawēd ī buland ī sahmgen*

*kē harw ahlaw ud druwand awiš madār.*

Do not rely on life, because, in the end, death will come upon you (*-t
\... abar*).

And dogs and birds will cut up the corpse, and the bones will fall on
the ground.

And for three days and nights, the soul sits at the headboard of (the
bed where) the body (lies).

And, on the fourth day, at dawn, (it goes) accompanied by Sroš-ahlīy the
good Wāy, and the powerful Wahrām

and with the opposition of Astwihād, the evil Wāy, the demons Drag-forth
and Drag-down,

and Wrath whose actions are according to his evil will and who does evil
things, he with the bloody club,

it goes to the Činwad bridge, tall and fearsome,

to which (*kē\... awiš*) every Righteous and wicked are destined to
come.

## Additional readings 7.2

From the *Dēnkard* 7.1.21 (from PV.2.4). -- Note the imperatives in
*-ē*.

*ud andar weh dēn pad gōwišn ī dādār Ohrmazd ō J̌am paydāg kū*

*ēg ān ī man gēhān frāyēn kū marag wēš bē kunē ud ēg ān ī man gēhān
wālēn kū frabihtar bē kunē*

*ud ēg az man padīrē gēhān srāyišn ud parwarišn*

*ud sālārīh ud abar-nigāhdārīh ēdōn bē kunē kū kas abar ōy ī did rēš ud
zyān nē kunēd*

And in the Good Dēn it is evident from the creator Ohrmazd's words to
J̌am:

'So further this world of mine!' i.e., make (its) number more! 'And then
increase this world of mine!' i.e., make it fatter!

'And then accept from me to protect and foster this world!'

'And guard it and look after it!' (i.e.) so that nobody can cause hurt
and harm to one another!

Do not practice sloth, so that your work and good deeds do not remain
undone!

Choose a woman of good family, for that one is the better one who in the
end is the one of better reputation!

Do not speak while eating, so that no heavy transgression against Hordad
and Amurdad befalls you!

Do not walk about without tying the kusti, so that no harm comes to your
bipeds and quadrupeds (those in your household on two and on four) and
no damage to your children!

Do not walk with one shoe, so that no heavy sin comes to your soul!

Do not urinate standing up, so that, on account of that sin, the demons
do not drag you to Hell!

Work hard, and eat from your good hard work, and give the gods and good
(people) (their) share!

# Lesson 8

## Spelling 8

### The phoneme / ǰ / (*ž*)

The sound *ž* may have existed in some words, especially words with
Avestan *-ž-*, but the evidence is not clear. MacKenzie, in his
*Dictionary*, assumes this *ž* belongs to the phoneme /ǰ/ (*Aǰdahāg*,
etc.), presumably by comparison with Manichean Middle Persian
(\<'jdh'g\>, etc.). Among the possible examples are the following:

WkaåDcÅ \<'cdh'k\'\> *Aǰdahāg* (*Aždahāg*) Av. Aži Dahāka (dragon slain
by Θraētaona, Pahl. Frēdōn)

:jadÍwY \<ywšd'sl\> *yōǰdahr* (*yōždahr*) "ritually clean" (Av.
*yaoždāθra*, ManMP. \<ywjdhr\>)

y\>ÍwlA , º\>ÍwlA \<hlwšd\> *xruǰd* (*xružd*) "hard, harsh"

MWtDCwlA \<hlwcdtwm\> *xruǰdtom* (*xruždtom*) "hardest" (Av.
*xruždišta*)

Wwaåd\<ßA \<'šgh'n\'\> *aǰgahān* (*ažgahān*) "lazy, indolent"

The sound may also have been used in *duž-*, a byform of *duš-* "evil,
bad," e.g.:

WwsÍwY \<dwšdyn\'\> *duǰdēn* (*duždēn*) "of evil *dēn*" (Av. *duždaēna*,
ManMP. \<dwjdynyy\>).

Examples of Avestan *-ǰ-* in Pahlavi include the two following common
terms referring to something bad:

WcŸJ \<syc\'\> *seǰ* "\*danger, \*damage" (Av. *iθiiajah*; sexual
impotence?)

WcŸjA \<'syc\'\> *aseǰ* "free from \*danger, \*damage" (Av. *aiθiiajah*)

##  Word formation 2. Prefixes and suffixes 2

#### *a-* (*an-*)

Adjectives denoting lack of something are formed from nouns or present
stems of verbs by means of the prefixes *a-* (-A \<'-\>) and, before
vowels, *an-* (-wA \<'n-\>) = "un-, -less, without," etc.

In the manuscripts, this *a-* is sometimes written separate or attached
without adapting its form to the following letter (e.g., ylMA \<'-mlg\>)
or in the form ë \<A-\> (e.g., mYB ë \<A-bym\>.

The opposites of these adjectives are formed by means of the suffixes
*‑ōmand* and *‑gen,* on which see Lesson 9. Nouns in *-īh* can in turn
be formed from such adjectives, e.g.:

*dān-* "to know" *adān* "without knowledge, ignorant" *adānīh*
"ignorance"

*petyārag* "adversary" *apetyārag* "without adversary" *apetyāragīh*
"adversary-less-ness"

*kanārag* "border, limit" *akanārag* "limitless" *akanāragīh*
"limitless-ness"

*zarmān* "old age" *azarmān* "unaging" *azarmānīh* "absence of aging"

*marg* "death" *amarg* "undying" *amargīh* "immortality"

*ōš* (*hōš*) "death" *ahōš* "immortal" *ahōšīh* "immortality"

*bīm* "fear" *abīm* "free from fear" *abīmīh* "freedom from fear"

*bēš* "harm" *abēš* "free from harm" *abēšīh* "freedom from harm"

*tazišn* "running, flow (of rivers)" *atazišn* "not flowing" *atazišnīh*
"fact/state of not flowing"

*ēr* "Aryan, Iranian" *anēr* (*an-ēr*) "non-Iranian" *anērīh* "not being
Iranian"

(spelled \<'n-'yl\>, less commonly \<'nyl\>)

From compounds:

*abar-dāštār* "supporting" *an-abar-dāštār* "without anything supporting
(it)

Words beginning with *h-* may take *an-* instead of *a-*, e.g.:

*hambasān* "opponent" *an-(h)ambasān* "having no opponents"

*haspīn* "rest, repose" *an-(h)aspīn* "incessent(ly)"

*hammōxt* "(sth.) learned" *an-hammōxt* "(sth.) not learned"

Words beginning with sibilant + consonant may take a prosthetic *e-*
(*a-*, *i-*?) and the prefix *an-*, e.g.:

*spās* "gratitude" *an-espās* "ungrateful"

*šnōhr* "gratitude" *an-ešnōhr* "ungrateful"

*šnās-* "to know (sth.)" *an-ešnās* "unknowing"

*spurr* "complete" *an-espurr* "incomplete"

#### *abē-*

Adjectives denoting lack of something can also be formed from nouns or
present stems of verbs by means of the prefix *abē-* (-YcÅ, -1YcÅ, -AcÅ
\<'p̄y-, 'p̄yḏ-, 'p̄'-\>) "without" (occasionally *bē* \<BRA\>,
Persianism?).

The opposites of these adjectives are formed by means of the suffixes
*-ōmand* and *-gen* "full of," on which see Lesson 9. Examples:

*mizag* "taste" *abē-mizag* "tasteless"

*bīm* "fear" *abē-bīm* "without fear" *abē-bīmīh* "fearlessness"

*wināh* "sin" *abē-wināh* "sin-less, having no sin" *abē-wināhīh*
"sinlessness"

*gumān* "doubt" *abē-gumān* "having no doubt" *abē-gumānīh* "state of
non-doubt"

*āstār* "sin" *bē-āstār* "without sin" (*DD*.16.14b)

#### *pad-* "with"

A few adjectives are formed with *pad-* ( WWP \<PWN\>).

They are not easy to recognize, as they look like prepositional phrases,
e.g.:

*bun* "beginning" *pad-bunīh* "being at the beginning"

*dād* "law" *pad-dād* "legitimate, according to the law"

*drōw* "lie" *pad-drōw* "lying, untruthful"

*dumb* "tail" *pad-dumb* "with tail" (cf. *a-dumb* "tail-less")

*gōhr* "substance, descent" *pad-gōhr* "of substance, of (good) descent"

*mizag* "taste" *pad-mizag* "tasty"

#### *hu-* \~ *duš-*

Nouns can be formed from other nouns by means of the prefixes *hu-* (-wA
\<hw-\>) and *duš-* (-ÍwY \<dwš-\>) and mean "a good X, a bad X," e.g.:

*pādixšāy* "king" *hupādixšāy* "a good king" *hupādixšāyīh* "a good
rule"

*dušpādixšāy* "a bad king" *dušpādixšāyīh* "a bad rule"

More commonly, adjectives are formed from nouns by means of the prefixes
*hu-* and *duš-* and mean "having good/bad X." Note that *duš-* becomes
*du(s)-* before *s* and, sometimes, *duǰ-* before voiced stops, e.g.:

*menišn* "thinking, thought" *hu-menišn* "having good thoughts"
*duš-menišn* "having bad thoughts\"

*gōwišn* "speaking, speech" *hu-gōwišn* "having good speech"
*duš-gōwišn* "having bad speech"

*kunišn* "action, deeds" *hu-kunišn* "having good deeds" *duš-kunišn*
"having bad deeds"

*dēn*, technical term *hu-dēn* "having a good *dēn*" *duǰ-dēn* "having a
bad *dēn*"

*sraw* "reputation" *husraw* "of good fame, famous" *dusraw* "of bad
fame, infamous"

Note the following common forms from Avestan:

*humad* (*humat*) *dušmad* (*dušmat*) = *hu-menišn* *duš-menišn*

*hūxt* *dušhūxt* = *hu-gōwišn* *duš-gōwišn*

*huwaršt* *dušhuwaršt* = *hu-kunišn* *duš-kunišn*

Sometimes the meaning is modified and cannot be predicted from the
individual components:

*čihr* "appearance" *hu-čihr* "beautiful" *duš-čihr* "ugly"

*čašm* "eye" *hu-čašm* "benevolent" *duš-čašm* "envious"

*āgāh* "aware" *duš-āgāh* "ignorant"

When added to an adjective with negative connotation, it means "very":

*zišt* "ugly" *duš-zišt* "very ugly"

#### * nā-* 'not"

The rare prefix *nā-* (-AW \<n'-\>) negates adjectives like *a-*, but
can sometimes be difficult to distinguish from *a-*:

*arzānīg* "valuable, worthy" *nā-arzānīg* "valueless"

*waxr* "crooked" *nā-waxr* "not crooked"

*kām-tazišn* "who runs according to his will" *nā-kām-tazišnīh* "not
running acc. to one's will" (souls in hell)

#### *-īg*, *-īk*

The most common suffix forming adjectives from nouns is *-īg*, with the
rare variant *-īk* (both WkY-/WI- \<-yk\'\>):

*āb* "water" *ābīg* "living in water"

*zamīg* "earth" *zamīgīg* "living on earth"

*hrōmāy* "a Roman" *hrōmāyīg* "Roman" (adjective)

*dōšox* "hell" *dōšoxīg* "denizen of hell, hell-bound"

*abzōn* "increase" *abzōnīg* "making increase" *abzōnīgīh* "increase"

*waran* "greed" *waranīg* "greedy" *waranīgīh* "greediness"

*tuwān* "ability, capability" *tuwānīg* "able, capable" *tuwānīgīh*
"(having) ability, capability"

*tār* "darkness" *tārīk* "dark" *tārīkīh* "darkness"

*nazd* "nearness, vicinity" *nazdīk* "near" *nazdīkīh* "vicintiy"

#### *-āg*

The suffix *-āg* (WkA- \<-'k\'\>) makes agent nouns from verbs:

*dān-* "know" *dānāg* "knowledgeable; a wise man" *dānāgīh* "being
knowledgeable"

*saz-* "fit" *sazāg* "fitting, appropriate" *sazāgīh* "being fitting,
appropriate"

*tuwān-* "be able" *tuwānāg* "mighty" *tuwānāgīh* "might"

*tuxš-* "be diligent, strive" *tuxšāg* "diligent" *tuxšāgīh* "diligence"

#### *-an*

The unproductive suffix *-an* (WW- \<-n\'\>) is found in a few inherited
nouns. It makes nouns from verbs:

*hanǰaman* "assembly" (Av. *haṇjamana-* from *ham-jam-* "come together")

*paymōzan* "garment" (cf. *paymōz-* "don, put on")

*xwaran* "meal, banquet" (cf. *xwar-* "to eat")

*stawan* in *Hōm stawan* "praise of the Hōm" (name of *Yasna* 9-11)

*yazan* "sacrifice" (*Ny*.3.8a, cf. OPers. *ā-yadana* "place of
sacrifice")

### Compounds 1

We have already seen many examples of compounds, that is, words formed
by combining other words, with or without suffixes. Some common types of
compounds are represented by the following:

*harwisp* "all" + *āgāh* "aware"

\> *harwisp-āgāh* "omniscient, all-knowing" \> *harwisp-āgāhīh*
"omniscience"

*rāst* "truthful" + *gōwišn* "speech"

\> *rāst-gōwišn* "of truthful speech, truthful" \> *rāst-gōwišnīh*
"speaking the truth"

*dām* "creation" + *dahišn* "establishing"

\> *dām- dahišn* \> *dām-dahišnīh* "establishment of the creation"

*kār* "work" + *nāmag* "written document"

\> *kār-nāmag* "book of deeds"

*uzdēs* "idol" + *parist-* "to worship"

\> *uzdēs-parist* "idol-worshipper" \> *uzdēs-paristišnīh*
"idol-worship"

\+ *kerd* "made with/from": *zarrēn-kerd* "made from gold, with gold
(thread, etc.)"

\+ *pēsīd* "adorned with": *harwisp-pēsīd* "adorned with every
(adornment)"

*zarrēn-pēsīd* "adorned with (adornments) of gold"

*asēmēn-pēsīd* "adorned with (adornments) of silver"

*gōhr-pēsīd* "adorned with jewels"

Pronouns + words meaning "manner, kind," etc.:

*čē* + *ēwēnag* 'way, manner" *čē-ēwēnag* "what kind of"

*ēdōn* + *čihr* "form, nature" *ēdōn-čihrag* "this form/type of (thing)"

## Grammar 8

### Nouns. The plural ending *-īhā*

The plural ending *-īhā* (aåD- \<-yh'\>) expresses "individual
plurality," e.g., *kōfīhā* "(all) the (individual) mountains." This
plural form takes the plural of the verb, e.g.:

*Spahān ud Pārs ud [kustagīhā]{.underline} ī abārīg*

"Spahān (Isfahan), Pārs, and [the other areas]{.underline}" (*KN*.1.2)

*xrafstar ī parrwar andar [sūrāgīhā]{.underline} ī zamīg šud hēnd*

"the winged evil animals went into [the holes]{.underline} of the earth"
(after *Bd*.6b.7)

*Tištar wārān ō [kišwarīhā]{.underline} wārēd*

"Tištar rains the rain onto [the continents]{.underline}" (after
*Bd*.16.4b)

*[zrēyīhā]{.underline} az wārān ī Tištar būd hēnd*

"[the oceans]{.underline} became (= came into existence) from Tištar's
rain" (after *Bd*.8.2)

*abārīg [kōfīhā]{.underline} az Harburz frāz rust hēnd*

"the other (= remaining) [mountains]{.underline} grew forth from
Harburz" (after *Bd*.9.3a)

*[ēdōn-čihragīhā]{.underline} nē garm nē sard*

"[things of this nature]{.underline} are neither warm nor cold"
(*WZ*.30.21)

### The postposition *rāy*

The postposition *rāy* (äL , áÒ \<l'd\>) plays a very important role in
Pahlavi syntax and has several functions. We have already seen it used
with "to be" to express *possession*. Other examples:

*[Pābag rāy]{.underline} pus-ēw [būd]{.underline} ī abāyišnīg* *[Pābag
rāy]{.underline} ēč frazend nē [būd]{.underline}*

"[Pābag had]{.underline} a nice son" (after *KN*.2.5/1.24) "[Pābag
had]{.underline} no child" (after *KN*.1.5)

Note: pus-ēw \... ī abāyišnīg.

*ud [ōy Wirāz rāy]{.underline} haft xwah [būd]{.underline}* *[amāh haft
xwah rāy]{.underline} brād ēn ēk [ast]{.underline}*

"and [that Wirāz had]{.underline} seven sisters" (*AWN*.2.1) "[we seven
sisters have]{.underline} (only) this one brother" (*AWN*.2.4)

Its other principal functions are:

[*rāy* "for the sake of" and indirect object (instead of
*ō*):]{.underline}

*tan [ruwān rāy]{.underline} bē abespārēd*

"he gives over (gives up) his body [for the sake of (his)
soul]{.underline}" (*MX*.14.25)

*pid ud mād [frazend ī xwēš rāy]{.underline} ēn kār ud kerbag pēš az
panzdah* (*pānzdah*) *sāl bē ē hammōzēnd*

"let the parents teach [their child]{.underline} these works and good
deeds before the age of fifteen (before fifteen years)" (after *PN*.34)

[*rāy* "about, regarding, as for":]{.underline}

*[may rāy]{.underline} paydāg kū kū gōhr ī nēk ud wad pad may pad
paydāgīh šāyēd madan*

"[regarding wine]{.underline}, it is manifest (well known) that (it has
bot) a good and bad essence, (and) by (drinking) wine it can become
manifest" (*MX*.15.20)

*[bāz ī spēd rāy]{.underline} gōwēd kū mār ī pad-parr ōzanēd*

"[about the white falcon]{.underline} it says that it kills the winged
snake" (*Bd*.24j.34)

[*rāy* "on account of, because of":]{.underline}

*harwisp-āgāhīh ī Ohrmazd rāy*

"because of Ohrmazd's omniscience, because Ohrmazd knows/knew all"
(*Bd*.1.9)

Note the following common combinations:

*čē rāy* "for what reason, why?"

*čē čim rāy* "for what reason, why?"

*ēd rāy (*+ *kū)* "for this reason that, so that"

*ēd rāy (*+ *čē)* "for this reason that, because"

*ān čim rāy* "for that"

*ham čim rāy* "for the same reason, for that very reason"

Examples:

*čē rāy mardōmān māh Frawardīn rōz ī Hordad az abārīg rōzīhā pad meh ud
weh ud grāmīgtar dārēnd*

"[why]{.underline} do people hold the day of Hordad (6th day of the
month) in the month of Frawardīh (1st month of the year) to be greater
and better and more dear that the other days?" (*MF*.1)

*mard ī ašō ēn mehīh [čē čim rāy]{.underline} ast*

"[why]{.underline} does the Righteous Man have this greatness?"
(*DD*.3.1)

*gōspand pad ēd hamāg sardag [ēd rāy]{.underline} dād [kū]{.underline}
ka Ganāg Mēnōy ēk bē abesīhēnēd ēk bē mānēd*

"animals were established in all these species, so that, when the Foul
Spirit destroys one, one remains" (after *Bd*.13.30)

*[ēd rāy]{.underline} sag xwānīhēd [čē]{.underline}-š 3 ēk-ēw az
mardōmān*

"[for this reason]{.underline} he it called 'dog', [because]{.underline}
one-third of it is from men" (*Bd*.13.28a)

*[ēd rāy čē]{.underline} duš-āgāh mard duš-āgāhīh ī xwēš pad menišn ēdōn
weh dārēd čiyōn dānāg dānāgīh ī xwēš pad menišn*

"\... [because]{.underline} an ignorant man in his mind regards his
ignorance as so much better, just as the knowledgeable (man regards) his
knowledge in his mind" (*MX*.53.3--4)

*[ān čim rāy]{.underline} ā-m wahišt ud Garōdmān bē dah*

"for that reason give me paradise and Garōdmān!" (*PR*.18f.25)

*[ham čim rāy]{.underline} gōwēnd kū Ohrmazd stārag ī zīndagīh ud Kēwān
stārag ī margīh*

"[for the same reason]{.underline}, they say that Ohrmazd is the star (=
planet) of life an Kēwān the star of death" (*Bd*.5b.13)

### Adjectives. Comparative and superlative

The comparative of adjectives ends in *-tar* (-LT \<-tl\>) and the
superlative in *-tom* (-MWT \<‑twm\>).

In Manichean texts, the suffixes became *-dar* and *-dom* after voiced
consonants, but Persian has the forms with *-t-*, which are used here,
e.g.:

Comparative Superlative

*abēzag* *abēzagtar* *abēzagtom* "pure, purer, purest."

*rēman rēmantar rēmantom* "polluted, more polluted, most polluted"

*xwār* *xwārtar xwārtom* "light, lighter, lightest" (also describing
sins)

*garān garāntar garāntom* "heavy (serious), heavier, heaviest" (also
describing sins)

When the adjective ends in *-t*, sometimes only one \<-t-\> is written,
e.g., *saxt-tar* "harder" spelled \<s'htl\> LtååJ beside \<s'httl\>
LTtååJ, *škefttar* "more violent, more terrible" spelled \<škyptl\>
LTcDkÍ beside \<škypttl\> LTTcDkÍ.

#### Irregular forms.

The following irregular ("suppletive'") comparatives and superlatives
should be noted carefully:

Comparative Superlative

*xūb* WPwA e\>W , lYpÍ *weh* (MwßAP) MwlaÅP *pahlom* (*pāšom*) "good,
better, best"

*wad* LTW , LtådL% , LtdL% *wattar* MWTW , MWtÒtådL% *wattartom*,
*wattom* "bad, worse, worst"

*xwālēn* WwylAwA WtjlAwA , MwlAwA *xwālom*, *xwālist* "sweet, sweetest"

*\
buland* YwLWB (cf. *bālāy* älAB "height") Wt∆dlAV , WtjlAV *bālist*
"high/tall, highest (point)"

*wazurg* g\<LWCW , AbL adM , sM *meh* WtŸja˜ , Wtja˜ , WtjsM *mahist*
"great, greater, greatest"

LtjM *mehtar*, MWtjM *mehtom* "greater, greatest,

Ltja˜ , Ltda˜ *mahītar*, *mahistar* most adult, oldest"

LtåjM *mahādar*, *mehādar* "more adult, older"

*kōdag* WKTWK LtjSK , LtJK , SK *keh*, *kehtar*, *kehisttar* WtjSK
*kahist* "small, smaller, smallest"

*was* YBK ßYW *wēš*, *wēštar* WtjßYW *wēšist* "much, more, most"

1âLP , äLP *frāy* WtŸjâLP , WtjâLP *frayist*, *frāyist* "more, most"

eLP , îÒP (*freh*) (*frahist*)

*garān* Wwa¬Y ¡AlY , älY *grāy* WtŸjâlY *grāyist* "heavier, heaviest"
(sin)

Ltå¬Y, LT1a¬Y, Ltda¬Y *grāytar*, *grātar* "more 'heavier' (sin)"

*dūr* iaÒ LTiaÒ *dūrtar* WtŸjAwY\> *dwayist* "distant, mre/most distant"

Notes:

There is also an adjective *weh* "good" different from *weh* "better,"
which is mainly used in the expression *weh dēn* "the good *dēn*," which
corresponds to Avestan *vaŋvhī daēnā* (the comparative *weh* corresponds
to Avestan *vahiiah*).

We also find comparatives and superlatives such as *pahlomtar* "better,"
*pahlomtom* "best."

*xwālom* is found only (?) in the expression *rāmišn xwālom*, which
renders Av. *rāman x^v^āstrəm* "peace with good pastures."

*mehādar* is also in *ŠGW*.14.40 as an epithet of Abraham. ManParth. has
*masādar*.

The various spellings of *frāy* and *frayist* indicate analogical
leveling. If the forms \<plyh, plhst\'\> are, indeed, for *freh*,
*frahist* \[thus MacKenzie, *Dictionary*\], they were probably changed
in analogy with *keh, meh* - *kahist*, *mahist*.

Note the expressions *pad wēšistīh*, *pad kamistīh* "at (the) most, at
(the) least."

Note that *garān* "heavy" is used in the literal sense, as well as of
sins, referring to the weight of the sin when the soul comes to the
Činwad bridge, where they are weighed. The comparative *grāy* is used to
denote an especially "heavy" sin and has its own comparative "more
*grāy*."

*dwayist* is found in the expression *pad dwayist* "at the most
distance" once (cf. OPers. *duvaištam*, Av. *dbōištəm*):

*čand [pad dwayist]{.underline} ān ī kē āsrō pad āsrō'īh az gēhān bē
rawād*

"how far at the most distant shall he who is a priest go away from the
animals to perform priestly duties?" (*Her*.4.1)

The following expressions characterize the soul going to Paradise. Here
*frāy-* is also sometimes spelled \<pl'-\>:

*frāy-humad frāy-hūxt frāy-huwaršt*

"having (thought) more good thoughts, having (spoken) more good words,
having (performed) more good acts (than bad ones)."

*awināh awināhtar* *awināhtom* "(more/most) free from sin"

*hutōhmag hutōhmagtar* *hutōhmagtom* "of good (better/best) lineage"

*hufrahaxt* *hufrahaxttar* *hufrahaxttom* "well (better/best)-trained"

*abēgumān* *abēgumāntar* *abēgumāntom* "(more/most) free from doubt"
