with Xwarrah"

*tom-arzānīg tom-arzānīgtar* *tom-arzānīgtom* "(more/most) worthy of
darkness"

*dūr-nigerišn* *dūr-nigerišntom* "whose sight (reaches) far/farthest"

*pad-wisp-āgāhīh* *pad-wisp-āgāhīhtar* "having (more)
all-awareness/omniscience"

#### Comparatives and superlatives from adverbs

*frāz* "forward" *frāztar* "more forward, future" *frāztom* "most
forward"

*abar* "above" *abartar* (*-dar*) "higher" *abartom* (*-dom*) "highest"

*azabar* "above" *azabartar* "farther above" *azabartom* "farthest
above"

*azēr* "below" *azērtar* "farther below" *azērtom* "farthest below"

Note: In the inscriptions, we find the form \<pl'stly\> *frāstar*, which
shows that the suffix was *-tar*, not *-dar*.

Note also

*ēw* "one" *ēwtom* MWtdA , MWTwˆÅ \<'ywtwm, HDtwm\> "one and the same,
equally" *bē* "out(side) *bēdom* MWtDV \<bytwm\> "outermost"

*fradom* MWtÒP "first" *abdom* MwYcÅ "final"

*nidar* LtDW "lower" *nidom* MWtDW "lowermost"

### Uses of the comparative: "than"

To express comparisons, "than," the preposition *az* or the conjunction
*kū*, occasionally *čiyōn*, is used, and very rarely *ī*. Note that *az*
is avoided before other prepositions, i.e., we do not find †"*az ō*"
"than to \...," only *kū ō*, *čiyōn ō*. Examples:

*ān mard [az]{.underline} man [meh]{.underline}*

"that man (is) [bigger than]{.underline} I"

*mard-ēw ī pad ān ēwēnag ī čiyōn nibišt abarmānd \... yazišn ī yazdān
[xūbtar]{.underline} rāyēnēd [az]{.underline} awēšān kē-šān abzār ud
hunar ī ōy nēst*

"a man who is excellent in the way that (it is) written (above) \...
conducts the sacrifice(s) to the gods [better than]{.underline} those
who do not have his skill and talent" (*DD*.43.7-8)

*spazgīh [garāntar kū]{.underline} ǰādūgīh*

"slander is a [heavier]{.underline} (sin) [than]{.underline} sorcery"
(*MX*.1.11)

*tan ka murd čē rāy [rēmantar kū]{.underline} ka zīndag*

"when the body is dead why is it [more polluted (and polluting)
than]{.underline} when alive" (*Dk*.5.23.19)

*andar gētīy mardōm kē 100 sāl bē zīyēd [kem kū]{.underline} ān kē 100
sāl nē zīyēd*

"in this world, people/a person who lives a hundred years, (are)
[less]{.underline} (= fewer) [than]{.underline} one who does not live a
hundred years" (*Dk*.9.10)

*u-š [xwaštar]{.underline} sahist ān bōy [čiyōn]{.underline} harwisp bōy
xwaš ī-š pad zīndagān pad wēnīg abar šud*

"and that smell seemed to him [more pleasant than]{.underline} every
pleasant smell that had come to his nose in life" (*AWN*.4.8)

*ān kē yašt nē kerd estēd u-š Itā ud Ašemwohū nē wurrōyēd guftan-iš
[garāntar]{.underline}-iz ast [čiyōn]{.underline} ān kē yašt kerd estēd
u‑š drōn nē wurrōyēd yaštan*

"he who has not performed the ritual, but does not believe in saying the
*iθā* and *aṣ̌əm vohū*, for him it is an even [more 'heavy']{.underline}
(sin) [than]{.underline} for him who has performed the ritual, but does
not believe in performing the *drōn* ritual" (*ŠnŠ*.5.5)

The *iθā āat̰ yazamaidē* "and thus we sacrifice" (*Yasna* 5.1 = 37.1) is
said as grace before meals; the *aṣ̌əm vohū* is a frequently recited
Avestan "prayer."

*ud ōy ī abārōn-dād ī [wēš]{.underline}-wināh [ī]{.underline}-š kerdag
kerbag pad ān kerbag zamānīg rāmišn rasēd*

"and upon the one who followed a depraved law and whose sins are [more
than]{.underline} the good deeds he has done, for those good deeds there
comes instant happiness" (*DD*.12.5)

[With relative pronouns]{.underline}:

*Ardā Wirāz ōwōn būd čiyōn mard-ēw [kē]{.underline} tā pad gētīy būd [az
ōy]{.underline} āsāntar ud xwaštar ud huramtar nē būd*

"Ardā Wirāz was like a man [than whom]{.underline}, while he was in this
world, there was no one more at ease, more pleased, and more cheerful"
(*AWN*.4.6)

##### With *ān ī az* "the one \...-er than":

*ān ī az tō keh* "that one who (is) smaller than you(rself), the one
smaller than you"

##### "The \...-er the better"

*harw čē [zūdtar]{.underline}* "as quickly as possible, the faster the
better" \$\$

### Uses of the superlative

The superlative is used to express 1. a high degree of something; 2. the
most oustanding of a group (+ possessive) or among (+ *az*) others,
e.g.:

*az nēmag ī dēwān bē āmad [gandagtom]{.underline} wād*

"from the direction of the demons came the [foulest]{.underline} wind"
(after *AWN*.17.8)

*kē yazdān [mahist]{.underline} ud kē mardān [pahlom]{.underline}*

"who is the [greatest]{.underline} of gods, and who is the
[best]{.underline} of/among men?"

*Ohrmazd az mēnōyān [abzōnīgtom]{.underline}*

"Ohrmazd, the [most life-giving]{.underline} (Av. *spəṇta*) of/among
beings in the world of thought" (*AWN*.101.7)

*man ēg andar ān ī amāh deh az mardōmān pad ǰādūgīh
[dūr-nigerišntom]{.underline}*

"then, on account of my sorcery, of/among the people in our village I am
the one [who sees the farthest]{.underline}" (*Dk*.7.3.21)

##### With *ān ī* and *ān ī az* "the most X (of)":

*čiyōn [ān ī bazzag-ēwēntom]{.underline} xrafstar ī rēmantom ī
gandagtom*

"like the evil animal [having the worst habits]{.underline}, the
filthiest, and the foulest" (*AWN*.17.9)

*kadār ast weh kadār wehtar ud kadār az harwispīn pahlom [ān
ī]{.underline} az harwispīn [pahlom]{.underline}*

"what is good, what is bettter, and what is [the best]{.underline} of
all" (*WZ*.22.3)

*dēn 7 parisp ast u-šān [ān ī bēdom]{.underline} Mānsr ud zand guft*

"the *dēn* has 7 enclosing walls, and [the outermost]{.underline} of
them is the sacred word and the *zand* (Pahlavi Avesta)" (*Dk*.6.215)

The adverb *pēš* 'before" is construed as a comparative, usually *pēš
az* or *pēš \... az*, but occasionally with *čiyōn*:

*pad kadār pēš azmāyišn pad mazdēsnān dēwēsnān*

*pad dēwēsnān [pēš]{.underline} ē azmāyānd [čiyōn]{.underline} pad
mazdēsnān*

"on which (of the two)---Mazdayasnians or worshippers of *dēw*s should
they experiment first?

Let them experiment on worshippers of *dēw*s [before]{.underline} on
Mazdayasnians!" (PV.7.37; about how to become a doctor)

-WwABkÍ \<ŠKBHWN-\> *nibay- nibast* "lie (down)"

-WtjÍ \<ŠDYTN-\> *wih*- *wist* "shoot (arrow)"

(-mAk) -WNBcD \<YCBEN-; k'm-\> *kām- kāmist* "wish" (impersonal)

### The verb: The Perfect

The present and past perfect are formed with the present and past of the
auxiliary *estādan est-*, e.g., -WnYWI WTWwlZW *šud est-* \<OZLWNt\'
YKOYMWN-\> "have gone":

##### The present perfect:

Singular Plural

1st *šud estam* MWnYWI WTWwlZW 1st *šud estēm* µYWnYWI WTWwlZW

2nd *šud estē* ìWnYWI WTWwlZW 2nd *šud estēd* WtDWnYWI WTWwlZW

3rd *šud estēd* WtDWnYWI WTWwlZW 3rd *šud estēnd* Y\>WnYWI WTWwlZW

##### The past perfect:

Singular Plural

1st *šud estād ham* MNwA WtÅWnYWI WTWwlZW 1st *šud estād hēm* µYNwA
WtÅWnYWI WTWlZW

2nd *šud estād hē* ìNwA WtÅWnYWI WTWwlZW 2nd *šud estād hēd* WtDNwA
WtÅWnYWI WTWwlZW

3rd *šud estād* WtÅWnYWI WTWwlZW 3rd *šud estād hēnd* Y\>NwA WtÅWnYWI
WTWwlZW

Note: A "doubly" characterized past perfect is occasionally found, e.g.,
*mad estād būd* "had come" (*AWN*.89.4).

The original meaning of this tense was [state resulting from previous
action or other event]{.underline}, e.g., *ēdōn nibišt estēd* "it is
written thus," with empasis on the [actual presence]{.underline} of
writing, not on the fact that it was written at some specific moment in
the past. Thus, *šud estēd* also means "he has gone," but with the
implication that "he is now away," as in English "he is gone."

When the main verb is [transitive]{.underline}, the perfect is
[passive]{.underline}. Examples:

*čiyōn gurd ī artēštār kē zrēy [paymōxt estēd]{.underline}*

"like a warrior (*artēštār*) hero (*gurd*) who [is dressed]{.underline}
in armor" (*Bd*.1a.7b)

*spāh homānāg kē ō kārēzār [baxt estēd]{.underline}*

"like an army that (has been and now) [is]{.underline}
[partitioned]{.underline} (distributed) for battle" (after *Bd*.2.3)

*pad kār-nāmag ī Ardaxšīr ī Pābagān ēdōn [nibišt estēd]{.underline}*

"in the book of deeds of Ardaxšīr son of Pābag [it is
written]{.underline} as follows" (*KN*.1.1)

*Ardawān andar kōšk [xuft estād]{.underline}*

"Ardawan (had gone to sleep and) [was lying asleep]{.underline} in a
pavilion" (after *KN*.3.14/2.13)

*Sāsān pad pīl-ēw ī ārāstag ī spēd [nišast estād]{.underline}*

"Sasan [was seated]{.underline} on a white, adorned, elephant"
(*KN*.1.9/1.10)

*ān hōm pad ān wan abar [rust estād]{.underline}*

"that *hōm* (had grown and) [was]{.underline} (now fully)
[grown]{.underline} on (*pad \... abar*) that tree" *Dk*.7.2.30)

4\. Translate into Pahlavi and write in Pahlavi at least sentences 1, 3,
5, 7, 9:

1.  In heaven the souls of the Righteous are unaging, undying, free from
    fear, and free from the Adversary.

2.  By his ability, diligence, knowledge, and wisdom, a good ruler keeps
    his land in peace and happiness.

3.  When the Roman army came against the land of Iran, it was greatly
    smitten, and many Romans died.

4.  When Tištar rains the rain on the (various) continents, the
    (various) oceans all become (= come into existence).

5.  About the dog they say that it came from the star-level from the
    direction of the star Ursa Major.

6.  The most happy among men is he whose wife is the best among women.

7.  (He) who gives less to the poor than to the rich, his sin is more
    than that of him who kills his own son.

8.  Because of your wish and action, I, who am your Dēn, am so (much)
    better and more sweet-smelling and more victorious and more free
    from harm as you see me.

9.  Ardawān had four sons: two were with their father and two had fled
    to Babylon (and were now there).

10. That evil which we see in Babylon, has all been done by the sin(s)
    of the Babylonians.

# Additional readings 8

## Additional reading 8.1

From the Pahlavi *Videvdad*: *PV*.3.15-17.

The \[\...\] indicates glosses added to the Pahlavi translations of the
Avestan text.

*pursišn. dādār ī gēhān ī astōmand ahlaw kū ōy mard gāh ī rist-keš.*

*passox. kē hēnd pad ēn zamīg ǰud-ābtom ǰud-urwartom yōǰdahr-zamīgtom az
hixr hušk-zamīgtom kū nam pad ān nēst*

*kamist-iz pad awēšān rāh franāmēnd pah ud stōr ātaxš-iz ī ohrmazd ud
barsom-iz ī pad ahlāyīh frāz wistard mard-iz ī ahlaw*

Q. O Righteous creator of the bony world of the living! Where is there a
(final resting) place for the man who is a carrier of the dead?

A. (The places) that are, on this earth, the most devoid of water, the
most devoid of plants, where the earth is the most (ritually) clean
(i.e.) from bodily secretions, where the earth is the driest (i.e.,)
there is no humidity on it,

and (where) they go forth the least on their paths, small and large
domestic animals and the fire of Ohrmazd and the *barsom* spread out in
proper fashion and Righteous men.

*dādār ī gēhān astōmandān ahlaw čand drahnāy az ātaxš čand drahnāy az āb
čand drahnāy az barsom pad ahlāyīh frāz wistard čand drahnāy az mard ī
ahlaw*

*30 gām az ātaxš ud 30 gām az āb ud 30 gām az barsom pad ahlāyīh frāz
wistard ud 3 gām az mardān ī ahlawān*

Q. O Righteous creator of the bony world of the living! How much
distance from the fire, how much from the water, how much from the
*barsom* spread out in proper fashion, and how much from the Righteous
man.

A. Thirty steps from the fire, thirty steps from the water, thirty steps
from the *barsom* spread out in proper fashion, and three steps from
Righteous men.

## Additional reading 8.2

From the *Ardā Wirāz-nāmag*: *AWN*.4.7-9. -- The conjunction *kū* "i.e."
introduces exegetical explanations ("i.e.").

*pad ōšībām ī sidīgar ōy ruwān ī ahlawān andar urwar ud bōy ī xwaš bē
wašt*

*u-š xwaštar sahist ān bōy čiyōn harwisp bōy ī xwaš ī-š pad zīndagān pad
wēnīg abar šud; ud ān bōy wād az rabihwintar rōn az nēmag ī yazdān bē
āyēd*

*u-š ān ī xwēš dēn ud ān ī xwēš kunišn ō padīrag āmad pad kanīg kerb ī
nēk pad dīdan ī hurust [kū]{.underline} pad frārōnīh rust estād
frāz-pestān [kū]{.underline}-š pestān abāz nišast ī dil ud gyān dōst
kē-š kerb ēdōn rōšn čiyōn pad dīdan hudōšagtar pad nigerišn
abāyišnīgtar*

At the third dawn, the soul of the Righteous wandered among nice
fragrent herbs.

And it seemed nicer to him that all the nice fragrance that had come to
his nose in life.

And the breeze of that fragrence is coming from the southern direction,
from the direction of the gods.

And his own *dēn* and his own deeds came toward him in a maiden's form,
beautiful to see, well-grown, i.e., she had grown up in goodness, with
forward bosom, i.e., her bosom sat well\[?\], and a friend to heart and
soul,

(a maiden) whose (*kē-š*) form was as bright as to be most pleasant to
see, most attractive to look at.

## Additional reading 8.3

From the *Ardā Wirāz-nāmag* 9.1-4

*ka sidīgar gām frāz niham pad huwaršt ānōh kū huwaršt pad mehmānīh ō
ānōh rasēm*

*rōšnīh ī bālistān bālist xwānēnd*

*ud wēnam ān ī ahlaw pad gāh ud wistarg ī zarrēn-kerd*

*ud mardōm būd hēnd kē-šān rōšnīh ō rōšnīh ī xwaršēd homānāg būd*

*pursēm az Srōš-ahlīy ud Ādur yazd kū ēn gyāg kadām ud ōy ruwān kē hēnd*

*gōwēd Srōš-ahlīy ud Ādur yazd kū ēn gyāg xwaršēd-pāyag*

*ud ōy ruwān hēnd kē pad gētīy hupādixšāy būd hēnd*.

When I take the third step in Good Deeds, we come to where Good Deeds
abide.

They call it the light of the highest of heights.

And I see the Righteous on couches and carpets made from gold.

And they were people whose (*kē-šān*) light was similar to the sun's
light.

I ask Srōš-ahlīy and the divine Fire: Which is this place, and who are
those souls?

Srōš-ahlīy and the divine Fire say: This place is the sun-level.

And those souls are (those) who were good rulers in this world.

# Glossary of words in the Texts and Exercises 8

[Idioms]{.underline}

*abāz dār-* (*dāšt*) hold back, keep back

*andar kun-* place, apply; + *andar* "into, onto"

*ast ī \... ast ī* one \... another, some \... others (Lesson 14)

*bē est-* stand (still)

*handāzag ī* like, similar to

*ō \... estād* turned to

*pad \... dār-* regard as \...

*pad \... nih-* establish as \...

*rāy ud xwarrah* expression taken from Avestan *ahe raiia xvarənaŋhaca*
"by his wealth and Xwarrah"; reinterpreted to mean something like
"luminosity and Xwarrah"; the Persian translations of the Avesta have
*nur o xorah* "Light and Xwarrah"; in the Pahlavi tradition this *rāy*
is understood as *tuxšāgīh* "diligence"

####  "Enclitic" numerals

The numeral "one" is regularly enclitic to its noun: 1- \<-1\> or Ä
\<-HD\> = *ēw*.

The numeral "two" is occasionally enclitic, e.g., 1ï¬AK \<k'l-2\> = *kār
dō* (*Dk*.5.24.16b, ms. DH 264v21), 1ïÅWK \<KRA-2\> *harw dō* (*PN*.41,
ms. MK f. 44v).

#### Derivatives in *-(g)ānag* "-fold"

These are often spelled as numerals with the ending \<-'nk\', -k'nk\'\>
*-gānag*, e.g.:

*ēkānag* (*ēgānag*) "single, identical"; also "submissive"

*dōgānag* \<dwk'nk\'\> "double, twins"

*segānag* \<3'nk\', sk'nk\'\> "triple, triplets"

*sadgānag ud hazārgānag* "a hundred-fold and a thousand-fold, by
hundreds and thousands"

Note also *hazāragīhā* "by thousands."

#### Fractions and percentages, multiplication

One "half" is *nēm* \<PRG, nym-\>.

Fractions are of the type *sē-ēk*, e.g.: *sē-ēk-ēw* ÄWwˆÅ3 \<3
'ywk\'-HD\> "one-third," *sē-ēk ī rōz* "one-third of the day."

*ka-š dēg abar nihēnd āb ud gōšt ēdōn abāyēd kerdan ī-š [pad
3-2]{.underline} andar bawēd*

"when one places a pot on it (the fire), one must put in water and meat
in such a manner that it is in it [at two-thirds]{.underline}"
(*PR*.37a.6)

*[pad 100 pad 1000 pad bēwar ēk-ēw]{.underline} bawēd kē pad ēn dēn
wurrōyēd*

"there will be (only) one [in a hundred, in a thousand, in ten
thousand]{.underline}, who believes in this *dēn*" (*ZWY*.4.31)

Percentage and multiplication are expressed by expressions with *bahr*
"part, share," e.g.:

*(az) ān-iz ī didīgar drōw-gōwišnīh dēwān ōz abar mad. u-šān mizag ī
xwarišn bē duzzīd ōwōn kū az [100 bahr ēw bahr]{.underline} mānd*

"and (by) the second lie, strength came to the *dēw*s, and they stole
\[ergativve, Lesson 14\] the taste of the food so that only 1% remained"
(*Bd*.14.20)

*ēk bahr ēk ēk 2 bahr 2 4* "1\*1 = 1, 2\*2 = 4"

*būd bawēd zamān-ēw ayāb gyāg-ēw kū [2 bahr 2 5]{.underline} ayāb
[3]{.underline} gōwīhēd*

"there may have been or is a time or place where [2\*2]{.underline} is
said to [= 5 or 3]{.underline}" (*ŠGW*.5.12, 14)

#### "Twice as," etc.

## Word formation 3. Prefixes and suffixes 3

#### *ham-* \~ *ǰud-*

Adjectives formed from nouns by means of the prefixes *ham-* (-ÂA
\<hm-\>) and *ǰud-* (-WtDwY \<ywyt\'-\>) mean "being of the same \...,"
"being of different/opposite \..." Nouns in *-īh* are common, e.g.:

*ham-dādestān* "agreed" *ǰud-dādestān* "disagreeing"

*ham-dādestānīh* "agreement" *ǰud-dādestānīh* "disagreement"

*ham-dēn* "having the same religion" *ǰud-dēn* "having a different (the
opposite) religion"

*ham-paywand* "relative"

*ham-kār* "collaborator"

*ǰud-kēš* "having different teachings"

*ǰud-wurrōyišn* "having a different belief"

*ǰud-ristag* "having different ways," *ǰud-ristagīh* "heresy"

In some words, *ǰud* has the meaning "keeping away" (for Avestan *vī-*),
e.g.:

*bēš* "harm" *ǰud-bēš* "keeping harm away" (Av. *vībaēša*)

*dēw* "demon" *ǰud-dēw* "keeping the demons away" (Av. *vīdaēuua*)

#### *hām-*

This prefix indicates totality, e.g.:

*kišwar* "land, continent" *hām-kišwar* "(in) the whole land

*Xwanīrah* "(the continent of) Xwanīrah *hām- Xwanīrah* "(in) the whole
continent of Xwanīrah

*šab* "night" *hām-šab* "the whole night"

*gēhān* "world" *hām-gēhān* "(in) the whole world"

#### *-ān*, *-agān*

These two suffixes **(WwAk- \<-k'n\'), WwaD- \<-g'n\'\>)** are used to
form adjectives meaning "son of":

*Ardašīr* *Ardašīrān* "son of Ardašīr"

*Pābag* *Pābagān* "son of Pābag"

*Šābuhr* *Šābuhragān* "son of Šābuhr"

The suffix *-ān* can also form "possessive" adjectives of names, e.g.:

*Isadwāstar* *hanǰaman ī Isadwāstarān* "the assembly of Isadwāstar"

*Zarēr* *kēn ī Zarērān* "revenge for Zarēr"; *ayādgār ī Zarērān* "the
Memorial of Zarēr"

*Wištāsp* *razm ī Wištāspān* "the battle fought by Wištāsp"

*Frāsyāb* *ǰādūgīh ī Frāsyābān* "the sorcery of Frāsyāb"

The suffix *-agān* is found also elsewhere, e.g.:

*Ādurbādagān* Azerbaijan

*āfrīnagān* name of a ceremony

*wāspuhragān* "in particular"

#### *-ēn*

Adjectives designating material and similar are formed from nouns by
means of the suffix *-ēn* ( WwY- \<-yn\'\>):

*zarr* "gold" *zarrēn* "of gold, golden"

*āhen* "iron" *āhenēn* "of iron"

*dār* "tree, wood" *dārēn* "of wood"

#### *-ōmand*

Adjectives meaning (things) "full of \..." are formed from nouns by
means of various suffixes, most commonly *‑ōmand* (YwMwA- \<-'wmnd\>).
Note that this suffix is spelled with initial \<'-\> as if a separate
word:

*ast* "bone" *astōmand* "having bones, bony" *astōmandīh* "fact of
having bones"

*ōz* "strength" *ōzōmand* "strong" *ōzōmandīh* "strength"

*xwarrah* "xwarrah" *xwarrahōmand* "full of Xwarrah" *xwarrahōmandīh*
"being full of Xwarrah"

*rāmišn* "joy" *rāmišnōmand* "full of joy" *rāmišnōmandīh* "joyfulness"

*sar* "head, beginning" *sarōmand* "having a beginning" contrast *asar*
"having no beginning"

*bīm* "fear" *bīmōmand* "fearful" contrast *abīm*, *abēbīm* "without
fear"

*kāmag* "will, wish" *kāmagōmand* "willing" contrast *akāmag*
"unwilling"

*dādestān* "law" *dādestānōmand* "law-abiding" contrast *adādestān* "not
law-abiding""

#### *-āwand* (*-āwend*) ( YwA- \<-'wnd\>)

This is an older version of *-ōmand* that survives in a few words, e.g.:

(Av. *ama-* "power") *amāwand* "powerful" *amāwandīh* "power"

*hunar* "skill, artistry" *hunarāwand* "skillful, artful" *hunarāwandīh*
"skill, artfulness"

*pādyāwand* "strong" *pādyāwandīh* "strength"

*xwēš* "(one's) own" *xwēšāwand* "a relative"

*zēnāwand* "vigilant" *zēnāwandīh* "vigilance"

(*dumb* "tail") *Dambāwand*, *Dumbāwand*, name of a mountain

#### *-gen*

This rare suffix (WWK-, WwYK- \<-kn\', -kyn\'\>; WwY\<-, WwS\<- \<-gn\',
-gyn\'\>) has a function similar to that of -*ōmand*. In New Persian, it
is *-gīn* \< \**-gēn*, but the Pahlavi spellings indicate a short vowel,
e.g.:

*andōh* "sorrow" *andōhgen* "sorrowful"

*bīm* "fear" *bīmgen* "scary" cf. *bīmōmand* "fearful"

*rēš* "wound, harm" *rēšken* "harmful"

*sahm* "terror" *sahmgen* "terrible, fierce"

*xešm* "anger" *xešmgen* "angry, quick to anger" (NP. *xašmgīn*)

*nam* "moisture, dew" *namgen* "moist" (NP. *namgīn*)

## Grammar 9

### "Other," "the others," "one \... another"

We have seen numerous examples of the use of *abārīg* (WIwAcÅ
\<'p̄'ryk\'\>) "*the* other(s)," that is, those that remain of a group or
class of objects after one part has been removed.

For "other(s)," i.e., something or someone different from something or
someone already mentioned, the word *anīy* WwaÅ \<AHRN is used. The word
is also frequently spelled Ä˝¸ \<ZK[ydy]{.underline}\>, which is
abbreviated to G˝¸ \<ZKḏ\>, ˝¸ \<ZK\> in less careful manuscripts:

WwAWwaÅ , WwaÅ \<AHRN, AHRN'n\'\> *anīy*, *anyān* "other, another,
others"

WwAcDWwaÅ , cDWwaÅ \<AHRNyc, AHRNyc'n\'\> *anīz*, *anīzān* "another,
too; others, too"

(Y˝¸) Ä˝¸ \<ZK[ydy]{.underline}\> *anīy* "other, another, others"

WwA˝¸ , WwaD˝¸ \<ZKy'n\', ZK'n\'\> *anyān* "the other(s)"

MWTÄ˝¸ \< ZK[ydy]{.underline}-twm\> *anītwm* "most others" (?)

Nir.65.1 has the plural form WwAIWwaÅ \< AHRNyk'n\'\>, perhaps for
*anīyān*.

Examples:

*abāg anīy mard xuft*

"she slept with [another]{.underline} man" (*AWN*.69.5)

*az frazendān (ī) Ēriǰ bē kanīg-ēw [anīy kas]{.underline} bē nē mānd*

"of the children of Ēriǰ [nobody]{.underline} but (*bē*) a young woman
remained" (*PT*.3.6)

*az 7 frazend ī Mihrōg bē man tā [anīy kas]{.underline} [nē]{.underline}
mānd estēd*

"of Mihrōg's seven children [nobody else]{.underline} but me (*bē man
tā*) is left" (*KN*.13.21/12.21)

*Wāy ī abarkār tarwēnīdārtom az [anyān]{.underline} dāmān*

"Wāy of lofty work is the one among the [other]{.underline} creations
who overcomes (evil) the most" (*PY*.0.9 etc.)

*[anīz]{.underline} was šahr ud šahrestānīhā ud mānīhā kerd hēnd*

"many [other]{.underline} lands, cities, and houses were made,
[too]{.underline}" (after *Bd*.32.9)

*ān ī pad xwēš nē nēk pad [anīzān]{.underline} nē kerdan*

"not to do to [others]{.underline} that which is not good for one's own"
(*Dk*.5.19.12)

##### *anītom* "most others" (?)

Noticed only once:

*anītom ka ōh gumānīg awēšān abēgumān hēnd ka bāzāy*

"most others, when (they are) doubtful in the usual way, have no doubt
when (a ritual fault is a sin worth) 'an arm'" (*Nir*.19.11e) -- "most
others" = "most other priests" or "in most other cases"

##### *anīy \... anīy* "one \... another, (the) one \... the other":

*ēg ān rahīy 2 rahīy būd mēnōy [anīy]{.underline} ud gētīy
[anīy]{.underline}*

"then that chariot became two chariots, [one]{.underline} in the other
world, [the other]{.underline} in this world" (*Dk*.7.6.11)

*ēdōn tō ātaxš \... ān wazr bar pad mēnōy hād abzār-it-ēw ī čiyōn ān
daham kē pad ān harwisp ox ī astōmand bē wardē ō ān ī asar rōšnīh ān
[anīy]{.underline} ud ō ān ī asar tārīkīh [anīy]{.underline}*

"thus, Fire, carry that cudgel in the other world, that is (*hād*), I
shall give you a tool like that, by which (*kē \... pad ān* "which by
that") you shall turn the entire bony existence: [the ones]{.underline}
to the eternal lights, [the others]{.underline} to the eternal darkness"
(*Dk.*9.11.12)

##### *ēw \... anīy* "one \... another, this and that":

*xwarišn kē zan ī daštān hu-frayād bawēd ēg-iš dādestān čē \... pad
adwadād [ēw saxwan ud anīy saxwan]{.underline} pad-iš*

"what is the legal position regarding the food that is beneficial to a
menstruant women? \... regarding 'unlawful abandonment' (*adwadād*) ---
there is [this and that word]{.underline} about it" (*ZFJ*.579)

##### *ēk-ēw \... ēk-ēw* "one \... one (= another)":

***amahrspandān \... hamē-zīndagān ud hamē-sūdān** [ēk-ēw]{.underline}
kū bē nē mīrēnd [ēk-ēw]{.underline} kū ōzad nē šāyēnd*

"'to the *amahrspand*s \... ever-living, ever-benefiting',
[one]{.underline} (reason) is this: they do not die;
[another]{.underline} is this: they can not be killed" (*PY*.4.4)

## The verb

### 

### The Symbols \<x1\> and \<x2\>.

In arameograms, instead of the usual 3rd person singular and plural
endings \<-yt\'\> and \<-d\>, two symbols are often used, now commonly
transcribed as \<x~1~\> and \<x~2~\>.

While \<x~1~\> has only the form x (or x\>), \<-x~2~\> has several
forms, the simplest being 9 or ¼, \~., and extended by \<y\> or \<d\>: þ
, Þ ; ž ,Ž. Instead of 9 (= Avestan *ą̇*) many manuscripts also use (, )
(= Avestan *ą*).

\<x~1~\> is used in the 3rd sing., while \<x~2~\> is used for the 3rd
plur., the past stem, or the infinitive.

In some manuscripts, \<-x~2~\> is also, very occasionally, used for the
2nd singular present indicative and imperative. A very few scribes
hardly use the symbols at all.

These symbols are used with arameograms that originally contained a
\<B\>, which was then spelled as \<Y\> (or \<‑Z-\>.

In some verbs, especially \<O[BY]{.underline}DWN-\>, the original
\<-B-\> has left a trace of its presence in a 'subscript hook' used by
some scribes under certain endings, e.g., æ- \<-m̨\>, tˇD- \<-yt̨\>, or
elsewhere.

Some common verbs of this type are:

-W\]ÇD \<[DB]{.underline}LWN-\> *nay- nīd* "lead" (inscr. nwwBd, nwlBd
\<DBRWN-, DBLWN-\>)

-WwlYKM, -WwlY\>KM \<MK[B]{.underline}LWN-\> *padīr-* *padīrift*
"receive" (inscr. nwlBkm)

-WwïΩM \<MZ[B]{.underline}NN-\> *frōš- frōxt* "sell"

-WwïÅW, -Wwï\>ÅW \<O[BY]{.underline}DWN-\> *kun- kerd* "do" (inscr.
nwdyBw)

(but not -WwïÅW, -Wwï\>ÅW \<OHDWN-\> *gīr- grift* "take"(!), inscr.
nwdhw)

-WWkˆH \<Š[B]{.underline}KWN‑\> *hil- hišt* "let, leave" (inscr. nwkBπ)

-W\]∂\>D\> , -W\]J \<Y[B]{.underline}LWN-\> *bar- burd* "carry" (but not
when with \<-B-\>: -WwLvY \<YBLWN-\>; inscr. nwlBy, Ps. NwlbY)

-WwïJwY \<YNS[B]{.underline}WN-\> *stān- stad* "take" (inscr. nwBsny)

-Wwï¸ \<Z[B]{.underline}NN‑\> *xrīn- xrīd* "buy"

#### The Turfan fragment

[Note: the students are not expected to learn what is in the section on
the Turfan fragment.]{.underline}

A single leaf from a manuscript containing a list of verbal arameograms
was found at Turfan. This is the oldest Pahlavi manuscript in existence.
The verbs are (on the left) \<HYTYWN-\> "fetch," \<YHSNN-\> "have,
hold," \<OZLWN‑\> "go," \<Y[B]{.underline}LWN-, YBLWN-\> "carry," (on
the right) \<D[B]{.underline}LWN-\> "lead," \<YNPKWN-\> "exit,"
\<HŠKHWN-\> "find."

The leaf was published by Kaj Barr in the *Bulletin of the School of
Oriental Studies* (*BSOS*) 8, 1936, pp. 391-40.

##### Origins of the symbols:

Since these symbols are used almost exclusively with arameograms that
contain an original \<-B-\>, it is not impossible that they originated
from the intersection of the "foot" of the \<B\> B with the endings at
some stage of the script (cf. inscr., nyB \<[BYN]{.underline}\> = x =
x~1~\>), and the two forms, when used for the 3rd singular (2nd plural)
and the 3rd plural, can conceivably be derived from \<‑yt\> and
\<-ynd\>, respectively, cf.:

*Psalms*: tYNWdYVW \<OBYDWNyt\> ⇾ xWwïdAW

*Psalms*: DNWdYVW \<OBYDWNd\> ⇾ žWwïdAW ,ŽWwïdAW

The Turfan ms., however, suggests the story may be more complicated, as
it features three different forms, two of which are also common in
economic documents on papyrus and leather.

Here, the three symbols are seen on the right: \<x~1~\> at the end of
line 3 (3rd sing.), \<x~2~\> at the beginning of line 3 (3rd plur.), and
x~3~ in the middle of line 6 (infinitive).

In the Turfan fragment, the oversized \<-t\> used at the end of lines

probably just a flourish, found also in the manuscripts, for instance,
final Æ is not uncommon in J2 and K5 and is very common in K20.

### The Passive

Originally, in Iranian languages, the passive was only used in sentences
in which the person or thing performing an action was not mentioned
specifically. That is, there were only constructions of the type "he is
being eaten," but [not]{.underline} "he is being eaten *by* a lion." In
this way, active constructions were reserved for sentences in which the
"performer" ("agent") was explicitly mentioned, e.g., "*Ahura Mazdā*
establishes the world," "*the soul* sees its *dēn*," "*they* think good
thoughts."

By the time of Pahlavi, this rule had been relaxed, and we find
constructions such as "he is led away by the demons." We will return to
these constructions later. Here, examples are given only of those
without "performer."

On the passive formation in *-īh-*, see Lesson 15.

#### Passive without "performer" with "to be/become."

A so-called "analytic" passive is formed with *būdan* "to be/become,"
e.g.:

*guft bawēd kū* "it is said that \..."

*abar amāh stahm-ēw abēčim [kerd bawēd]{.underline}*

"for no reason violence [will be done]{.underline} to us" (*AWN*.2.6)

*ka xrafstar ōzanēnd ahrimen [bēšīd bawēd]{.underline} čē xrafstar hamāg
az tan ī ahrimen*

"when one kills evil animals, Ahrimen [is (will be) hurt]{.underline},
because evil animals are all from Ahrimen's body" (after PT.28. *Handarz
ī Dastwarān ō Weh-Dēnān* 29)

*mard-ēw kē duxt-ēw ī purnāy pad zanīh bē ō mard-ēw dahēd duxt nē
ham-dādestān sālārīh bē ōy [dād bawēd]{.underline} ayāb nē*

"a man who gives a daughter (who has come) of age as wife to a man (but)
the daughter does not agree, (then) [is]{.underline} guardianship
[given]{.underline} ([has it]{.underline} thereby [been
given]{.underline}) to him or not?" (*RAF*.10.1)

*az bīmīhā ān ēk bīm rāy [dād]{.underline} šāyēd [būd]{.underline} (ī)
az bīm ī dōšox rāy ō arzānīgān tis dahēd*

"among the various fears, it can [be given]{.underline} for that one
fear: he who, for fear of hell, gives something to those worthy"
(*RAF*.74.3)

*drōw az tan bērōn kun u-t tan [wirāst]{.underline} ud ruwān [bōxt
bawēd]{.underline}*

"expel lies from (your) body, and your body [will be
restored]{.underline} and your soul [will be saved]{.underline}"
(*Dk*.3.56.2)

#### Past transitive verbs without "performer" as passive.

When a past [transitive]{.underline} verb is used [without a
"performer,"]{.underline} it is passive, e.g.:

*ēn ān mard ī-š pus andar kārēzār [ōzad]{.underline}*

"this (is) that man whose *(ī-š* "who his") son [was killed]{.underline}
in the battle"

*šusr ī gāw abar ō māh-pāyag [burd]{.underline} ānōh bē [pālūd
hēnd]{.underline}. ud az ān šusr gōspand ī purr-sardag [frāz
brēhēnīd]{.underline}*

"the bull's semen [was brought]{.underline} to the moon-level (and)
there it [was purified]{.underline} \[*note plural*\]; and from that
semen the animal of many-species [was fashioned forth]{.underline}"
(*Bd*.13.4)

*an pādixšāy [kerd ham]{.underline}*

"[I was made]{.underline} authoritative (was placed in charge)" (Kerdīr)

*hamāg mardōm ō dar ī ādur Farrbay [xwānd hēnd]{.underline}*

"all people [were called]{.underline} to the house of the Farrbay fire"
(*AWN*.1.16)

#### 

#### The 3rd plural expressing indefinite subject ("one")

When the "performer" is unknown, one can also use an indefinite 3rd
plural: "they say" = "it is said," "they killed him" = he was killed,"
e.g.:

*gōwēnd kū* "they say, it is said"

*ud az tan ī Gayōmard rōšnīh ōwōn bē šud čiyōn āhen ī garm ī suxr ka-š
pōlābd abar [zanēnd]{.underline} ud syā bē bawēd*

"and from Gayōmard's body light went out as (when) [they
strike]{.underline} steel on a redhot iron and it becomes black"
(*Bd*.7.11)

*kas pad wēmārīh nē mīrēd bē pad zarmānīh ayāb [ōzanēnd]{.underline}*

"no one will die from illness, other than from old age or (if) [they
kill]{.underline} them (= [they are killed]{.underline})" (*Bd*.33.37)

*ka-š ǰud az hunsandīh ī sālārān [frēbēnd ud nayēnd]{.underline}*

"when [they deceive]{.underline} her and [lead]{.underline} her (away)
without the pleasure (of the husband) (= when she = the wife [is
deceived and led]{.underline} away)" (*MHD*.30.2)

[Note the combination of intransitive + indefinite verb:]{.underline}

*harw čē abēzag ō Garōdmān šawēd ud harw čē druwand ō dōšox
[abganēnd]{.underline}*

"everything that is pure goes to Garōdmān, and everything that is wicked
[they throw]{.underline} (= is thrown) into hell" (*Bd*.28.10)

### Impersonal expressions

Impersonal expressions are sentences without grammatical subjects
(English "it is necessary, it is possible, etc.). Most impersonal
expressions involve a [3rd singular verb]{.underline} or a
[noun]{.underline} or an [adjective]{.underline} (*tuwān*, etc.).

The person it is necessary, etc., *for* can be expressed by a noun, an
independent pronoun, or an enclitic pronoun.

Plural nouns take the ending *-ān*.

When the person is expressed by a relative pronoun (*kē*), an enclitic
pronoun can be added to clarify the person.

Impersonal expressions include:

*abāyēd*, *abāyist* "it behoves/behoved X (to), X should, must"

*kāmed*, *kāmist* "wants, wishes"

*sahēd*, *sahist* "seem (to \...), seem (OK to \...)"

*šāyēd*, *šāyist* "be appropriate; be possible (for X to do)"

*wurrōyēd, wurrōyist* "believe"

*wizīrēd* "it is avoidable"

*awizīrišnīg* "unavoidable, doing without (*az*)."

*tuwān* "it (is/was) possible (for)"

Impersonal expressions are often combined with an infinitive (see Lesson
10).

In the English translation, the impersonal expression must often be
turned into a personal one.

Note that *pādixšāy* "authorized" (often used in the same kind of
contexts as *šāyēd*) is a normal adjective.

Note also that the past stems *abāyist* and *šāyist* are frequently
written as if "*abāyīd*" and "*šāyīd*," but this is probably a special
way of spelling *-āyist* (see Lesson 5).

Examples:

*čand-[itān]{.underline} [tuwān]{.underline} pad kerbag kerdan tuxšāg
bawēd*

"as much as [it is possible for you]{.underline} (= you can), be
diligent in performing good deeds!"

*ān mard u-[m]{.underline} and [sahist]{.underline} čand 3 mard
nēzag-bālāy*

"that man [seemed]{.underline} [to me]{.underline} as large as three men
the height of a spear" (after *Dk*.7.3.52)

*ka-š zan ud xwāstag ī-[š]{.underline} abāyišnīg [sahist]{.underline}
dāštan āgāhīh mad*

"when information came of a woman or property that [seemed to
him]{.underline} good to have" (*Dk*.9.21.13)

*harw čē-[t kāmag]{.underline} ast xwāh tā-t daham*

"ask everything [you wish]{.underline}, so that I shall give it to you!"
(after *Bd*.4.6)

*ēk ka-[š]{.underline} tis [kāmēd]{.underline} guftan*

"one, when [he wants]{.underline} to say something" (*Dk*.9.2.4)

*u-šān ārzōgīhēd kū kāč nē zād būd-ēnd*

"and they desire: if only they had not been born!" (after *Dk*.3.178.8)

*nohom [kē]{.underline} pad harw kēš [wurrōyēd]{.underline} ud
paristīdan kāmēd*

"ninth, [he who]{.underline} (*kē*) [believes]{.underline} in every
teaching and wishes to worship (in it)" (*MX*.35.12)

*[kē-š]{.underline} [wurrōyēd]{.underline} xwarēd ud [kē-š]{.underline}
nē [wurrōyēd]{.underline} nē xwarēd*

"[he]{.underline} [who]{.underline} (*kē-š*) [believes]{.underline}
shall eat, and [he]{.underline} [who]{.underline} [does]{.underline} not
[believe]{.underline} shall not eat"

*kē tis wēš gōwēd kū ān ī dānēd ān-iz ī dānēd [mardōmān]{.underline} nē
[wurrōyēd]{.underline}*

"he who says more than what he knows, (then), also what he knows [people
will]{.underline} not [believe]{.underline}" (*Dk*.6C.2)

*ka-m frāz mad hēnd pad ān paymōzan ī zarrēn-pēsīd ī asēmēn-pēsīd ī
brāzišnīgtom az harwisp paymōzanān u-[m]{.underline} burzišnīgtar
[sahist]{.underline}*

"when they come forward to me in that (those) gold-embroidered,
silver-embroidered garment(s), most radiant of all garments, [it seemed
to me]{.underline} most praiseworthy" (*AWN*.12.6)

*ka [wizīrēd]{.underline} abāg wattarān ham-kunišn \... nē bawišn*

"when [one can avoid]{.underline} it, one should not be collaborators
with bad ones" (*Dk*.6C.22)

*[nōg-widurdān]{.underline} \... [az]{.underline} yazišn paristišn
[awizīrišnīg]{.underline}*

"[the newly departed cannot do without]{.underline} sacrifices and
worship" (*DD*.80.3)

#### Impersonal *andar abāyēd* expressing need and necessity

In this impersonal expression, the person who needs to do something is
often an enclitic pronoun; "needed [for]{.underline}" is expressed by
*pad*, e.g.:

*Ohrmazd ēdōn gōwēd kū ka ēbgad āmad ān ī xwēš hamēmāl pad kōxšišn frāz
gīrēd kū nōg framān [andar nē abāyēd]{.underline}*

"Ohrmazd says as follows: When the Invasion has come, (each) seizes his
own opponent to fight with, that is, a new command [is not
needed]{.underline}" (*Bd*.3.12)

*gōwēd pad dēn kū hōm ī spēd [pad]{.underline} fraškerd-kerdārīh [andar
abāyēd]{.underline}*

"it says in the *dēn* that the white *hōm* [is needed for]{.underline}
making Fraškerd" (after *Bd*.24a.1)

*Ohrmazd rāy gōwēd kū Wāy-iz abzār-ēw būd ī-[š]{.underline}
[pad]{.underline} dām-dahišnīh [andar abāyist]{.underline}*

"it says about Ohrmazd that Wāy, too, was a tool that [he
needed]{.underline} [for]{.underline} establishing the creation"
(*Bd*.1.45)

*u-[š]{.underline} pānagīh ī awēšān \... [awizīrišnīg]{.underline}
[andar abāyēd]{.underline} bē dād*

"and [he cannot avoid]{.underline} (*a-wizīrišnīg*) [having
to]{.underline} (*andar abāyēd*) provide (*dād*) protection for them"
(*DD*.53.6)

*[Ohrmazd]{.underline} abzār-ēw pad akārēnīdan zadan ī Gannāg Mēnōy
[andar abāyist]{.underline}*

"Ohrmazd needed a tool for incapacitating and striking down the Foul
Spirit" (*WD*.10.3)

Note *abd sahist* "seemed wondrous (to)," *škoft sahist* "seemed amazing
(to)."

*abar čiyōnīh ī kōfān. gōwēd pad dēn kū nazdist kōf frāz rust Harburz ī

It says in the *dēn*:

(As) the first mountain, Harburz "allotted-by-the-allotter" grew forth,
and, afterward, all the mountains grew forth from it in (the space) of
18 years.

Harburz kept growing to the completion of (= altogether for) 800
years---

200 years (up) to the star-level, 200 to the moon-level, 200 to the
sun-level, and 200 to the highest of heaven.

That is (*čiyōn*), the other mountains are grown forth from Harburz,
2244 mountains in number (= in total).

## Text 9.4

After the *Bundahišn*: *Bd*.14.8. -- As M&M grew up from the earth in
the form of a rhubarb plant, two *xwarrah*s grew up between them.
Ohrmazd is asked which grew up first, the body or the *xwarrah*. Mss.
TD1, ff. 40r-41v, TD2, p. 101, DH, ff. 186v-187r.

*čiyōn gōwēd kū kadār pēš dād xwarrah ayāb tan*

*Ohrmazd gōwēd kū xwarrah pēš dād ud tan pas ō ān dād estēd*

*andar tan dād kū xwēškārīh bē brēhēnīd tan bē ō xwēškārīh dād*

As it says: Which was established before (= first): the *xwarrah* or the
body?

And Ohrmazd says: The *xwarrah* was established before, and the body was
afterward established for it.

It was established in the body, i.e., one's duties were fashioned,
(then) the body was established for one's duties (in order that one
might do one's duties).

In this text, the direct translation from the Avestan (next page),
preserving the Avestan word order, is followed by short explanations
(glosses), some introduced by *kū* "that is."

The Avestan Text:

*huuarəxšaētəm aməṣ̌əm raēm* We sacrifice to the immortal sun, wealthy

*auruua.aspəm yazamaide* with fleet horses.

*āa ya huuarə raoxšne tāpaiieiti* Then, when the sun warms (the world)
in the light,

*āa ya huuarə raocō tāpaiieiti* Then, when the sun warms the light,

9.4. Translate into Pahlavi and write in Pahlavi at least sentences 2,
4, 6, 8, 9:

1.  When I praise Righteousness, then the demons are scorned.

2.  Before the Renovation, Ohrmazd needs Frēdōn for the striking of
    Dahāg.

3.  Ahrimen and the other demons and lie-demons will be stricken and
    killed.

4.  Everything that was said there in that assembly was written (down)
    clearly.

5.  If it seems (good) to you (all), tell me in more detail what is
    written here in this book.

6.  Another day, Ardaxšīr was standing on a chariot, and all the other
    people were sitting on horses (all) around him.

7.  The one who does good deeds, he goes forth to Paradise, and he who
    does evil deeds, him they throw into Hell.

8.  Do not speak lying speech, because, if you speak lying speech,
    Astwihād will drag you to the worst existence, and there you will
    experience (see) much unhappiness.

9.  When I came to Paradise, a group of departed ones came toward me,
    and, from the souls of the Righteous, a light went out like that of
    the sun, the moon, and the stars; and they went about joyfully in
    the light of the intermediate space (the atmosphere).

Then the Foul Spirit rose up together with all the demons against the
light ones.

And that sky appeared to them in the other world when it had not yet
been established as 'bony'.

Out of envious desire, he made an assault on it.

The sky stood on the star-level, (but) was dragged down into the void,
which, it was written in the beginning, was between the "principles" of
the light ones and the dark ones, so that it stood as much as one-third
from inside the sky above the star-level.

And like a snake, the sky jumped beneath this earth and was shattered
and broken.

Q. The '*hōm* that restores the dead', with which they restore the dead
and with which they make the Final Body, where does it grow?

And for what action (purpose) is the Kar fish appointed?

A. The '*hōm* that restores the dead' grows in the Warkaš Sea in the
deepest place.

and 99,999 fravashis of the Righteous have been appointed for its (*-š*)
protection.

And the Kar fish turns around it (*-š \... pērāmōn*) and keeps frogs and
other evil animals away from it (*-š \... aziš*).

The number: 9 ud 70 \[for 90\] ud 900 ud 9000 ud 9 bēwar

= 9 + 90 + 900 + 9,000 + 90,000 = 99,999 (= 100,000-1).

## Word formation 4. Prefixes and suffixes 4

#### ^1^*-āy*, *-āyīg* 

The suffixes ^1^*-āy* (*-ā*) *-āyīg* (Ä- \<-'d\>, \<-'d, \[W∂ÎdA-\]
WiÄ-, WiA- \<-'d(y)k\'\>) make adjectives from geographical names::

*hrōm* "Rome" *hrōmāy* (*hrōmā*) "a Roman" *hrōmāyīg* "Roman"

\**muzr*, *misr* *muzrāyīg* "Egyptian"

*bābēl* "Babylonia" *bābēlāyīg* "Babylonian"

*asūrestān* "Assyria" *asūrāyīg* "Assyrian"

#### ^2^*-āy* 

The rare suffix ^2^*-āy* (Ä- \<-'d\>) mostly makes nouns corresponding
to adjectives denoting size:

*drahnāy* "length"

*drāzāy* "length" (rare) cf. *drāz* "long" (distance, cf. *darg* "long"
time)

*pahnāy* "width, thickness" cf. *pahn* "broad, thick"

*bālāy* "height" cf. *buland* "high"

*zofāy* "depth" cf. *zafr*, *zofr* "deep"

*drūnāy* "harvesting" cf. *drūdan* "to reap, harvest"

Note also *zan-rēbāy* "\*seduction" (*Dk*.5.9.9 \< *rēb-* 'to
defraud"?), as well as the Aramaic loan word *nakkīrāy* "denying" and
the adverb *agāmāy* \<'k'm'y\> "unwillingly" (see Lesson 18).

#### *-gar*, *-gār* 

The suffixes *-gar* ( LK-, lY- \<-gl, -kl\>) and *-gār* ( lAk-, laD-
\<-g'l, -k'l\>) mostly make adjectives and nouns meaning "doer of X,
making X." Examples:

*pērōz* "victorious" *pērōzgar* "victorious"

*yōǰdahr* "ritually pure" *yōǰdahrgar* "who makes ritually pure"

*warz* "cultivation, farming" *warzīgar* "cultivator, farmer"

*kerbag* "good deeds" *kerbakkar* \<krpkkl, krpkgl\> "doer of good
deeds" (Man. \<kyrbkr\>)

*bazzag* "bad deeds *bazzakkar* \<bckkl, bckgl\> "doer of bad deeds,
evil-doer" (Man. \<bzkr\>)

*kām* "wish, desire" *kāmgār* "who does what he wishes"

*wināh* "sin, crime" *wināhgār* "sinful, guilty" (oppos. *awināh* "who
has no sins")

*ayād* "memory" *ayādgār* "memorial"

*rōz* "day" *rōzgār* "time" (as it passes day by day)

#### *-tār/-dār*, *-tārīh/-dārīh*

Nouns of agent (performer of action) in *-tār/-dār* ( lAT- \<-t'l\>) are
formed from past stems of verbs by replacing the final *-t* or *-d* with
*-tār* or *-dār*, respectively.

Negative nouns in *a-* and abstract nouns in *-īh* (elAT- \<-t'lyh\>)
are frequently formed from such agent nouns:

*bōxtan* "deliver" *bōxtār* "deliverer" *bōxtārīh* "deliverance"

*warzīdan* "work, labor, perform" *warzīdār* "laborer, sb. who
performs/does sth." *warzīdārīh* "performance"

*xwardan* "eat" *axwardār* "not eating, without eating"

*pahrēxtan* "guard (against)" *pahrēxtār* "staying away from"

*dīdan* "see" *dīdār* "seeing, a view (of)"

*madan* "come" *madār* "bound/destined to come, sb. who comes
frequently"

In compounds:

*āyaft-xwāstār* "sb. who seeks rewards" *āyaft-xwāstārīh* "the seeking
of rewards"

*kerbag-warzīdār* "sb. who performs deeds" *kerbag-warzīdārīh* "the
performing of good deeds"

These nouns can take direct objects, e.g., *druzān wānīdārtom* "one who
most often overcomes the lie-demons" (*StS*.17.9)

Some nouns in *-tār/-dār* have passive meaning, e.g.:

*griftan* "seize" *griftār* "prisoner"

*frēftan* "deceive" *frēftār* "(easily) deceived"

*dīdan* "see" *dīdār* "visible," cf. *dūr-dīdār* "visible from afar"

*bastan* "bind, close (road)" *bastār* "closed (road)"

#### *-estān*

This common suffix, spelled WwAtJ- \<-st'n\'\> or WwAtjG- \<-yst'n\'\>
(occasionally WwAtjA- \<-'st'n\'\>) makes nouns of place:

*Asūrestān* "Assyria, Syria" *Hūzestān* "Khuzistan" *Tabarestān*
"Tabaristan"

*Čīnestān* "China" *Sagestān* "Sistan" *Turkestān* "Turkistan"

*Hindūstān* "India" *Sō(g)westān* "Sogdiana"(?)

*šahr* "realm" *šahrestān* "town"

*hērbed*, a priestly teacher *hērbedestān*, lit., place for priestly
studies

*aspestān* "(horse) stable" *gōstān* "cow pen"

*uštar-estān* "camel-stable" \[but: *pahast* "sheep stall" \< *pah*\]

In a few words, the function of the suffix is indeterminate, e.g.:

*dādestān* "law, judgement" cf. *dād* "law"

*zamestān* "winter" cf. *zamčīg* "of winter, winterly"

*bārestān* "patient" *bār* "burden"

Note also names o*f Avestan texts*, all listed with short descriptions
in *Dēnkard* book VIII:

*Hērbedestān*, rules connected with priestly studies

*Nīrangestān*, rules connected with the performance of rituals

*Zaxmestān*, *Rēšestān*, rules dealing with bodily assault and harm
(text not extant)

*Hamēmālestān*, rules dealing with bodily assault and harm (not extant)

*Pasuš-horwestān*, rules for dealing with sheep and shepherd dogs
(partly extant)

*Stōrestān*, rules for dealing with domestic animals (partly extant)

*Arzestān*, rules for determining value (partly extant)

*Waxšestān*, rules for gift exchange, compensation (*waxš* "interest"),
etc. (not extant)

#### *-bān* (WwAP- \<-p'n\'\>) "guardian of"

*darbān* "door guard" *marzbān* "border guard"

*pāsbān* "watch guard, watcher" *zēndānbān* "prison guard"

#### *-bed* (WTP- \<-pt\'\>) "lord of, master of"

*mānbed* "house-master" *spāhbed* "master of the army, general"

*wisbed* "town-master" *hērbed* "priest" (Av. *aēθrapaiti* "master of
learning")

*dahībed* (*dehbed*) "lord of the land" *mowbed* "high priest" (Av.
\**moγupaiti* "master of the Magi")

#### *-war* ( LW- \<-wl\>)

This fairly rare suffix (from *-bar* "carrying") mostly makes nouns and
adjectives from nouns. Examples:

*waxš* "word" (Av. *vāxš*) *waxšwar* "prophet"

*nēzag* "spear, lance" *nēzagwar* "spear/lance-carrying"

*kēn* "vengeance" *kēnwar* "vengeful"

*āz* "greed" (demon: *Āz*) *āzwar* "greedy"

Note:

*mādag* "substance" *mādagwar* "especially"

#### *-wār* (lAW- \<-w'l\>)

This suffix makes adverbs of manner. Examples:

*sazāg* "fitting, appropriate" *sazāgwār* "fittingly, appropriately"

*xwadāy* "lord, ruler" *xwadāywār* "lordly, in a manner befitting a
lord"

*ham* "same" *hamwār* "always"

#### *-čār*, *-zār* ( lAC- \<-c'l\>) "place of"

*uzdēsčār* "place of idols, idol temple" *ǰašnzār* "place of
celebrations"

## 

## Grammar 10

### Demonstrative pronouns (recapitulation)

##### Near-deictic "proximal" ("this, these"):

*ēn* NwY , NwY\> \<Z̲NE\> "this"

*ēd* \[Ä\] AwA **\<**HNA ('y)\> "this"

*im* Nwï\>Ò , NwïÒ **\<**LZ̲NE\> "this" *imēšān* WwaHNwïÒ
\<L[Z]{.underline}NEš'n\'\> "these"

##### Far-deictic "distal" ("that, those"):

*ōy* nLW \<OLE\> "that" *awēšān* WwaHnLW \<OLEš'n\'\> "those"

*ān* ˝¸ \<ZK\> "that (there)"

The pronouns *ēn* and *ān* can be preceded by *ham* to add emphasis:
"this/that very."

Only *ōy* and *im* have plural forms: *awēšān* and *imēšān* (Manichean
also *imīn*).

*ōy* is rarely plural; instead *awēšān* tends to be used as general
plural, both as personal pronoun (alone) and demonstrative pronoun (with
a noun).

*ōy*, *awēšān* is also used as a personal pronoun "he, she, it; they."

*ēn*, *ēd*, and *ān* can be used with singular and plural nouns,
including nouns in *-ān*.

*ēd* is commonly used to refer to the text or the situation in which a
sentence is spoken: "this one in question, this that we have been
talking about, the following," etc.

*im* "this" is the least frequent of the near-deictic pronouns; it is
mainly used in expressions such as *im rōz* "this day, today." The
plural *imēšān* is very rare and only used with nouns in *-ān*.

Examples:

*[ān]{.underline} sāl wārān bawēd*

"that year there will be rain" (in predictions) (*PR*.48.13)

*[ēn]{.underline} dašt nēk ud gōr ēdar was*

"this plain is fine and wild asses are plentiful here" (*KN*.2.18)

*pad gōwišnīh ī ohrmazd paydāg kū [ēd]{.underline} tō mašīy gāw u-t
[ēd]{.underline} ǰōrdā*

"in/by the statement of Ohrmazd it is manifest: This is your cow, Mašīy,
and this (is) your barley" (*Dk*.7.1.11)

*Gayōmard daxšagōmandīh [ēd]{.underline} kū mardōm az ōy tōhmag pad
[ān]{.underline} hangōšīdag zād hēnd*

"Gayōmard's 'having a mark' is this (the following): people were born
from his seed in that similar manner" (*Bd*.1a.16)

*Ādur-mihr guft kū druz-ēw Āz stahmagtar ud xwarišn-ēw [ham
ēn]{.underline} xwārtom ī amāh nūn xward* *[ham ān]{.underline}*

"Ādur-mihr said: 'One lie-demon, (namely) Greed is the most violent, and
one food is the lightest (namely) [this very one]{.underline} that we
have eaten now, (yes) [that very one]{.underline}' " (*Dk*.6d.2)

Note expressions such as *ēn nām* "this fame," that is, "the fame for
this deed" (*AWN*.2.7), *pēš az ān nibištan* "before that writing," that
is, "before writing (all) that" (*Dk*.8.1.4)

##### *ōy*, *ān* "that, the other," *ēn \... ān* as "this \... that," and *ēk \... ān* "one \... the other":

*gōy [ōy kanār ī]{.underline} Ardaxšīr ōbast*

"the (polo) ball fell [on the other side]{.underline} of Ardaxšīr"
(*KN*.14.6)

*hutuxšīh [ān 3 pēšag]{.underline} hayār*

"the artisanate (is) the helper of [those]{.underline} (= the other)
[three estates]{.underline} (priests, warriors, farmers)" (*Dk*.3.27)

*ka pad [ān kust ī Tērag]{.underline} andar šawēd kišwar ī Sawah ud
Wōrūbaršn ud Wōrūǰaršn nēm-ēw az Xwanīrah tābēd*

"when (the sun) sets [on that]{.underline} (= the other)
[side]{.underline} of (Mount) Tērag, it shines on the continents of
Sawah, Wōrūbaršn ud Wōrūǰaršn, and half of Xwanīrah" (*Bd*.5b.11)

*ka zarmān mard [pad ēn darag]{.underline} andar šawēd aburnāy ī
15-sālag [pad ān dar]{.underline} bērōn āyēd*

"when an old man goes in [through this]{.underline} (one)
[door]{.underline}, he comes out through [that]{.underline} (other)
[door]{.underline} as a 15 year-old youth" (*Bd*.32.11)

*2 mard ēk abāg did pahikār ud harw 2 brād hēnd [ēk]{.underline} gōwēd
kū pidar ī man wāhmān 2 xwāstag \*ō man dād \... ud nūn-iz
[ān]{.underline} pusar ōwōn gōwēd \...*

"two men had a legal fight one with the other, and the two (of them)
were brothers; [the one]{.underline} says 'my father such and such gave
two pieces of property to me \... and now [that]{.underline} (= the
other) son says thus \..." (*Purs*.53.1)

*kerbag ī az [ēn]{.underline} gāhānbār tā [ān]{.underline} gāhānbār
kunēd ēw-kardag bē bawēd harw ēk ēk ōh bawēd*

"the *kerbag*s he makes from this Gāhānbār to that (= another, the
next?) Gāhānbār will be connected, (and) each one will be in the usual
way" (Nir.42.5b; about the merit accruing from celebrating the
Gāhānbārs)

##### *ēd rāy* (*ē rāy*) "for this reason," *pad ēd dār-* "to think, estimate (that)":

*[ēd rāy]{.underline} star ī agumēzagīh xwānēnd*

"[for this reason]{.underline} they call (them) 'the stars un(touched
by) the Mixture'" (after *Bd*.2.11)

*[pad ēd dārēnd]{.underline} kū ēk-tāg hēnd*

"[they think]{.underline} that they are alone" (*Bd*.27.57)

##### *ka \... ēd (ī) kā*, *ēd (ī) ka \... ēd (ī) kā* "whether \... or" (rare):

*ān anāgīh ī [ka]{.underline} kerbakkar [ēd ka]{.underline} bazakkar ud
[ka]{.underline} tuxšēd [ēd ī ka]{.underline} nē tuxšēd [ēd
ka]{.underline} hunsand ud [ēd ka]{.underline} nē hunsand ud pas a-kām
\... rasēd*

"[whether]{.underline} one does good [or]{.underline} one does evil,
[whether]{.underline} one is diligent [or]{.underline} not diligent,
[whether]{.underline} one is content [or]{.underline} discontented, that
evil (= death) will then come (even) against one's wish" (*DD*.14.3)

*Abarg guft [ēd ka]{.underline} bē* (= *pad*) *kēr dārišn bē gīrēd [ēd
ka]{.underline} pad dast dārišn bē ō an-Ērān kunēd pad gyāg tanābuhl ud
pad sāl-drahnāy margarzān*

"Abarg said: [whether]{.underline} he takes (the child) by virtue of
'possession by penis' (as the father), [or]{.underline} he hands it over
to non-Iranians by virtue of 'possession by hand' (as the one who
actually has the child), (in either case) he is *tanābuhl* and after a
year *margarzān*" (*ZFJ*.593)

(about a man who has sex with a non-Iranian woman and she becomes
pregnant)

*[ēd ka]{.underline} pus [ēd ka]{.underline} mard ī šahr pad 3-gōwišnīh
gōwēd kū xwāstag-dār ham hamē xwāstag-dār bawēd*

"[whether]{.underline} a son [or]{.underline} a man of the (same)
town/land says with three utterances: 'I am in possession of the
(inherited) property', (he is to be believed and) will be (regarded as)
the one in (legal) possession of the property" (*MHD*.41.6)

##### 

##### *adār-ēw* !lAtÅ \<'t'l-1\> "whichever (of two)":

This rare word, which rhymes with *kadār-ēw* "which of two," looks like
a demonstrative adverb, but renders the Avestan relative adverb *yatāra*
"the one of the two who = whichever of two" (?):

*ēg gōwēd dōst ō ōy dōst ān ī pad bālišn nibāyān kū ul tō ēst čē wigrād
man*

*[adār-ēw kē]{.underline} pēš ul estād ā-š bē rawišnīh ō ān ī pahlom
axwān*

"then the friend says to (his) friend, the one lying on his pillow: 'get
up! for I am awake'

[the one who]{.underline} (= whichever of the two) has gotten up first,
he will be going to the Best Existence" (*PV*.18.26)

###  The verb. The infinitives

Infinitives are formed in two ways:

1\. "short" infinitives are identical with the past participle

2\. "long" infinitives are formed from the past stem by adding *-an*:

WWT- \<-tn\'\>, WWtÅ- \<-'tn\'\>, WWtD- \<-ytn\>, WWtJ-, WWt∆D-
\<-(y)stn\'\>.

Since the only orthographic difference between the short and the long
infinitives is the final stroke, they cannot always be distinguished,
but we know from Manichean Middle and modern Persian that they both
existed, e.g.:

*griftan* WWTWwïÅW , WWTplY \<glptn\'; OHDWNtn\'\> "to take, seize"

*nišastan* WWtJWW}YtD \<YTYBWNstn\'\> "to sit"

*madan* WWt˜ \<mtn\'\> "to come"

*āmadan* WWTWWtåD \<YATWNtn\'\> "to come"

*kerdan* WWTWK \<krtn\'\> "to do"

*framūdan* WWTnLP \<plmwtn\'\> "to command, order"

*estādan* WWtÅWnYWI \<YKOYMWN'tn\'\> "to stand"

*pursīdan* WWtŸJWWP \<pwrsytn\'\> "to ask"

*frēstīdan* WWtDWWwïH \<ŠDRWNytn\'\> "to send"

*dwārīdan* WWtdlA\|wY \<dwb'lytn\'\> "to run" (esp. evil beings)

*dwāristan* WWtjlA\|wY \<dwb'lstn\'\> "to run"

Notes:

Remember that the verb *madan* "come" (= *āmadan*) has no present stem.

Recall also that the infinitive may take the ending \<-x~2~\>.

The infinitive *pargandan* "scatter, sow" is spelled WwY\>WkLP
\<plkndn\'\>.

### Uses of the infinitive

European speakers on non-English languages (and Pahlavi) will all have
to learn that there correspond in English two forms to their
infinitives: the infinitive (*to sing*) and the *ing*-form of the verb
(*sing-ing*). Conversely, English-speakers should realize that, to
translate a Pahlavi infinitive, either an English infinitive or an
*ing*-form can/must be used. Keeping this in mind will make it easier to
understand the following examples.

Note also that the Pahlavi infinitive sometimes needs to be translated
into English as a passive infinite.

#### Infinitive as subject, direct object, possessive

Since the inifinitive is a nominal form of the verb, it can be used in
all the functions of a regular noun. In English, *ing*-forms are often
preferred in some of these functions, e.g.:

subject: *to sing/singing can be hard work*

direct object: *I like to sing/singing*, *he commanded the army to
attack*

possessive: *the art of singing*, *a time of rejoicing*

with prepositions: *in order to sing*

with adjectives: *able to sing*, *authorized to leave*

On the whole, Pahlavi infinitives, too, work in this way!

##### Infinitive as subject and predicate:

An infinitive is often found as subject in impersonal expresssions \[on
these, see below\], but rarely otherwise.

##### Infinitive as predicate:

*fradom sūd ī az Gayōmard [ōzadan]{.underline} ī Arzūr ud abespārag
kerdan ī tan ī xwēš meh-dādestānīhā ō Ahrimen* *[būd]{.underline}*

"the first benefit from Gayōmard [was to kill]{.underline} Arzūr and
surrender his own body to Ahrimen obeying a higher law (requirement *or
similar*) (*meh-dādestānīhā*)" (after *MX*.26.14-15)

##### Infinitive as direct object:

*nūn-it nimāyam [būdan]{.underline} ī ristāxēz ud tan ī pasēn*

"now I (will) show you [the becoming]{.underline} (= coming into
existence) of the Resurrection and the Final Body (= how the R. comes
about)" (after *AWN*.5.7)

#### Infinitives governed by prepositions

These constructions are very common:

*[abar agārēnīdan]{.underline} ī abārōn-dādīh ud wad-kunišnīh ī Banīg
Srāyēl*

"[about how to undo]{.underline} the evil laws and evil deeds of Banī
Isrāyīl" (*Dk*.5.1.5)

*xwarrah pad ān hangām mad ō Waēgird ī Hōšang ī pēšdād [abar
winnārdan]{.underline} andar gēhān dād ī dehgānīh ud gēhān warzīdārīh ud
dahībedīh ī gēhān pānagīh*

"at that time, the Xwarrah came to Waēgird son of Hōšang Pēšdād
[about]{.underline} (= for the sake of) [establishing]{.underline} in
the world the law of landownership, the cultivation and overlordship of
the world, which (is = that is) the protection of the world"
(*Dk*.7.1.16)

*ōh-iš [az guftan kerdan]{.underline} paydāg*

"thus it is manifest to him [from what is said and done]{.underline}"
(*Purs*.26.2)

*[pad marnǰēnīdan]{.underline} tag abar kerd*

"he attacked [in order to destroy]{.underline} (it)" (*Bd*.1.15)

*Ardawān spāh ud gund ī ārāstag abāg pus ī xwēš ō pārs [pad
griftan]{.underline} ī Ardaxšīr frēstīd*

"Ardawān sent an equipped army and force with his own son to Pārs [in
order to seize]{.underline} Ardaxšīr" (*KN*.3.22)

*ān ī weh ōstigāntar winnerdan [pad]{.underline} wattarīh [škastan
wišuftan]{.underline}*

"how to establish more firmly what is good [by breaking and
scattering]{.underline} (what is) bad" (*Dk*.3.229.18)

*mardōm [pad]{.underline} kerbag [kerdan]{.underline} tuxšāgēnēd kē dāšn
ō kerbakkarān kunēd*

"he who makes gifts to those who do good makes people be diligent [in
doing]{.underline} good things" (after *Dk*.9.67.5)

*[pēš az madan]{.underline} ī ō gāw ohrmazd mang ī bēšāz ō gāw pad
xwardan dād*

"[before coming]{.underline} = [before he]{.underline} (the Adversary)
[came]{.underline} to the bull, Ohrmazd gave the bull medicinal hashish
to eat" (after *Bd*.4.20)

*ud nasāy sag nimūdan nīrangīg čim ēk ēn kū a-wiškinn awēšān druzān ī
tan agārēnīdārān kē nasuš-iz xwad hēnd pad ōy tan gāh dāštan ud [tā
waštan]{.underline} ī az nasāyīh [abāz madan]{.underline} ī did ō kār ud
sūd ī gēhān šāyēnd*

"and one ritual reason for showing (a corpse) to a dog is this:
uninterruptedly (*a-wiškinn*), those lie-demons who are what makes the
body useless (*agārēnīdārān*), who are (nothing but) the Nasuš itself,
are able to (*šāyēnd*) keep (their) place in that body [until the
changing]{.underline} from being *nasāy* (and) [returning]{.underline}
(= until it changes and returns) again to service and profit for the
world of the living" (*Dk*.5.24.28)

#### Infinitives with *rāy*, *pad \... rāy* "in order to, for \... -ing"

*[gumān kerdan]{.underline} ī mardōmān pad ēn dēn [rāy]{.underline}*

"in order [to make]{.underline} people [doubtful]{.underline} about this
*dēn*" (*AWN*.1.3)

*ohrmazd guft kū nē šāyēd kerd čē tūr ī brādarōxš ī karb ī ahrimen [ōzad
ī tō rāy]{.underline} dād ān a-marg bē bawēd*

"Ohrmazd said: it is not possible (to give Z. immortality), because
(then) Tūr ī Brādarōxš, the evil priest (*karb*) whom Ahrimen
established [in order to kill you]{.underline}---he will become immortal
(too)" (*PR*.36.6)

*harw kas \... wistāx bawišn kū hagriz tis aw-iš nē rasēd ī aw-iš [madan
rāy]{.underline} zyān*

"everybody should be confident that nothing will ever come to (= happen
to) him (*aw-iš*), which, [because it comes]{.underline} to him, (there)
is harm" (*Dk*.6.28)

*ān āb pad fraškerd rist [wirāstan rāy]{.underline} andar abāyēd*

"that water is needed at the Fraškerd [in order to restore]{.underline}
the dead" (*Bd*.12.12)

*ān ī ka kār frārōn hudānāg [pad]{.underline} hu'īh [burd]{.underline} ī
dānišn ō kār [rāy]{.underline} pad ēk-brahmīh estēd ī-š paymān*

"when it is that the activity is good (and the performer) is
'well'-knowledgeable, [by bringing]{.underline} knowledge to an activity
with/by 'well'-ness, he finds himself (*estēd*) in 'being of one manner
(*brahm*),' which is his 'mean'" (*Dk*.3.144.4)

#### Infinitives with subject and direct object

Since the infinitive is a verbal form, it can also have a 'subject'
(who/which performs the action of the infinitive), a direct or indirect
object and sometimes all three, as in these English examples:

"(about) [Ohrmazd's creating mankind]{.underline}"

= "(about) the fact that Ohrmazd \[Subj.\] created mankind \[Dir.
Obj.\]," "(about) how Ohrmazd created mankind"

"(at the time of) [Z.'s giving the *dēn* to the world]{.underline}"

= "at the time when Z. \[Subj.\] gave the *dēn* \[Dir. Obj.\] to the
world \[Indir. Obj.\]"

These infinitives may be translated by *ing*-forms, but quite often as
subordinate clauses. There are several examples in the preceding
sentences (find them!), and here are some more:

##### Infinitive with 'subject':

The 'subject ' of an infinitive usually follows the infinitive and is
connected to it by *ī*. Other words may intervene:

*abar [madan ī]{.underline} pad harw zamān [Astwihād]{.underline} ō
ōšōmandān kē ōš mad estēd kē-iz nē*

"about [Astwihād's coming]{.underline} at every time both those to whom
death has come and those not"

= about [how Astwihād]{.underline} \... [comes]{.underline} *or* "about
[the fact that A. comes]{.underline}) to mortals" (*Dk*.9.12.17)

*pas az [madan]{.underline} ī gizistag Aliksandar ī Hrōmāyīg*

"after [the coming]{.underline} of the accursed Alexander, the Roman" =
"after A. came \..."

*xešmgen mard hāmōyēn wināh ud bazag ō menišn ōbadēd tā [bē nišast ī
xešm]{.underline}*

"all (kinds of) sins and evil deeds fall into the thoughts of a wrathful
man until [the subsiding of (his) wrath]{.underline} = "until (his)
wrath subsides)" (*MX.*1.18)

##### Infinitive with 'subject' and direct object:

Note that the direct object can be separated from the infinitive at
quite a distance:

*[muštan ī wād āb]{.underline} ō zrēy*

"[the wind's]{.underline} \[Su\] [sweeping (of) the water]{.underline}
\[DO\] into the ocean (= how the wind sweeps \...)" (*WZ*.3.33)

*ka hangām ī [xwarišn xwardan ī ān kirm]{.underline} bawēd ēdōn kunē*

"when the time comes of [Kirm's eating food]{.underline}, then you
(shall) do thus (= as follows)

= "when the time for that Kirm \[Su\] to eat food \[DO\] \..."
(*KN*.8.14)

*abar [kerd ī Kāy-Us xwadāyīh]{.underline} pad čērīh abar būm ī haft pad
dēwān ud mardōmān*

"about [Kāy-Us's exercising kingship]{.underline} by valor over demons
and men on the seven(fold) earth"

= [how]{.underline} Kāy-Us \[Su\] by valor [exercised
kingship]{.underline} \[DO\] \..." (*Dk*.9.22.4)

*abar [xwardan ī artēštārān]{.underline} rōz ī kārēzār
[gōšt]{.underline}*

"about [soldiers']{.underline} \[Su\] [eating meat]{.underline} \[DO\]
on the day of battle" (*Dk*.8.26.12)

*handarz ī [abar]{.underline} nē [guftan ī]{.underline} andar xwarišn ud
xwārišn [saxwan]{.underline}*

"the advice [about not speaking a word]{.underline} while eating and
drinking" (*Dk*.9.9.2)

*abar garān-wināhīh ī [mard nibāg]{.underline} az an-ērān [abāz
duzzīdan]{.underline} ka-š xwēš pus*

"about the gravity of the sin of (= incurred by) [a man]{.underline}
\[Su\] [stealing back a hostage]{.underline} (*nibāg*) \[DO\] from
non-Iranians when it is his own son" (*Dk*.8.20.120)

##### Infinitive with 'subject', direct object, and indirect object (with *ō*):

*abar [nimūdan ī Ohrmazd ō Zarduxšt dāmān]{.underline} pad tan ī pasēn*

"about [how Ohrmazd]{.underline} \[Su\] [showed Zarduxšt]{.underline}
\[IO\] [the creations]{.underline} \[DO\] at the final body"
(*Dk*.9.35.14)

#### Infinitive in impersonal constructions

On the constructions of impersonal verbs, see Lesson 9 \[see also Lesson
12 on personal forms of 'impersonal' verbs\]. These often take the short
infinitive. Examples:

##### With *abāyēd* "one should, one must it behoves":

*[pidar ud mādar]{.underline} frazend ī xwēš rāy ēn and kār ud kerbag
pēš az 15 sāl bē [hammōxtan abāyēd]{.underline}*

"[a father and mother should teach]{.underline} these many (= all the
following) actions and good deeds to their own child before it reaches
fifteen years (of age)" (*PN*.34)

*u-[šān]{.underline} \... [guftan abāyēd]{.underline}* "[it behoves them
to say]{.underline}"

##### With *šayēd* "it is appropriate, it is possible, one can":

*pad tārīkīh ēdōn tārīk ī pad dast [frāz šāyēd grift(an)]{.underline}*

"(hell) is so dark with respect to darkness that [grasping]{.underline}
it with the hands [is possible]{.underline}

= [it is possible to grasp]{.underline} it with the hands" (*AWN*.18.4;
mss. short and long inf.)

*wināh wizārišn rāy čand weh [šāyēd]{.underline} kerbag
[warzīdan]{.underline}*

"[to perform]{.underline} good deeds the best (*čand weh*) [one
can]{.underline} in order to atone for (one's) sins" (*MX*.52.9)

*[Ardašīr widerdan nē šāyist]{.underline}*

"[Ardaxšīr was unable to cross]{.underline} (over)" (*KN*.8.6/6.24)

Note that *šāyēd* need not take an infinitive:

*nasāy ka andar āb wišuft estēd ān ī [šāyēd]{.underline} bērōn [bē
āwarēnd]{.underline} ān ī nē šāyēd dādestān čē*

"when a dead thing is broken up in (a body of) water, what is the legal
position of that which [they can bring out]{.underline} = [can be
brought out]{.underline} and that which cannot?" (*RAF*.38.1)

##### With *tuwān* "it is possible":

*u-[tān griftan nē tuwān]{.underline}*

"and (it will) [not]{.underline} (be) [possibl]{.underline}e for you =
[you will not be able to seize]{.underline} (him, them, etc.)"
(*KN*.4.12/3.10)

*ān-and dušmen az šahr [abāz dāšt kē tuwān]{.underline}*

"[who can hold]{.underline} so many enemies [back]{.underline} from the
land?" (*AZ*.63)

*pad ēn hamkārīh [dēwān]{.underline} andar ēbgadīh ayōxšust [wanīy
kerdan nē tuwān]{.underline} bawēd*

"by this collaborations (between Šahrīwar and other deities), during the
Invasion, [the demons will be unable to destroy]{.underline} the metal"
(*Bd*.3.19)

*nē harwisp-kerdār hē Ganāg Mēnōy kū-[t]{.underline} man [nē tuwān
marnǰēnīdan]{.underline}*

"(Ohrmazd said) you are not omnipotent, Foul Spirit, i,e.,
[destroying]{.underline} me [is not possible for you]{.underline} = [you
are unable to destroy]{.underline} me" (*Bd*.1.23)

##### Other:

*ēk ka-[š]{.underline} tis [kāmēd guftan]{.underline} ēk
ka-[š]{.underline} tis [kāmēd xwāstan]{.underline}*

"one, when [he wants to say]{.underline} something (and) one when [he
wants to seek]{.underline} something" (*Dk*.9.2.4)

*čē [sazēd būdan]{.underline}* "what can it be?" (*KN*.4.16/3.14)

#### Infinitives with other adjectives and nouns 

The adjectives and nouns that take infinitives are mostly the same as in
English.

*Srid guft kū nē [ādūg]{.underline} ham bē [ōzadan]{.underline} čē-m
az-iš garzišn bē abaxšīh pad dil*

"Srid said: I am not [able to kill]{.underline} (the bull); for, because
of (*az \... bē*) its complaint, I have (*-m*) pity in (my) heart"
(*WZ*.4.17)

*ka mēwag xormāy ayāb angūr yašt harw mēwag [pādixšāy
xwardan]{.underline}*

"when one has sacrificed fruit---dates or grapes---(one is) [authorized
to eat]{.underline} every fruit" (*MX*.15.18)

##### With nouns:

*drust āmad hē tō ardā wirāz ka-t ahanūz [āmad zamān]{.underline} nē
būd*

"welcome, Righteous Wirāz, (who have come) when it was not yet [the
time]{.underline} for you [to come]{.underline}" (*AWN*.4.1)

*ōy kē-š pad ēn frahang ud rāz [hammōxtan kāmag būd]{.underline}*

"he who whose [wish]{.underline} it was [to be taught]{.underline} in
this learning and secret

= who [wished to be taught]{.underline} in this learning and secret"
(*Bd*.0.5)

*čiyōn dūdag kadag-bānūg ast bē ō stūr [gumārdan nē niyāz]{.underline}*

"since there is (an authorized wife), (namely) the house-mistress of the
family, there is [no need to appoint]{.underline} her as guardian (of
her non *compos mentis* husband)" (*DD*.53.9)

*pad [ēmēd ī]{.underline} kār wēš [ayāftan]{.underline}*

"[in the hope to get]{.underline} (= [of getting]{.underline}) more
work" (*DD*.87.9)

*Wāy ān ī andar harw 2 dām petyārag [bē burd xwēškārīh]{.underline}*

"Wāy's [duty]{.underline} is [to remove/removing]{.underline} the
adversities in both creations" (*Bd*.3.6)

*u-m \... [xwēškārīh ud frēzwānīh]{.underline} ēn*

*kū ohrmazd pad astīh \... ud akanāragīh ud abēzagīh ahrimen pad nēstīh
ud wanī-būdīh [menīdan]{.underline}*

"and my [duties and obligations]{.underline} (are) these: [to
think/thinking]{.underline} about Ohrmazd as being, as limitless and
pure, (but) about Ahrimen as not being and as someone that will be
destroyed" (*PN*.3)

#### Infinitive with verbs

The most common verb taking an infinitive is "to order, command
(somebody [to do]{.underline})," "to give," "say," "to know, be able,"
"begin," and others:

*ēdōn [framāyēd nibištan]{.underline}*

"he orders (him) to write as follows"

*āwarēnd wiš ud zahr ī mār ud gazdum ud abārīg-iz xrafstar ī pad dōšox
[u-š xward dahēnd]{.underline}*

"they bring venom and poison from snakes, scorpions, and the other evil
animals in hell and [give him to eat]{.underline}" (*MX*.1.191)

*ka [gād]{.underline} ēw-bār [dahēd]{.underline} bīm pad tan ēwar*

"when [she offers him to have sex]{.underline} once, fear (= danger) to
the body is certain" (because she may conceal her menstruation) (after
*PR*.34d.2)

*kē yazd [šnāxtan gōwēd]{.underline} u-š čiyōnīh nē dānēd \... az
yazd-šnāsīh dūr*

"he who [says he knows]{.underline} god, but does not know how he is, is
far from knowing god" (*Dk*.3.109.9)

*kē pad āsn-xrad ud gōšōsrūd-xrad [abar nigerīdan dānēd]{.underline}*

"he who [knows]{.underline} (how) [to look]{.underline} at (something)
by (both his) 'inborn wisdom' and the 'wisdom acquired through the ear'"
(*Dk*.6B.11)

*hudānāg [būdan]{.underline} ud kār ud kerbag [čāštan nē
dānēd]{.underline}*

"he [does not know]{.underline} (how) [to be]{.underline} well-knowing
and [to teach]{.underline} works and good deeds (*Purs*.45.2)

*xwaršēd Mūš parīg ō rahīy ī xwēš bast \... kū tā wināh
[kerdan]{.underline} kam [tuwānist]{.underline}*

"the Sun bound the witch Mūš to his own chariot \... in order that [she
should be able to do]{.underline} less sin" (*Bd*.5.5)

*ud az ēdar [niwennīhēd guftan]{.underline} abar rēmanīh ī bahrān ī
andar-iz zīndagīh ī tan az tan murd ud ǰudāg bawēnd*

"and from here we start (*niwennīhēd* "it is started") to speak about
the pollution of the parts that, also during the life of the body,
become dead and separated from the body" (after *Dk*.5.24.19b)

In one (famous) example, *kāmēd* appears to be used with the infinitive
as future (a construction found in some Persian dialects):

*pad dēn gōwēd kū dušpādixšāyīh ī awēšān [sar kāmēd būdan]{.underline}*

"it says in the Religion that their evil rule [will come to an
end]{.underline}" (*Bd*.33.23)

#### Infinitives in enumerations

This usage is often indistinguishible from the use identical with the
participle of necessity, e.g.:

*pad gētīy fradom pad dēn āstawān [būdan]{.underline} didīgar [zan
kerdan]{.underline} ud paywand ī gētīy [rāyēnīdan]{.underline} \... ud
pad ēn abēgumān [būdan]{.underline}*

"in this world, firstly, [to have]{.underline} (= having *or* one should
have) faith (*āstawān būdan*) in the *dēn*; secondly, [to
marry]{.underline} and [to arrange]{.underline} (= marrying and
arranging *or* one should marry) continuation of one's line in this
world \... and [to be]{.underline} (= being) without doubt (= have no
doubt *or* one should have no doubt) about this (= the following)"
(*PN*.4)

*harw šab 3 bār pad hamāg ram [madan]{.underline} \... harw rōz bāmdād
bē [raftan]{.underline} \... andar gōspandān [nigerīdan]{.underline} ān
ī wēmār ud rišt \... gōspand dādīhā [darmānēnīdan]{.underline}
[sālārēnīdan]{.underline}*

"[to get to]{.underline} (*or* one should go to, etc.) the entire flock
three times every night \...; [to go]{.underline} among the cattle every
day at dawn \...; [to check out]{.underline} the cattle that are sick
and hurt; [to give them medication]{.underline} according to the rules;
and [to be their guardian]{.underline}" (*Dk*.8.23.5; the duties of the
cattle owner)

#### Infinitive ≈ participle of necessity in *-išn*

In legal texts, the infinitive is often used similar to the participle
of necessity in *-išn* "which needs to be done" (Lesson 13) and can
often be translated in English by a passive infinitive "is to be done,"
e.g.:

*ēn dādestān abāg wizīr ī \... azabar-nibišt estēd
[nigerīdan]{.underline}*

"(as for) this judgement together with the opinion \...., what is
written above [is to be looked at]{.underline} (= see what is written
above)" (*MHDA*.8.84)

*ōy ī margarzān wināh andar radān [garzišn]{.underline} ud tan bē
[abespārdan]{.underline}*

*ǰud az radān tan bē abespārd nē bawēd*

"he who has a *margarzān* sin, [should complain]{.underline} to the
judges and (his) body [is to be surrendered]{.underline};

the body is not surrendered other than (to = only to) the judges"
(*ŠnŠ*.8.2)

### The use of derived nouns instead of subordinate clauses

The nouns in *-īh*, especially those made from compounds, are often used
much in the same way as infinitives. They can, and should, often be
translated as full clauses. Note especially the use of *rāy* in such
constructions:

*u-m [mardōmīh]{.underline} az Mahrīy ud Mahriyānīy*

"and my [being a human]{.underline} being (comes) from (being descended
from) Mahlīy ud Mahliyānīy = I am a human being because I am (descended)
from Mahlīy ud Mahliyānīy" (*PN*.2)

*did Ahrimen gōwēd kū bē hāzam harwisp ox ī astōmand ō
[adōstīh]{.underline} ī tō [dōstīh]{.underline} ī man*

"then Ahrimen says: 'I will lead the entire bony existence [to being
unfriendly]{.underline} to you, (but) [to being friendly]{.underline} to
me (not being your friend \...)'" (*WZ*.1.7)

*sag [pad hamēstārīh]{.underline} ī gurg-sardagān ud
[pānagīh]{.underline} ī gōspandān [kerdan]{.underline} rāy dād estēd*

"the dog has been established ('created') [in order to
oppose]{.underline} the wolf-species and [to protect]{.underline} the
domestic animals" (after *Bd*.24.38)

Note how phrases are changed into adjectives and adjectives are changed
into nouns:

*harwisp-āgāh* "all-knowing"

\> *Ohrmazd harwisp-āgāhīh [rāy]{.underline}* "[because]{.underline} of
Ohrmazd's all-knowing-ness = because Ohrmazd knows/knew all"

*garān wināh* (*wināh ī garān*) "a heavy sin"

\> *mard ī garān-wināh* "a heavy-sin man = a man who commits (and is
guilty of) heavy sins"

\> *garān-wināhīh ī ān mard [rāy]{.underline}* "[on account
of]{.underline} the heavy-sin-ness of that man = [because]{.underline}
that man had committed (and was guilty of) (such) heavy sins"

*mard-ēw kē-š gōwišn rāst* "a man whose speech is truthful"

\> *mard ī rāst-gōwišn* "a truthfully-speaking man"

\> *[pad]{.underline} rāst-gōwišnīh ī ēn mard* "[through]{.underline}
the truthfully-speaking of this man = [because]{.underline} this man
speaks the truth"

*wišād dwār-* "run about untied (i.e., without tying the kusti)

\> *wišād-dwārišnīh wināh ī garān* "going about (with the kusti) untied
is a heavy sin"

*bē tuxšāgīh ka-š yazd* (or *dād*) *nē abāg pad gētīy abēbar*

The knowledgeable man asks the divine Wisdom:

Is it possible to make the property of this world one's own through
diligence?

The divine Wisdon answers:

Through diligence, it is not possible to make one's own that goodness
that has not been (already) assigned (as such by the divine).

But that which has been (so) assigned comes earlier by diligence.

But diligence in this world, when/if it does not have the gods (or the
law?) with it, bears no fruits.

But, *afterward*, in the other world, it comes to (one's) aid and
increases (the good deeds) on the scale.

The knowledgeable man asks the divine Wisdom: Who is the poorer among
the rich, and who is the richer among the poor?

The divine Wisdon answers: Of the rich, he is the poorer who is not
content with what he has and worries about how (his) things (belongings)
can become more.

And, of the poor, he is the richer who is content with what has come (to
him and he now has) and does not think about how (his) things (=
belongings) can become more.

4\. Translate into Pahlavi and write in Pahlavi:

1.  When we arrived in (= to) Babylon, we came to a river which we were
    not able to cross.

2.  It says in the Avesta that, in Ērānwēz, the winter is ten months and
    the summer two months.

3.  Until the resurrection and the Final Body, one must be in Hell in
    much evil and many kinds of punishment.

4.  Gōbedšāh's house is in Ērānšahr in the continent of Xwanīrah, but
    there is (one) who says he was ruler of Sogdiana, which is on the
    road from Xwarāsān to China.

5.  In the *Hērbedestān* there is much talk about (*abar*) how to become
    a priestly teacher, and the *Nīrangestān* is about how to perform
    the *yasna* to the gods properly.

6.  The accursed king of the Xionians orders the scribe to write as
    follows in a letter: You must relinquish that Mazdayasnian religion!
    If not, we will come against you with 10,000 Turanian warriors and
    we will kill all the Iranians.

7.  In this world, one should, first, believe in the *dēn*; second,
    marry; third, cultivate the earth; fourth, tend (cultivate) cattle
    according to the law; fifth, one-third of the day and one-third of
    the night go to school and inquire about (ask) the wisdom of the
    Righteous; one-third of the day and one-third of the night be
    diligent in one's duties, and one-third of the day and one-third of
    the night be happy and relax.

and it has one branch in Xwarāsān.

Mount Padišxwārgar (is) the one in Tabarestān and Gēlān and those parts.

*Weh-rōd pad Xwarāsān bē widerēd ud pad Sind būm šawēd ud pad Hindūstān
ō zrēy rēzēd*

*u-š ānōh Mihrān rōd xwānēnd ud Hindūgān rōd-iz xwānēnd.*

*Frād rōd bunxān az wimand ī Hrōm pad Asūrestān widerēd ud ō Daǰlit
