The river Weh passes through Xwarāsān and goes to the land of Sind, and
it pours into the sea in India.

There they call it the Mihrān river, and they also call it the river of
the Indians.

The source of the river Euphrates (is) from the border with 'Rome', and
it passes through Asūrestān and flows into the Tigris. And it is called
'Frād' because it produces something to drink (all) over the earth.

Cf. Avestan *frāda-* "to further, make prosper."

### Additional reading 10.2

From the *Hērbedestān*, about the vicissitudes of accompanying a woman
(wife of his teacher) away from her home to pursue religious studies.

/ ABwY\< WwaÅW tÂA WkLcÅ WklAkßA tÂA WtDwYkAcÅ áÒ µlaHwY\> WWTWtŸ:J tÂA

WtDWtŸ:J aÒ :jaÅ x ÍcÅ WtDWwsaD aÒ q WkmaD ÍcÅ xW\]ÇD EwÍwˆ˜ WWTWtŸ:J
WWP ÍtÂA WtDWWwaD ã

/ ABwY\< WwaÅW tÂA WkLcÅ WklAkßA tÂA :jaÅ WWP tÂA

*ka gādan dōšāram rāy abāgēnēd ka āškārag apparag ka nihān duzz.*

*ān bawēd ka-š pad gādan-menišnīh nayēd u-š ǰāmag abar nē dārēd u-š
andar hāsr nē gāyēd*

*ka pad hāsr ka āškārag apparag ud ka nihān duzz*

When he accompanies (her) because of desire to have sex with (her), if
it is in the open (he is) a 'robber', if in secret a 'thief'.

The above obtains when he leads her with the *intention* of having sex
with (her), but he does not lift her garment and does not have sex with
her *within* a league (from her house).

If he has sex with her *at* one league (or farther), (then) if it is in
the open, he is a 'robber' and if in secret a 'thief'.

Notes:

The terms 'robber' and 'thief' are technical legal terms and clearly
refers to offences committed openly ('robber') or in secret ('thief').

*ān bawēd* is a technical term meaning "that obtains, that is the case
(when)."

*gādan-menišnīh* "thinking about having sex," i.e., he *thinks*: "I
shall have sex," is a common way of expressing "intention" in Pahlavi.

Note the contrast *andar hāsr* "within a league" and *pad hāsr* "at a
league('s distance)."

### Additional reading 10.3

From the *Rivayat of Ādur-farrbay*: *RAF*.20. Questions and answers.
Note that *ka* "when" is often close to "if."

WtdAcÅ x EnßYW WWP nÍPW \^ NtåÅ WPwˆÅ nÍPW \^ NTWV WN AWvY / Ww˙JWWP

/ WWTWK EnßYW WWP vmaÅtJ WWP WwaHnLW áhAtÅP AWvY ã

/ aÒ WPwˆÅ WtDWWwaD esY\>WtDwA \^ WKPWK xWwˆÅW tÂA

*pursišn. mard kē duxt ī xwēš ayāb xwah ī xwēš pad zanīh andar abāyēd*

*ān mard pādixšāy awēšān pad stahmb pad zanīh kerdan.*

*ka kunēd kerbag ī xwēdōdahīh bawēd ayāb nē.*

Q: A man who needs his daughter or sister as wife, is that man
authorized to make her his wife by force?

When he does it, will there be (for him) merit of "*xwēdōdah*" (= for
performing *xwēdōdah*)?

Notes:

He presumably "needs" them for legal purposes: most probably to produce
an heir, perhaps for reasons of property and/or inheritance.

*xwēdōdah*, or next-of-kin marriage, was (apparently) widely practiced
in Sasanian Iran, although often, it seems, for purely practical (legal)
purposes.

*passox. čiyōn an dānam. xwah ayāb duxt pad ān ēwēnag pad stahmb zan
kerdan pādixšāy.*

*ka kunēd zanīh xūb, kerbag ī xwēdōdahīh ōh bawēd.*

*ka šōy nē hamdādestān kerdan nē pādixšāy ud wināh.*

A: As I know (it): He is authorized to make a sister or daughter his
wife in that manner by force.

When he does, then the wife-hood is "good," and he gets (the merit of)
the good deed in the usual way (*ōh*) for performing *xwēdōdah*.

When (her) husband does not agree, he is not authorized, and it is a
"sin."

Notes:

*pādixšāy* means "authorized (by law)."

Note that the suffix *-īh* in *xwēdōdahīh* serves to *quote* the word
(legal term) *xwēdōdah*.

Note the use of *ōh* to mean "in the usual, standard, way."

Note the use of *xūb* "good" to mean "valid, in order."

Q. Where is Gōbedšāh?

A. Gōbedšāh is in Ērānwēz in the continent of Xwanirah.

And from the feet to the waist he is a bull, and from the waist up
human.

And he always sits on the sea shore and sacrifices to the gods and pours
libations into the sea,

on account of which (= and therefore), by that libation pouring,
countless evil animals die in the sea.

For if, God forbid, he should not perform that sacrificing and should
not pour the libations into the ocean so that those countless evil
animals are destroyed, then whenever it rains, it rains evil animals
like rain.

### Additional readings 10.5-7: On the three-legged donkey

Several central terms for pollution and purification are found in the
texts below:

*nasāy*: dead matter, originates from bodies of humans and animals; it
is polluted by the female demon Nasuš, who needs to be exorcised by
washing (*šōy- šust*) or by a dog looking at the dead being/thing.

*daštān*: menstrual discharge.

*hixr*: excreted or vomited matter, hair and nails.

*pāk*: clean, about polluted objects that have been washed or have
become clean naturally, e.g., having lain outdoors for a specific time
period.

*yōǰdahr*: ritually clean and usable for ritual purposes, e.g., wood for
firewood.

*gōmēz*: cow's or bull's urine, used in addition to water to wash
polluted objects: first *gōmēz*, then water.

# Lesson 11

**Note:**

At this stage the students should start familiarizing themselves with
the use of MacKenzie's *Dictionary* if they have not already done so.

A pdf is currently available at
http://www.rabbinics.org/pahlavi/MacKenzie-PahlDict.pdf.

## Spelling 9

### The allophones /e/ and /o/

As already mentioned in lesson 1, MacKenzie introduced the use of the
vowels *e* and *o* in his *Dictionary*. MacKenzie assigned them, in
particular, to words in which the spelling of the vowel varies in the
manuscripts, although he did not do so consistently, e.g.:

*men-* "think" and *menišn-* "thought": usually spelled \<myn-\>,
occasionally \<mn-\>

*zofr* "deep": usually spelled LPU \<zwpl\>, occasionally LpZ \<zpl\>,
cf. *zofāy* ÄPU \<zwp'd\> "depth"

*homānāg* "similar (to)": spelled WkAwa˜WA \<hwm'n'k\'\> and WkAwaÂA
\<hm'n'k\'\>

*abaxšāyīdan*, *aboxšāyīdan* "forgive; withhold": spelled -áhAcÅ
\<'p̄hš'd-\> and -áhAWcÅ \<'p̄whš'd-\>

*škeft* or *škoft* "amazing(ly), very; harsh": spelled WTPkÍ \<škpt\'\>,
\<škypt\'\> TpYkÍ, and TPWkÍ \<škwpt\'\>

*padifrāh* or *pādofrāh* "punishment": spelled saÒPtÅP / aåÒPtÅP
\<p'tpl's/h\>

or saÒPWtÅP / aåÒWPtÅP \<p'twpl's/h\>

*pādixšāy* or *pādoxšāy* "authoritative": spelled áHAtÅ \<p'thš'd\> or
áHAWtÅ \<p'twhš'd\>

*pornāy*, *abornāy* "adult, minor (child): spelled ÄwLP , ÄwLcÅ \<pln'd,
'p̄ln'd\>,

more commonly ÄwLWP , ÄwLWcÅ \<pwln'd, 'p̄wln'd\>

Here, we will use the spellings *abaxšāyišnīh/abuxšāyišnīh*
*pādifrāh/pādufrāh*, *pādixšāy/pāduxšāy*, and *purnāy*,
*abarnāy/aburnāy*.

### Short *-u-* spelled without \<-w-\>

This spelling is found in a few words in MacKenzie's *Dictionary*, but
it is doubtful. The most common is *dudīgar* "second," after Manichean
\<dwdygr\>, with analogical \<dw-\> after *dō* "two," but the Pahl. form
is clearly *didī-gar* (from OPers. *duvitīya-*). Other words are
*drubušt* "fortress," most often spelled \<dlpwšt'\> *darbušt* (rarely
\<dlwpwšt\'\>), *kandāg* \<knd'k\> "magician," Man. \<*qnd'-*\> (MacK.
*kundāg* after NPers. *kondā*), *rubūd* \<lpwt\'\> for *rabūd* "rob,"
and *sidāb* \<st'p\'\> "rue" (NPers. *sodāb*).

The words *gund* "troop" and *gung* "deaf" are often spelled without
\<w\> (Mack.: \<gwnd\>, but \<g(w)ng\>), notably in the *Kār-nāmag*, but
these may be examples of influence from Persian.

## Grammar 11

### Plural of nouns and adjectives

Pahlavi originally had two cases, one reserved for [the (grammatical)
subject, i.e., the word with which the verb agrees]{.underline}, as well
as words qualifying the subject, and one for the other syntactic
functions.

The cases are distinguished in the 1st person pronoun *an* ∼ *man*; in
the plural of nouns and adjectives, where the oblique takes the ending
*-ān*; and in the family terms (see below).

The cases are commonly referred to as "direct" and "oblique," a
terminology that says little about either form or function. Thus, it may
be simpler just to remember that *an* "I" is only used as subject of
verbs and that the plural forms in *‑ān* are used when the noun is
[not]{.underline} the (grammatical) subject of a verb.

The older paradigm is thus as follows:

Singular Plural 1st person "I, me"

Subject *yazd* ***yazd** an*

Non-subject ***yazd** yazdān man*

The subject case is also used for the predicate of the verb "be,
become," as well as with verbs such as "be called," and for appositions
to the (grammatical) subject and the predicate, as well as the vocative.

The [direct object]{.underline} is sometimes in the subject case,
sometimes in the non-subject case. In this Introduction, we will simply
follow the manuscripts on this point.

The main uses of the non-subject case is as indirect object, as
possessor (including in *ān ī* constructions), after/before
pre/postpositions, and in impersonal expressions.

In the manuscripts, the forms in *-ān* are often used as subject as in
modern Persian, see below.

Examples:

*[pōryōtkēš]{.underline} hamāg pad ēn ham-dādestān bē [būd
hēnd]{.underline}*

"[the teachers of old have all been]{.underline} agreed about this"
(*DD*.40.6)

*[awēšān ātaxš ī sōzēnd]{.underline} ī xwarg [nē kunēnd]{.underline} ā
čē*

"[those fires which burn which make]{.underline} no embers what (are
they)?" (*PR*.35c.7)

*[amahrspand dārēnd]{.underline} dāmān, [baxšēnd]{.underline} rāy ud
xwarrah ō gēhān, ēdōn-iz abārīg [mēnōy yazd]{.underline}*

"[the amahrspands maintain]{.underline} the creations,
[bestow]{.underline} Light and Xwarrah on living beings, thus also [the
other gods]{.underline} in the other world" (*Dk*.3.51.3)

*ān paydāg kū Zardušt ān zamān [abāg yazdān]{.underline} wēš būd estād
u-š [yazd]{.underline} āšnāgtar [būd hēnd]{.underline}*

"that is manifest: at that time, Zardušt had been more [with the
gods]{.underline}, and [the gods were]{.underline} more familiar to him"
(after *PY*.9.1)

*az pāy pēšārwār ma kun kū pad dād ī [dēwān]{.underline} griftār nē bawē
u-t ān wināh rāy [dēw]{.underline} ō dōšox nē kešēnd*

"do not urinate standing, so that you do not become 'seized' by the law
[of the demons]{.underline} and [the demons]{.underline} do not drag you
to hell for that sin!" (*MX*.1.39-41)

#### Plural of adjectives

Adjectives used with nouns ending in *-ān* can take no ending or the
ending *-ān* (*-īn*, see below).

*2 srišwādag [Ēr deh]{.underline} ahlaw hēnd ud ēk druwand*

"[the Iranian towns]{.underline} are (i.e., will be) two-thirds Rightous
and one(-third) wicked" (*Dk*.7.9.13)

*pad abāz-estišnīh ī ān ī dēwān bēš ud ān-iz ī [mardōmān ī
wadag]{.underline}*

"to withstand the hostility of the demons, as well as that of [bad
people]{.underline}" (*PY*.68.8)

*ō [abēzagān mardōmān]{.underline}* "to pure people"

*[ahlawān mardān zanān]{.underline} yazam. [driyōšān mardān
zanān]{.underline} yazam [druwandān mardān zanān]{.underline} nē*
*yazam*

"I sacrifice for the Righteous men and women. I sacrifice for the poor
men and women; I do not sacrifice for wicked men and women" (after
*Dk*.7.3.38, cf. *WZ*.12.6, below)

When adjectives are used as nouns, they regularly take the ending, e.g.:

*ēn mard [wehān ud arzānīgān ud driyōšān]{.underline} padīrēd u-šān tis
dahēd*

"this man receives the good, worthy, and poor and gives them something
(after *AWN*.68.3)

*kē hučašmīh ī [wehān]{.underline} xwāhēd ud xwad-iz pad wehīh ī andar
[wehān]{.underline} wēnēd hučašm bawēd*

"he who seeks the benevolence of the good, he will himself, too, be
benevolent because of the goodness he sees in the good" (*MX*.36.17)

*u-š ham-ōwōn pad rōšnīh kāmag čiyōn pad-iz [tārān]{.underline}*

"and he desired (*-š kāmag \... pad*) the light, as (he desired)
[dark]{.underline} (places)" (*WZ*.1.3)

#### The plural ending *-īn* with pronouns and nouns

In early Pahlavi, there were two alternative endings for oblique plural
*-ān*: *-īn*, and *-ūn*, e.g., *zanīn* "of/to the women," *ǰehīn*
(*ǰahīn*) "of/to wicked women," *frazendīn* "of/to the children," and
*dušmenūn* "of/to the enemies."

In Book Pahlavi, the ending *-īn* survives in the numerals (Lesson 9),
the pronominal forms *harwīn* and *harwispīn* from *harw* and *harwisp*
"every, all" and *čandīn* from *čand* "how many?" (the forms *harwist*,
*harwistīn* are also common), as well as sporadically in nouns:

*abar ō [harwispīn kišwar]{.underline} kē haft*

"onto all the seven continents" (*PY*.65.5) -- Note that *kišwar* does
not have the ending.

***čandīn mardān pad āfrāh ō zōd radīhā** kū pad yašt-ēw rāspīg čand
dastwarīhā*

"(with) how many men to inform the main priest (*zōd*) is according to
the *rad*s (ritual models), i.e., for one ritual, how many auxiliary
priests (*rāspīg*) (are) according to sanctioned practice?" --- Here
*čandīn mardān* renders Av. *cuuaiti narąm* "how many men?"

*ātaxš ī [zanīn]{.underline} nišāst sālārīh pad zan*

"guardianship of a fire endowed (lit. enthroned) of (by)
[women]{.underline} (rests) with the woman (who endowed it)"
(*MHDA*.50.4.15)

*ahlāyīh yazam ahlawān driyōšān mardān [zanīn]{.underline} yazam*

"I sacrifice for the Righteousness of Righteous, poor men and women"
(*WZ*.12.6, cf. *Dk*.7.3.38, above)

*ud ōy-iz druz ī hu-zahagīh marnǰēnīdār ī zāyišn wizūdār pādīrāngar ī
mādagān petyāragtom [ǰahīn]{.underline} srādag*

"and that lie-demon too which destroys easy birth, ruins and impedes
birth, the greatest adversary of females, the species [of evil
women]{.underline}" (*Dk*.5.24.19b)

Note *duzz duzzīn appar apparīn* "thief of thieves, robber of robbers"
(*PV*.4.1).

####  The "family terms" 

In Iranian languges in general and Pahlavi in particular, the family
terms *father*, etc. (cf. Lesson 7), have some irregular forms (cf. Eng.
*brother*, *brethren*).

In early Pahlavi, they took the ending *-ar* in the plural, but also in
the singular in the same positions that plural nouns take *-ān*, hence
they are also called *r*-stems. This distribution is still often found
in the Pahlavi texts:

Singular Plural

Subject *pid* ***pidar***

Non-subject ***pidar*** *pidarān*

The word *pus* "son" was originally not an *r*-stem, and so had *pus* in
the singular and non-subject plural. In the texts, it is often declined
as an *r*-stem, however, and in *PR*.26.2, all the mss. have *pusarīn*
instead of *pusarān*.

The *Psalter* also has *pidarūn* \<ptlwn\>.

Examples:

*[az pidar]{.underline} nāmburdār bāš bē harw-ēwēnag [mād]{.underline}
ma āzār*

"carry the name [of (your) father]{.underline}, but do not bother (your)
[mother]{.underline} in every way!" (*PKX*.2c)

*[pidar]{.underline} ī gēhān hēd*

"you are [the]{.underline} [fathers]{.underline} (= parents) of living
beings" (*Bd.*14.11)

*pus ī Frēdōn rāy xānag az abarmānd [ī pidarān]{.underline} was būd*

"Frēdōn's son had many houses [from (his) parents'/fathers']{.underline}
inheritance"

*awēšān rasēnd kē [pus]{.underline} ī Zarduxšt [hēnd]{.underline}*

"those will come who [are the sons]{.underline} of Zarduxšt
(*Dk*.7.8.50)

*pas gōwēd kay-Wištāsp-šāh kū agar [hamāg pus ud brād]{.underline} ud
wispuhrag ī man kay-Wištāsp-šāh [murd bawēnd]{.underline} ēg-im ēn
abēzag dēn ī mazdēsn bē nē hilam*

"then King Kay Wištāsp says: if [all my sons, brothers, and princes are
to die]{.underline}, I shall not relinquish this pure Mazdayasnian
*dēn*" (*AZ*.68)

*[awēšān pusarān ud brādarān]{.underline} ud wispuhragān ī tō rām-šahr
kay-Wištāsp-šāh andar ān diz bē framāy nišastan*

"O King Kay Wištāsp, of peaceful land, order [those your sons,
brothers]{.underline}, and princes to sit in that fortress!" (*AZ*.62)

*ka pad kāmag abāg zanān [pusarān duxtarān]{.underline}* \<BREl'n
BRTEl'n\> *xwaš bē šāyēd nišastan pad rāh ī tō*

"when one can sit pleasantly at will with one's wives, sons, and
daughters, it is by way of (≈ through) you (Mihr)" (after *StS*.16.16)

###  Feminine nouns and adjectives.

A few nouns and adjectives have special feminine endings. These are
found mainly in the oldest manuscripts of the *Pahlavi Avesta*:

*ahurānīy* "lady" (Av. *ahurānī-*, fem. of *ahura-* "lord").

*ahlaw*, fem. *ahlawēnīy* (J2, K5), *ahlawīy* \<'hlwbwy\> (Mf4, Pt4),
plur. *ahlawīyān* \<'hlwbwy'n\> (Mf4, Pt4; also in *StS*.19)

*ašō* \<'šwk\'\>, fem. *ašōnīy* \<'šwknyḏ\> (*NM*.1.7.10).

*mānbed*, fem. *mānbedīn* (*PVr*.3.3), *mānbedīy* (*PVyt*.3.5c \[17\]
\<m'nptyh\>), Av. *nmānō.paθnīm/paθniiå*.

*Frawāg*, fem. *Frawāgīy* (*Bd*.14.33, *IndBd*. *Fravākayn* in Avestan
script).

Examples:

***mādagān rad gōwam dēn ī mazdēsnān** \... **kē-iz dō-padištān
ahlawēnīy/ahlawīy** kū zan-ēw ī nēk u-š rad ī mādagān gōwam **ēn zamīg
kē ān ī amāh** dahišn ud **burdār** u-š rad ī mādagān gōwam*

"'(as) model of the females I say the Mazdayasnian *dēn* \... and
who(ever) is a Righteous (woman) among bipeds,' i.e., a good woman, her
I say (is) the model of the females, (namely) 'this earth who is our
carrier/womb,' her I say (is) the model of the females" (*PY*.13.1)

*ma \... rasād ō ātaxš ma ō āb ma ō zamīg ma ō gōspand ma ō urwar ma ō
mard ī ahlaw ma ō nāyrīg ī ahlawēnīy/ahlawīy*

"let her (the corpse demon) not come \[subj.\] upon the fire nor the
water nor the earth nor the animals nor the plants nor the Righteous man
nor the Righteous woman!" (*PV*.9.33)

*ēn-iz xwāham az xwābar Ohrmazd dādār ī harw nēkīh kū-mān ān hayārīh ī
az [ahlawīyān]{.underline} ī wehān ī abzārān ī abzōnīgān frawahr
bowandagīhā awiš rasād*

"this too I ask of merciful Ohrmazd, the Creator of every goodness, that
that assistance from the [Righteous]{.underline}, good, strong,
beneficent *frawahr*s \[female!\] may come to us in full measure
(*bowandagīhā*) (*StS*.19.11)

### The use of endings in the manuscripts.

All our Pahlavi manuscripts were written in or after the 13th century,
that is, well into the modern Persian period, when the case distinctions
had been lost. In early modern Persian, therefore, the forms in *-ān*
simply indicated plural, and the family terms could take the shorter or
longer forms, for instance, according to metrical requirements or at the
whim of the writer.

The pronoun *an* "I" had simply disappeared by then and been replaced by
*man*.

This practice shows up in the Pahlavi manuscripts, as well, but, in good
manuscripts based on strong traditions, the older distribution of the
forms is still very common, e.g.:

*[amahrspandān ud yazd]{.underline} bē rasēnd ud nē niyōšēnd ud bē
padīrēnd*

"the amahrspands and the gods arrive and do not listen, but accept"
(*ŠnŠ*.9.10)

[In the exercises in this Introduction, the students are expected to use
the original distribution.]{.underline} Examples of actual usage in the
texts will be found in the manuscript samples given from this lesson on.

###  Interrogative pronouns and adverbs

Interrogative pronouns and adverbs are made from the same stems as
relative pronouns (*k-*, *č-*), as in English, e.g. *who*, *which*,
etc.:

*kē* WN \<MNW\> "who?"

*kē'ān*/*ke'ān* WwAWN \<MNW'n\'\> "whose?"

*ān ī kē* WN Y ã \<ZK Y MNW\> "whose?"

*kadām* µATK \<kt'm\> **"**which?"

*kadār* lATK \<kt'l\> **"**which (usually of two)?"

*[kē]{.underline} ham ud [kē]{.underline} xwēš ham*

"[who]{.underline} am I, and [whose]{.underline} am I (= who do I belong
to)?" (*PN*.1)

*awēšān [ān ī kē]{.underline} ruwān*

"[whose]{.underline} souls are those?" (after *AWN*)

*[kē]{.underline} hē ud az [ke'ān]{.underline} hē*

"[who]{.underline} are you, and from [whom]{.underline} are you?"
(*PY*.43.7; *Dk*.7.3.55 spelled \<MNW ZK\>!)

*az [kadām]{.underline} paywand ud tōhmag ham*

"of [which]{.underline} lineage and descent am I?" (*PN*.1)

*zamīg [kadār]{.underline} gyāg mustōmandtar*

"[which]{.underline} place (of/in) the earth is more oppressed?" (*or*
"as for the earth, which place \...") (*Bd*.9.11)

*[kadār]{.underline}-itān sūdōmandtar sahēd*

"[which]{.underline} (alternative) seems more profitable to you?"
(*Bd*.3.26)

*[kadār]{.underline} ast weh [kadār]{.underline} wehtar ud
[kadār]{.underline} az harwispīn pahlom*

"[which]{.underline} is there (that is) good, [which]{.underline} is
better, and [which]{.underline} is best of all?" (*WZ*.22.3)

Note *kadām gyāg* "in which place?":

*[kadām gyāg]{.underline} brēhēnīd Ohrmazd pad bun-dahišn ǰōrdāy*

"[in which place]{.underline} did Ohrmazd fashion barley at the first
creation?" (after *Dk*.8.31.30)

*kay* tÂïÅ \<AYMT\> "when?"

*kū* à \<AYK\> "where?"

*az kū* "from where, whence?"

*ō kū* "to where, whither?"

*abar čē ud pad čē ud ō čē ud [az kū]{.underline} ud [ō kū]{.underline}
abāz [ō kū]{.underline}*

"about what and with what and to what and [from where]{.underline} and
[to where]{.underline} (and) back [to where]{.underline}?"
(*Dk*.3.222.1)

*az bunīh [kū]{.underline} būd ham ud [kay]{.underline} mad ham ud ēdar
čē kunam*

*ud [kay]{.underline} bē šawam ud čim bē šawam ud ka bē šawam [ō
kū]{.underline} šawam*

"from the beginning, where was I? and when did I come? and what am I
doing here?

and when do I go (from here)? and why do I go? and, when I go, to where
do I go?" (*Dk*.6E.3)

Note also *kū gyāg* "where?":

*ka ān ī ahlaw bē widerēd ruwān šab ī fradom ud didīgar ud sidīgar kū
gyāg nišīnēd*

"when the soul of the Righteous passes away, where does it sit the
first, second, and third nights?" (*DD*.23.1)

*ēn mardōm [az kū gyāg]{.underline} abāz āxēzēnd*

"these people (who died), [from where]{.underline} will they rise
again?" (*ŠnŠSup*.17.11)

*ahlawān ud druwandān ō kū gyāg šawēnd*

"[to where]{.underline} do the Righteous and the wicked go?" (*DD*.19.1)

*čē* nM \<ME\> "what?"

*čē rāy* áÒ nM \<ME l'd\> "for what reason, why?"

*čē ēwēnag* WKwYwïÅ nM \<ME 'dwynk\'\> "what kind of?"

*pad čē ēwēnag* WKwYwïÅ nM WWP \<PWN ME 'dwynk\'\> "in what way? how?"

Note: On *če'ān-iz* "anything," see Lesson 12.

*[čē]{.underline} dānē kū*

"[what]{.underline} do you know (about the fact) that?" (= "how do you
know that?") (*Dk*.6.214)

*ān 2 aswār ī ō ēn kustag rōn āmad [čē zamān]{.underline} bē widerd*

"[when]{.underline} did those two horsemen who came in this direction
pass through?" (*KN*.4.9)

*awēšān [kē]{.underline} hēnd ud [čē rāy]{.underline} ēdar estēnd*

"[who]{.underline} are those and [why]{.underline} do they stand here?"
(*AWN*.6.2)

*kū pad gyān ī xwadāyān kōxšēnd [pad čē]{.underline} dārē*

"when they make an attempt upon the life of lords, [how]{.underline} do
you regard it?" (cf. *pad ēd dāram* "I consider, I think (that)") (after
*KN*.10.9)

*čand* YWC \<cnd\> "how much, how many?"

*čim (rāy)* MC \<cm\> "why?"

*čiyōn* WwSC \<cygwn\> "how?"

*[čand]{.underline} āyēnd xyōn az bunag [čand]{.underline} aswār āyēnd
[čand]{.underline} mīrēnd ud [čand]{.underline} abāz šawēnd*

"[how many]{.underline} Xyōns will be coming from the camp? [How
many]{.underline} will come on horseback? [How many]{.underline} will
die? And [how many]{.underline} will go back?" (*AZ*.65)

*Ahrimen drāyēd kū druwand bē ō gilistag ī man [čim]{.underline} āmad
hē*

"Ahrimen howls: O wicked one, [why]{.underline} have you come to my
den?" (*PR*.23.33)

*mard ī ašō ēn mehīh [čē čim rāy]{.underline} ast*

"[why]{.underline} does the Righteous Man have this greatness?
(*DD*.3.1)

The question words can be placed at the end of the question (as in
modern Persian), e.g.:

*ān mard ī-š abāg pad asp [kē]{.underline}*

"[who]{.underline} is that man who is with him on the horse?"
(*KN*.3.19)

*Kang-diz [kū gyāg]{.underline} estēd war ī ǰamkerd [kū]{.underline}
kerd estēd tan ī Sām [kū gyāg]{.underline} nibayēd ud mānišn ī Srōš kū*

"the wise man asked the Spirit of Wisdom: [where]{.underline} is the
Kang fortress? [where]{.underline} is the bunker made which J̌am made?
[where]{.underline} does Sām's body lie? and where is Srōš's dwelling?"
(*MX*.61.1-5)

*dōšox [čiyōn]{.underline} ud [čand]{.underline}. ud ahlawān andar
wahišt dādēstān [čē]{.underline} ud nēkīh [az čē]{.underline}*

"Hell is how and how many? And what is the judgement for/of the
Righteous in Paradise, and [from what]{.underline} is the goodness
(there)?" (*MX*.6.4)

##### Substantivized forms:

See also Lesson 17 for these forms, e.g.:

*(Srid) abāz ō Kāy-Us šud u-š az [čē-ēwēnagīh]{.underline} āgāhēnīd*

"Srid went back to Kay Us and informed him of how it was" (*WZ*.4.15)

*ān zand āgāhīh \... pas abar xīr kē gēhān dārēd pad wizārišn ī [čē'īh
ud čiyōnīh]{.underline}*

"that awareness of the Zand \... is next about the stuff that the world
of the living contains, with an explanation of [what and how it
is]{.underline}" (*Bd*.0.0)

### Alternative questions

These are formed with *ayāb* "or," e.g.:

*ēn yazišn ō yazdān rasēd [ayāb]{.underline} ō dēwān*

"does this sacrifice come to the gods [or]{.underline} to the demons?"

Regular questions can also be formulated as alternative questions by
adding *ayāb nē* "or not," where *ayāb nē* does not necessarily have to
be translated, e.g.:

*tō ēd dānē* *[ayāb nē]{.underline}* "do you know this [or
not]{.underline}?"

*pad tuxšāgīh xīr ud xwāstag ī gētīy ō xwēš šāyēd kerdan [ayāb
nē]{.underline}*

"is it possible to appropriate the things and possessions of this world
by diligence [or not]{.underline}?" (*MX*.21.2)

### Negative questions

*[nē]{.underline} wād tō dād āb tō dād gil tō dād ātaxš tō dād harw tis
tō dād*

"[did you not]{.underline} establish the wind, the water, the clay, the
fire, and everything?" (*PR*.36.7)

### Indirect questions

Indirect questions are regular questions preceded by *kū* (cf. Lesson
4), e.g.:

*gōw [kū]{.underline} ān 3 tis [čē]{.underline}*

"say: those three things (are) [what]{.underline}? = say what those
three things are!" (*Bd*.36A.1)

*abar bē šnāxtan ī-š waččag [kū]{.underline} kadām gōspand*

"about knowing its child: [which]{.underline} animal? = about how he is
to know to which animal the child belongs" (*Dk*.8.23.7)

*abar xwānam zamīg ud az-iš xwāham ast ud gōšt ud pay ī Gayōmard ud
abārīgān.*

*gōwēd zamīg kū čiyōn rasēnam, ka nē ēn bē dānam [kū]{.underline}
[kadār]{.underline} ān ī ōy ast ud [kadār]{.underline} ān ī ōy*

"(Ohrmazd said:) I shall call up the earth and request from her the
bones, flesh, and tendons of Gayōmard and the others. The earth says:
How shall I make that happen, when I do not know (this:)
[which]{.underline} are this one's bones and [which]{.underline} are
that one's?" (*WZ*.34.8)

### Alternative indirect questions

These are of various types, e.g.:

*čiyōn gōwēd kū [kadār/kadām]{.underline} pēš dād xwarrah
[ayāb]{.underline} tan*

"as it says (in the *dēn*): [which]{.underline} was established first:
the Xwarrah [or]{.underline} the body? (*Bd*.14.8)

*ašmāh dānēd [kū]{.underline} ēn yazišn ō yazdān rasēd
[ayāb]{.underline} ō dēwān*

"do you know: does this sacrifice come the gods [or]{.underline} the
demons?" (= [whether]{.underline} this sacrifice comes to the gods
[or]{.underline} the demons?" (after *AWN*1.15)

*āfrāh ī dēn zēnāwandīhā abar tuxšēd tā dānēd* *[kadār ayāb]{.underline}
ahlaw [ayāb]{.underline} druwand wurrōyēd meh*

*kū kasān [ayāb]{.underline} ān ī ahlaw tuxšāgīhātar wurrōyēd
[ayāb]{.underline} ān ī druwand*

"apply yourselves vigilently to the instructions of the *dēn* so
that/until you know [which]{.underline} (of the two):
[either]{.underline} a Righteous [or]{.underline} a wicked believes
greater = whether a Righteous or a wicked person believes more
(diligently) than (other) people, (i.e.) whether the Righteous one or
the wicked one believes the most diligently" (*PN*.53 + *PY*.31.17)
(note the word order, cf. Lesson 4)

*dōšox azēr ī zamīg az azabar abar asmān u-š dar ul ō zamīg*

*ēn [kū]{.underline} abar bērōn asmān ast [ayāb nē]{.underline} ā-m nē
rōšnag*

"Hell is under the earth, (but) up above the sky (beneath the earh), and
it has a door up to the earth;

[whether]{.underline} 'above' (means) outside the sky [or
not]{.underline} is not clear to me" (*PV*.3.7)

### Relative pronouns and relative clauses

Of the three relative pronouns *kē*, *ī*, and *čē*, the relative pronoun
*čē* is relatively rare; it is used mainly when the referent is not
specific (that which, everything that, whatever).

Relative pronouns are most often used as subject, direct object, and
possessive (genitive).

Relative pronouns usually have an "antecedent," that is, a noun,
adjective, or pronoun that they refer to. The antecedent may be separate
and quite a distance from the relative pronoun, e.g.:

*Ardawān rāy [kanīzag]{.underline}-ēw abāyišnīg būd [kē]{.underline} az
abārīg kanīzagān āzarmīgtar ud grāmīgtar dāšt*

"Ardawān had a (certain) attractive (servant) [girl]{.underline},
[whom]{.underline} he held (= who was to him) more beloved and more dear
than the other girls" (*KN*.3.1)

*amāh haft xwah rāy [brād]{.underline} ēn ēk ast [kē]{.underline}-mān
zīyišn ud dārišn*

"we seven sisters have (only) this one brother, [who]{.underline} is our
life (= livelihood) and upkeep" (*AWN*.2.4)

*ān [menišn]{.underline} agriftār ud [kunišn]{.underline} griftārōmand
[čē]{.underline} mardōmān pad kunišn kunēnd*

"[that thought]{.underline} (is) intangible and (that)
[action]{.underline} tangible [which]{.underline} people perform in
their action (= when they act)" (*PN*.25)

*kē* and *ī* often alternate in the same sentence, e.g.:

*Ādur yazd ō Ardā Wirāz war-ēw nimūd ud guft ēn [ān āb]{.underline} ast
[kē]{.underline} az [ān esm]{.underline} bē tazīd [ī]{.underline} tō
abar ō man nihād*

"the divine Fire showed Ardā Wirāz a lake and said: this is [that water
which]{.underline} flowed from [the firewood that]{.underline} you laid
on me" (after *AWN*.10.8)

##### *ī ast* "that is":

*4 pēšag ī ast āsrōnīh ud artēštārīh ud wāstaryōšīh hutuxšīh*

"the four estates, that is: priesthood, military, husbandry, artisanate"
(*Dj*.7.1.20)

#### Indefinite relative pronouns

Sometimes the antecedent is missing, in which case we must translate the
relative pronoun as "he who, someone who, whoever" and "that which,
something which, whatever," e.g.:

*pad ēd dāram kū wahišt ast ud dōšox ast ud [kē]{.underline} ruwān weh
ān ō wahišt šawēd ud [kē]{.underline} ruwān wattar ān ō dōšox ōftēd*

"I think that Paradise and Hell exist and (he) [whose]{.underline} soul
is good goes to Paradise and (he) [whose]{.underline} soul is bad falls
into Hell"

*ōy ēdōn homānāg čiyōn [kē]{.underline} sar ī mardōmān pad dast dārēd ud
mazg ī mardōmān xwarēd*

"he is like (someone) [who]{.underline} holds people's heads in his
hands and eats people's brains" (*MX*.1.49)

*ud [čē]{.underline} andar ān dar*

"and (that) [which]{.underline} is in that chapter"

*[kē]{.underline} kamēd kū [čē]{.underline}-š az yazdān xwāhēd abērtar
windēd, yazišn ī yazdān gōwizār ē kunēd*

"[(he) who]{.underline} (= whoever) wishes that he more often gets
(that) [which]{.underline} (= whatever) he asks of the gods, let him
perform a detailed sacrifice to the gods" (*Dk*.6.125)

[Indefiniteness]{.underline} can be emphasized by adding *ēč* before the
relative pronoun, e.g.:

*[ēč kē]{.underline} būd hēnd ud [ēč kē]{.underline} bawēnd [ud
ēč]{.underline} kē hēnd*

"[whoever]{.underline} have been, [whoever]{.underline} will be, and
[whoever]{.underline} are" (*PN*.21)

[Indefinite alternatives]{.underline} are expressed by repetition of
*kē*, *čē*, and *kū*, e.g.:

##### *kē \... kē*:

*hāmōyēn dām ud dahišn ī dādār Ohrmazd \... [kē]{.underline} zāyišnīg ud
[kē-iz]{.underline} ārōyišnīg*

"the entire creation of the Creator Ohrmazd \... (be it that)
[which]{.underline} is still to be born and (that) [which]{.underline}
is still to grow (*or* whether still to be born and still to grow)"
(*MX*.48.23)

*ud 57 sāl Sōšāns rist hangēzēnēd ud harwisp mardōm hangēzēnēnd
[kē]{.underline} ahlaw [kē]{.underline} druwand mardōm harw kas az ānōh
ul hangēzēnd*

"and for 57 years Sōšāns will raise the dead, and they will raise all
people, (be it those) [who]{.underline} (are) Righteous (be it those)
[who]{.underline} are wicked (people), everybody will be raised from
there" (*Bd*.34.7)

##### *čē \... čē*:

*tar-menišnīh ī dēn abāz-stāyišnīh az-iš nē dāštan ī dastwar
xwad-dōšagīhā raft*

*abārīg andar ham dar čiyōn pad hangerdīg [čē]{.underline} ag-dēnīh [tā
čē]{.underline} a-dēnīh nām*

"scorning the *dēn*, 'back-praising' (oneself) from it, not having a
*dastwar*, behaving bstinately,

(and all) the other things of the same sort, as called succinctly
[whether]{.underline}/[be it]{.underline} 'having an evil *dēn*'
[or]{.underline}/[be it]{.underline} even (*tā čē*) 'having no *dēn*'"
(*Dk*.5.9.5)

*ud pas az Gayōmard andar zamān zamānag \... hamē bahr az-iš*

*čand dānišn āgāhīh ud kunišn bōzišn ī mardōm ī ān āwām kē padiš ō
paydāgīh mad abāyišnīg būd*

*[čē]{.underline} pad ham-pursagīh ī ō dādār ud [čē]{.underline}
waxš-abar-burdārīh ī abartarīg pad dādār framān*

"after Gayōmard, at various times \... a few parts (were revealed) from
it (= the *dēn*):

as much knowledge and science and action that was needed for the
salvation of the people who appeared in that age,

[be it]{.underline} through conversation with the Creator, [be
it]{.underline} through the prophecy from on high, at the order of the
Creator" (*Dk*.7.1.8)

##### *kū \... kū*:

*ēn dēn \... andar hamāg gēhān [kū]{.underline} abēzagīhā ud
[kū]{.underline} gumēzagīhā rawāg kerd estēd*

"this *dēn* was propagated in the whole world, [in some
places]{.underline} in its pure state, i[n other places]{.underline} in
a mixed state" (*Dk*.5.24.14)

#### "Case forms" of relative pronouns

The relative pronouns do not have case forms, and possession and other
syntactic functions can be expressed in the clause, either by a pronoun
or by a possessive or prepositional phrase (cf. Lesson 4 on "whose"),
e.g.:

*harw [kē-š]{.underline} ān wād [pad]{.underline} wēnīg abar šawēd bē
larzēd ud bē ōftēd*

"everybody ([who]{.underline} up [his]{.underline} nose ⇾) up
[whose]{.underline} nose that wind goes, trembles and falls"
(*AWN*.18.4)

*ān widarg kū abar āmad xwad ast rāh ī ō dōšox [kē pad ān]{.underline}
dwārēnd dēw ī druwand*

"that passage where (Ahrimen) came up is itself (= is nothing but) the
road to Hell, ([which on that]{.underline} ⇾) [on which]{.underline} the
wicked demons run" (*WZ*.2.5)

*nēk ōy [kē az ān ī ōy]{.underline} nēkīh kadār-iz-ēw nēkīh*

"good for him ([who from his]{.underline} ⇾) [from whose]{.underline}
goodness (comes) whichever goodness (= any goodness there is)" (Pahl.
*Aṣ̌əm vohū*)

*ēn ruwān ī awēšān mardōmān hēnd [kē-šān]{.underline} kerbag ud wināh
rāst būd*

"these are the souls of those people (who their ⇾) [whose]{.underline}
good and bad deeds were equal" (*AWN*.6.3)

*ēn mardōm būd hēnd [kē-šān]{.underline} rōšnīh ō rōšnīh ī xwaršēd
homānāg būd*

"these were people [whose]{.underline} light was similar to the light of
the sun" (*AWN*.9.2)

Cf. adverbial clauses of place:

*stāyēm gar ī buland [kū]{.underline} [ānōh]{.underline} hōm rust estē*

"I/we praise the lofty mountain ([where there]{.underline} ⇾)
[where]{.underline} you, Hōm, have grown" (*PY*.10.3)

[Note that prepositions do not usually precede the relative
pronoun]{.underline}, but come later in the clause, e.g.:

*zan ān wattar [kē abāg]{.underline} pad rāmišn zīyistan nē šāyēd*

"the worst wife is she [with whom]{.underline} it is not possible to
live in peace" (*MX*.32.14)

*gāw zōd rafēd [kē]{.underline} [andar]{.underline} dārišn*

"the bull attacks the priest, [in]{.underline} [whose]{.underline}
keeping (it is)" (*PY*.11.1)

*mān homānāg [kē]{.underline} harw tis [andar]{.underline} pāyēd*

"like a house [in which]{.underline} he guards everything" (*Bd*.1A.6)

*ramag [ī]{.underline} gōspand ēw [andar]{.underline} kē nasāy ǰūd estēd
nē dānēd kū kadām*

"a herd [in which]{.underline} (is) a sheep that has chewed *nasāy*,
(and) one does not know which" (*ZFJ*.437)

Not: "a herd of sheep 'in which' *nasāy* has been chewed \..."

### 

### The use of Pre- and postpositions with enclitic pronouns 1

This and subsequent sections on this topic contain some of the trickiest
syntax of Pahlavi and needs to be studied carefully.

Most prepositions, simple and combined, can govern an enclitic pronoun,
e.g.:

*u-m kāmist [pad pēš]{.underline}-[iš]{.underline} namāz burdan*

"and I wished to bear homage [before]{.underline} [him]{.underline}"
(*AWN*.11.4)

*mard-ēw was wazurg [abāg]{.underline}-[iš]{.underline} pad asp nišast
estād*

"a very large man was sitting [with him]{.underline} on the horse"
(*KN*.4.22)

As we have seen before, [pre]{.underline}positions often turn up as
[post]{.underline}positions, as when they govern relative pronouns and
enclitic pronouns. This also happens in other cases, where it is
sometimes difficult to decide whether we are dealing with a postposition
or a preverb, e.g.:

##### Following the pronoun directly:

*u-[šān]{.underline} [mayān]{.underline} tuhīgīh būd*

"and [between]{.underline} [them]{.underline} was emptiness" (*Bd*.1.5)

*u-[šān]{.underline} [pērāmōn]{.underline} dēwār bē estēnīd*

"and around them a wall had been set up" (*Dk*.7.2.23)

cf.

*pērāmōn ī Sāsān estēnd*

"they stand around Sāsān" (*KN*.1.9)

##### Separated from the pronoun:

*u-š kōšk asēmēn ud dandānag zarrēn u-[š]{.underline} 14 kōf
[andar]{.underline}*

*u-[š]{.underline} 7 rōd nāydāg [andar]{.underline} u-[š]{.underline}
haft murw kē-š pānagīh pad xwadāyīh šāyēd kerdan [andar]{.underline}*

"and (castle Kang) has a silver turret and golden crenelations, and
there are 14 mountains [inside it]{.underline}

and seven deep rivers [inside it]{.underline}, and (there are) seven
birds [inside it]{.underline}, which it can (*-š \...šāyēd*) protect
(*pānagīh \... kerdan*) by its reign" (*PR*.49.7)

##### With relative pronoun:

*tis-iz ēč ast ī hamāg āhōgēnīd estēd
[kē]{.underline}-iz-[iš]{.underline} gōhr [andar]{.underline} gumēxt
estēd*

"there is something that is all polluted and also (something) ([which
into it]{.underline} ⇾) [into which]{.underline} jewels are mixed, as
well (*-iz*)" (after *Bd*.18.13)

#### *az*, *ō*, and *pad* governing enclitics

The prepositions *az* "from," *ō* "to," and *pad* "on, with" regularly
govern the 3rd singular enclitic pronoun. More rarely they govern other
enclitic pronouns.

In these functions, these three prepositions are usually written
phonetically, not with arameograms, although spellings with arameograms
are found in a very few manuscripts, e.g.:

*az-iš* ÍcÅ \<hcš\> "from him, her, it"

*pad-iš* ÍTP \<ptš\> "on him, her, it"

*aw-iš* ÍBwA \<'wbš\> "to him, her, him"

Examples:

***[aw-]{.underline}*:**

*andar ēw rōz mard ēn hamāg tis (ī) bē [aw-iš]{.underline} rasēd \...*

"in one day, this man, all these things (that) come [to him]{.underline}
\..." (*PR*.28c.1)

*darbuštīh āsmān kerd kū petyārag [aw-iš]{.underline} gumēxtan nē tuwān*

"the heaven was made (to be) a fortress, so that the Adversary was not
able to mingle himself [into it]{.underline}" (*Bd*.4.27)

*rasēd [aw-išān]{.underline} sūd ī az frārōnīh*

"the benefit of honesty comes [to them]{.underline}" (*Dk*.9.39.6)

*abar wizīn ī artēštārān rōzīg artēštārān stōr ud ǰāmag abzār \... ī
[aw-išān]{.underline} dahišn*

"about the selection of the soldiers' daily (needs): the soldiers'
beasts, clothes, tools \... which should be given (*dahišn*) [to
them]{.underline}" (*Dk*.8.26.2)

***[az-]{.underline}*:**

*ud ēn-iz nihang-ēw [az-iš]{.underline}*

"and this too is a chapter [from]{.underline} (i.e., in)
[it]{.underline}" (*Dk*.7.8.11)

*ēn frašn [az-iš]{.underline} pursīd kū*

"this question was asked [of him]{.underline}"

*3 zrēy ī meh ud 30 zrēy ī keh [az-iš]{.underline} būd*

"three great seas and 30 small seas arose [from it]{.underline}"
(*Bd*.6B.17)

*az aspān astar ī az asp ud xar ī ō ēč [az-išān]{.underline} nē homānāg*

"among horses, the mule, which (is) from a horse and a donkey, (is) not
like any (*ēč \... nē*) [of them]{.underline}" (after *Dk*.3.80.16)

*ud Ohrmazd ō Zardušt guft kū yazdān stāy u-šān hamīh xwāh*

*ud dēwān harw [az-išān]{.underline} ǰudāgīh dōš*

"and Ohrmazd said to Zardušt: Praise the gods and seek their company!

And, (as for) all the *dēw*s*,* choose separation [from
them]{.underline}!" (*Dk*.9.24.13)

Note the use of *az-išān* to indicate some of an indefinite group:

*pōryōtkēš ī az-išān*

"a teacher of old from (among) them" = "one of the teachers of old"
(*Dk*.3.294.4)

***[pad-]{.underline}*:**

*zamīg ka suft Gannāg Mēnōy [pad-iš]{.underline} dwārist*

"when the earth was pierced, the Evil Spirit rushed [through/into
it]{.underline}" (after *Bd*.4.28)

#### *az*, *ō*, and *pad* with enclitics [not]{.underline} governed by the preposition

Other enclitic pronouns when not governed by the preposition, can also
be attached to it. In these cases, the prepositions are usually spelled
with arameograms, e.g.:

*az awēšān gyāg* \> *az-išān gyāg* \<MN-š'n\' \... \> "from their place"

*ō man xānag* *\> ō-m xānag* \<OL-m \... \> "to my house"

*ān ī abyōxt ō-[m]{.underline}* \<OLm\> *dānišn ud mānd
pad-[im]{.underline}* \<PWNm\> *ayādīh*

"that which was attached to [my]{.underline} knowledge and remained in
[my]{.underline} memory" (*DD*.36.48)

*ka mānd estād [ō-š]{.underline}* \<OLš\> *zāyišn 3 rōz*

"when there remained 3 days [to his]{.underline} birth" (*Dk*.7.2.56)

*ud paydāgīhist wazurg abdīh [ō-šān]{.underline}* \<OLš'n\'\> *harw dō*

"and a great wonder was manifested [to]{.underline} the two [of
them]{.underline}" (*Dk*.7.2.48)

*[ō-mān]{.underline}* \<OLm'n\'\> *harw dō'ān sūd abgārīhēd az-iš*

"[to]{.underline} both [of us]{.underline} profit will accrue from it"
(after *Bd*.1.20)

*nām ī Zarduxšt xwānīhist abar zamīg [pēš az-iš]{.underline}* \<MNš\>
*hampursagīh pad 30 sāl*

"the name of Z. was sounded over the earth [before his]{.underline}
conversation (with Ohrmazd) at thirty" (*WZ*.49)

*dād estēd [ō-šān]{.underline}* \<OLš'n\'\> *hayārīh az andarrōn tan bōy
ud [pad-iš]{.underline}* \<PWN-š\> *wīr nērōg xwāstār ud ayāftār*

"the conscience (*bōy*) was given [for their]{.underline} aid inside
(*az andarrōn*) the body and [by]{.underline} the power of
[its]{.underline} memory it is the seeker and the obtainer"
(*Dk*.3.60.2)

*āsmān pad ēwēnag ī warr-ēw nihuft dāšt ud 6 amahrspand
[pad-iš]{.underline}* \<PWN-š\> *ham-bašnīh paydāg būd hēnd*

"(he) wore the sky like a piece of clothing, and the six Amahrspands
appeared [in his]{.underline} same height (= as being of the same height
as he)" (*WZ*.22.9)

##  The verb: Shortened Forms of the 3rd person

In addition to the usual forms and endings of the 3rd person singular,
some unusual forms and endings also exist.

Shortened forms of the 3rd singular are relatively common in some texts,
notably in the *Pahlavi* *Videvdad*, e.g.:

º\>LV , ºLV , y\>LB *bard* = *barēd* "carries" \[also tÒWB M51b in
*IndBd*.34\]

GwaD\> , G\>waD\> *dānd* = *dānēd* "knows"

--\>WWK , GWWK , G\>WWK *kund* = *kunēd* (Man. *kwnd*) \[occasionally
WTWWK \<kwnt\'\>\]

º\>pL , G\>pL *rawd* = *rawēd* "goes"

ï\>ÇD\> , Y\>zY\> *dazd* = *dazēd* "burns" (*PV*.5.9)

ï\>¸P *pazd* = *pazēd* 'cooks" (*Nir*.49.17)

ï\>ÇJ *sazd* = *sazēd* "passes" (time; *PV*.5.10, 18.16)

ï\>¸T *tazd* = *tazēd* "runs, flows" (*PV*.13.48i)

º\>LwA , ï\>ÒwA *xward* = *xwarēd* "eats" (*PV*.13.45a)

ï\>ÇD *yazd* = *yazēd* "sacrifices" (*PV*.18.43)

WtDB *bēd* = *bawēd* (common, especially at the end of lines)

WtD\> , WtD *dat* = *dahēd* (common in PV; Man. *dat* and *tad*!)

WthAC *čāšt* = *čāšēd* "teaches" (*PY*.19.12, *AWN*.12.5, *Dk*.3.16.2,
etc.)

WtHwA *hōšt* = *hōšēd* "dries out" (*PV*.16.2N; *Psalter* \<hwšty\>)

WtÒwLP *parward* = *parwarēd* "nurtures, raises (*PV*.14.16,
*IndBd*.14.30)

WthAWT *tuxšt* ? = *tuxšēd* "strives" (*PR*.28c.3 beside *tuxšēd*)

In the manuscripts, *dānd* is sometimes written with the arameogram as
\`\>WWtDwA \<[YD]{.underline}OYTWNd\> or with extra \<w\>\'s as
\`\>WWwaD\> \<d'n\"d\> (making it look like \<YHWWNd\>!). See Exercise
11.1 sentence 10!

The form *bēd* is also used in the 2nd plural imperative.

It is likely that the form \<YHWWNyt\'\> was also commonly read as
*bēd*, as the two forms alternate in the manuscripts.

Similarly, we occasionally find 1st sing. \<bym\> for \<YHWWNm\>
(PV.18.32; K1 end of line), 1st plural *bēm* \<bym\> for \<YHWWNym\> and
3rd plural *band* for \<YHWWNd\> (PV.7.24). The Pahlavi *Psalter* has
1st plural *bam* \<bmy\>.

For *šāyēd* the mss., not infrequently, have \<šyt\'\>, but it is not
clear whether this is a genuine form or a typo.

### Text 11.3

From the *Pahlavi Videvdad*: *PV*.4.1 L4 48v-49r

Go to http://ada.usal.es -- click on Manuscripts view -- pull down the
Work tab to V -- pull down the Book tab to 4 -- pull down the Paragraph
tab to 1 -- Go to + V_P (on the left) -- Click on L4. This will take you
to the first picture. You will find the text one line down from where it
says 4.1 in the right margin. -- When you have read the first page,
click on the \< sign to advance to the next page. -- Click on the images
to enlarge. -- Skip the Avestan text! Do the same for M3.

The Avestan text: "He who to a man who gives him greetings does not bear
the greeting in return/back, he becomes a thief of the greeting, a
violator of the greetings-bearer."

*niyāyišn* here renders Avestan *nəmō* "homage, reverence, greetings,"
cf. Av. *nəmas^ə^ tē* "homage/greetings to you!"

The first part contains the rendering of the Avestan plus glosses; the
second part contains the commentary.

***kē ō mard ī niyāyišnōmand** tis abāyēd dādan ā-š **nē niyāyišn abāz
bard** kū-š ne dahēd*

***duzz ī*** \[L4, M3 *duzzīh*\] ***niyāyišn bawēd** ān ī-š pad ēd
menišn bē stānēd kū abāz ne daham* {M3 + *ēn*}

***u-š apparīh (ī)*** \[L4 \<'p̄l\>, M3 \<QDM\>!\] ***niyāyišn az
barišn** ka xwāhēd gōwēd ay ast-im u-t nē daham*

*ēn az Abestāg paydāg ān bawēd ka gōwēd ay* \[not in M3\] *tis-iz dah,
ud tō-iz ka abāyēd ā-t daham*

*ud pad ēd* \[in L4 correction\] *menišn bē stānēd kū abāz ne daham,*

{M3 repeats: *ud* \<LKWM\> for \<LKc\> *kē ast ā-t daham ud pad ēd*
*menišn bē stānēd kū abāz ne daham*}

*ka kas nē dānd, pad hāsr duzz* \[M3 CwL for CwY\>\]*; ud ka kas dānēd,
pad hāsr apparag*

*ka xwāhēd, gōwēd ay nēst-im, pad gyāg duzz*

*ka gōwēd ay ast-im u-t nē daham, pad gyāg duzz ī duzzīn ud appar*
{*ud*} *apparīn* \[M3: *apparag duzz ī appar ī apparīn*\]

### 

Ms. readings in \[\...\]. Text in {\...}: ignore!

The text is about a man who is greeted by another and the various
reactions to the greeting by the man who receives the greeting. It is
somewhat elliptic, e.g., *ka xwāhēd* "when he wishes \[to receive the
greeting\]."

11.3. Translate into Pahlavi and write in Pahlavi at least sentences 2,
4, 6, 8, 9:

1.  A wise man is like a good field (earth) on which one sows (throws)
    seed and many fragrant plants and tall trees come up from it.

2.  Then Ahrimen rose up from the depth in order to smash Ohrmazd's
    creation, but he was thrown back down into the darkness of Hell.

3.  When the adversary had run in, the sky feared him like a sheep the
    wolf; he came upon the fire in the form of a fly.

4.  If I become the gods' helper, the gods will make me their own, and I
    will not fear (my) enemies, but be confident in the goodness of this
    world and the just judgement in the other world.

5.  The Righteous in paradise are clothed in gold-adorned,
    silver-adorned, jewel-adorned garments, shinier than all (other)
    garments.

6.  He who digs a well for (his) opponents falls into it himself, and he
    will not be able to come out of it, but will die in it from (because
    of) hunger and thirst.

7.  Do you know why the sky is above and the earth is below and the
    atmosphere is in between and whether it is possible go from this
    world to the other?

*kadām-iz-ēw* ÄcÂATK \<kt'mc-HD\> "whichever, any \... at all/soever"

all/soever"

all/soever"

l"

Examples:

own good diligence may not be ruined" (*MX*.1.46-47)

*ēn ruwān ī ōy druwand mard kē-š pad gētīy xwāstag nē az frārōnīh bē az
tis ī [kasān]{.underline} duzdīd*

"this is the soul of that wicked man who (*kē-š*; ergative, Lesson 14),
in this world, did not (acquire) wealth from good behavior, but stole
from (other) [people's]{.underline} stuff" (*AWN*.46.3)

##### *kas*, *tis* negated:

*[nē]{.underline} bōxtēnd az-iš [kas-iz]{.underline} bē kē ruwān bōzēd*

"[nobody]{.underline} will be saved from him (Astwihād) except (*bē*) he
who saves his soul" (*Dk*.9.16.2)

*pas az ān ī ka druz ō dām dwārist bē Zardušt tā az gētīyān [kas-iz
nē]{.underline} dīd haft kišwar*

"since the Druz rushed onto the creation, other than (*bē \... tā*)
Zardušt, [nobody]{.underline} of those in this world has seen the seven
continents" (*PR*.46.9)

*pad [kas-iz kas]{.underline} afsōs ma kunēd*

"do not deride anybody at all" (*PN*.43)

*u-šān [ēk-iz]{.underline} passox [nē]{.underline} kerd*

"and not a single one of them answered" (*Bd*.26.38)

*Akōman handēšīd kū-m [nē tis]{.underline} warzišn kē-š ō man guft
Wahuman*

"Akōman reflected: I must make/do [nothing]{.underline} that Wahuman
told (*-š \... guft* "he said", ergative, Lesson 13) me (to do)"
(*WZ*.8.14)

*yazd ō mardōmān bē nēkīh ēnyā [tis-iz]{.underline} ǰuttarīh
[nē]{.underline} dahēnd*

"the gods give [nothing at all]{.underline} (producing) contrariety to
people, only (*bē \... enyā*) goodness" (*MX*.51.15)

*ruwān ī ahlawān pas az ān ī ka gyān az tan bē šawēd \...
[tis-iz]{.underline} duš-xwārīh [nē]{.underline} bawēd*

"for the soul of the Righteous, after (*pas az ān ī ka*) the breath-soul
leaves the body, there will be [no]{.underline} discomfort [at
all]{.underline}" (*PR*.24.1)

*tis pad [tis-iz tis nē]{.underline} dārēd*

"he does not consider anything as [anything]{.underline} at all,"
approx. "he does not consider anything at all worth worrying about"
(*Ōšnar* 20)

[Double negatives]{.underline} occur occasionally, perhaps as a scribal
error, e.g.:

*[nē kas]{.underline} az mardōmān ahlaw ud garōdmānīg [nē]{.underline}
bawēd kē-š gāhān nē warm kerd* "[no one at all]{.underline} among men
becomes Righteous and Garōdmān-bound who has not performed (*-š \...
kerd* "he has done") the Gathas" (*PR*.17b.1)

##### Note also *ēk-iz \... nē* aÒ \... CKwïÅ \<'ywkc \... LA\> and *ēw (\...) nē* aÒ (\...) Ä \<HD (\...) LA\> "not (a single) one":

*ēg pursīd az awēšān kū amāh kē brēhēnīd hēm, u-šān [ēk-iz]{.underline}
passox [nē]{.underline} kerd*

"then (one) among them (the *amahrspand*s) asked: 'who fashioned
us?'---and [not one]{.underline} of them answered" (*MX*.26.38-39)

*ka-š nasāy [ēk-iz]{.underline} čarbišn gumēxtagīh andar
[nēst]{.underline} ud ka šud [ēw nē]{.underline} paydāg, tanūr
hixrōmand*

"when there is no *nasāy* and [not a single]{.underline} fattiness
mixture in it (*-š \... andar*) and [not one]{.underline} (piece of
skin) has manifestly come loose, the (legal position of) the oven (is)
'contains *hixr*'" (*RAF*.109.2; when one burns a hand on the oven)

*ēč* (*hēč*) cdA \<'yc\> "any (at all)"

*ēč kas* ˙dA cdA \<'yc AYŠ\> "anybody"

*ēč tis(-ēw)* MwYN cdA \<'yc MNDOM\> "anything"

*ēč kē* WN cdA \<'yc MNW\> "whoever"

##### *ēč* non-negated:

*[ēč kē]{.underline} būd hēnd ud [ēč kē]{.underline} bawēnd ud [ēč
kē]{.underline} hēnd*

"whoever have been, whoever will be, and whoever are"

##### *ēč* negated:

*ān ēk rāh gīrēd ī ahlāyīh ud [ma]{.underline} pad frāxīh ud
[ma]{.underline} pad tangīh ud [ma]{.underline} pad ēč rāh az-iš wardēd*

"take that one path, that of Righteousness, and [do not]{.underline}
turn from it in any way, [(n)either]{.underline} in well-being
[(n)or]{.underline} (when) in a tight spot (distress)!" (*AWN*.101.8)

*abar wināh ī hamēmālān bē andar xwad-iz hamēmāl pad [anīy
ēč]{.underline} kerbag [nē]{.underline} tōzīhistan*

"about sins against one's fellow men: it is [not]{.underline} to be
redeemed by [any other]{.underline} good deed except (one done) to that
fellow man himself" (*Dk*.8.17.9)

*yazd [ēč kas]{.underline} pad hammōg ī dēwān [nē]{.underline} hišt*

"God has [not]{.underline} left [anybody]{.underline} to the teaching of
the demons" (*Dk*.5.24.14a)

*pad [ēč]{.underline} rāh ud pad [ēč tis]{.underline} sūdagīh
[nē]{.underline} kerdan*

"one is not to practice neglect in any way and in any matter = in
[no]{.underline} way and in [no matter]{.underline} is one to practice
neglect" (*WD*.89.5)

*Ardaxšīr [ēč tis-ēw]{.underline} [nē]{.underline} paydāgēnīd*

"Ardashir revealed nothing" (*KN*.14.7)

*andar zamānag ī spurr-wehīh [ēč]{.underline} dard bēš pad
[ēč]{.underline} čār ō [ēč]{.underline} dām handāxtan [nē]{.underline}
šāyēd*

"in the time of complete goodness, no pain (and) harm can by any means
be plotted against any creature" (*DD*.36.102; at the end of the world)

*hamāg*, plur. *hamāgān* WkaÂA \<hm'k\'\> "all"

*harw*, plur. *harwīn* AWK \<KRA\> "every, all"

*harw ēk* WKwïÅ AWK \<KRA 'ywk\'\> "each one"

*harw dō* 2 AWK \<KRA 2\> "both"

*harw kas* ˙dA AWK \<KRA AYŠ\> "everybody"

*harw tis* MwYN AWK \<KRA MNDOM\> "everything"

*harw kadār* lATK AWK \<KRA kt'l\> "whichever" (of two)

*harw kē* WN AWK \<KRA MNW\> "whoever"

*harw čē* nM AWK \<KRA ME\> "whatever"

*harw čiyōn* WwSC AWK \<KRA cygwn\> "in whatever way, how(so)ever"

*harwisp*, plur. *harwispīn*, *-ān* WcJwAWK \<KRAwsp\'\> "every, all"

*harukīn*, *harkīn* (rare) WwYklA , wYKwlA \<hlwkyn\'\> "all" (ManMP
*hrwkyn*, *hrwqyn*)

Note the frequent use of plural verbs with *harw*.

*ud ham-kāmagīh ī 7-ān amahrspandān rāy ān čē ēk handēšēd ēg

"Hordad is the *rad* of the years, months, and days, because (*az ēn
kū*) he is the *rad* of [all things]{.underline}" (*Bd*.26.103)

*[harw ēk]{.underline} 100 sāl bē zīst [hēnd]{.underline}*

*Pašang ud Wēsag [harw 2]{.underline} brād būd hēnd*

"Pašang and Wēsag were [both]{.underline} brothers" (*Bd*.35.18)

*[harw kas]{.underline} dōst bāš*

"be a friend to [everybody]{.underline}!" (*DD*.93.6)

*[harw kas]{.underline} az-iš hammōxtār hēnd*

"everybody---they are learners (= learn) from him" (*Bd*.3.3)

*Ahrimen [harw tis]{.underline} pad zyān ī Ohrmazd kunēd*

"Ahrimen does [everything]{.underline} for the harm of Ohrmazd"
(*DD*.93.8)

*petītīgīh hamē ka kunēnd [harw čiyōn]{.underline} kunēnd ud pēš ī [harw
kē]{.underline} kunēnd*

"as long as they perform repentance, [however]{.underline} they do it
and before [whomever]{.underline} they do it \..." (*ŠnŠ*.8.13)

*[harw čē]{.underline}-t kāmag ast xwāh tā-t daham*

"ask [whatever]{.underline} you wish, so that I shall give it to you!"

[harwisp]{.underline} dahišn ī Ohrmazd-dād*

"I shall soil the water, the fire, the plant, and the
[entire]{.underline} creation Ohrmazd set in place" (*Bd*.4.4b)

##### *harw čē* with comparative "the -er \... the -er":

This construction, which is quite common in modern Persian, is rare in
Pahlavi, e.g.:

*asp ud gāw ud mēš ud buz ud abārīg sardag ī gōspandān [harw
čē]{.underline} gušn [meh]{.underline} mādag bar [weh]{.underline}
dahēd*

*zarrēn ud sēmēn ud abārīg ayōxšustīg ǰāmag [harw čē pāktar ud
an-āhōgtar]{.underline} ēg-iš wāng [xwaštar]{.underline}*

"horses, cattle, sheep, goats, and the other kinds of domestic animals,
[the bigger]{.underline} the male, [the better]{.underline} offspring
the female will give;

a bowl of gold, silver, and the other metals, [the purer and more
unsullied]{.underline}, [the more beautiful]{.underline} the sound"
(after *Dk*.6.90)

##### *har(w)kēn* "all"

*kerbag ī az ēn gāhānbār tā ān gāhānbār kunēd ēw-kardag bē bawēd harw ēk
ēk ōh bawēd*
